+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter Seven: The Antares Proposition The transfer vessel *Corvus Meridian* had no windows in the passenger compartment, which Arthur Neegan decided was deliberate. A man who cannot see where he is going cannot argue about the route. He sat in a chair of quilted grey synthetic that smelled faintly of ozone and other men's anxiety, and he watched the only thing there was to watch: a small display screen set into the bulkhead, cycling patiently through system diagnostics in green monospaced text. `REACTOR PRIMARY — NOMINAL` `ATTITUDE JETS 1–8 — NOMINAL` `HULL INTEGRITY — 100.0%` `AZRA CATALYST BED — 0.04 g — WITHIN TOLERANCE` He read that last line three times. Four hundredths of a gram. On Mars, in the leaseholds, that quantity of Azra represented eleven years of a labourer's indenture, and this ship carried it as *tolerance* — a rounding error, a smear of dust in a lead honeycomb, quietly hurrying the decay of some isotope so that the *Corvus Meridian* might shave nine days off a Hohmann transfer. Arthur had spent his adult life calculating overburden ratios and drill-bit fatigue. He understood, in the abstract, the arithmetic of empires. He had never before been *inside* it. They had come for him at 0510, Tharsis time. Six of them, in soft-soled boots, with sidearms holstered and helmets politely tucked beneath their arms — and on the shoulder of each grey coverall, worked in silver thread, the sunburst-and-caduceus of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. *Diplomatic.* Arthur had laughed at that, once, at a union hall on Isidis, when an older man had said that Antares kept its diplomats the way a hunter keeps his dogs: for the sole purpose of finding things and holding them still. The captain of the retinue had been almost gentle. *Mr. Neegan, you are invited.* And when Arthur had asked whether he might decline, the man had considered the question with genuine, courteous interest, as though it were a novel and rather charming philosophical position, and had then said: *We'd very much prefer you didn't make that necessary.* `LIFE SUPPORT — NOMINAL` `GUEST COMPARTMENT — SECURED` *Guest.* Arthur rubbed the ochre dust that would never wash entirely out of his knuckles and waited. --- The room they brought him to did not belong on a ship. It belonged in an old photograph of Earth. Real wood panelling — or a forgery so expensive as to be morally equivalent — and a long table of black glass, and above it a chandelier of concentric brass rings that turned slowly, throwing soft mobile shadows. Gravity here was perhaps two-thirds Martian: a centrifuge ring, then, spun for the comfort of people who mattered. At the far end sat a woman in a plain dark suit with no insignia at all, which told Arthur more than any sunburst could have. She was perhaps sixty, with iron hair cut short and the flat, unhurried eyes of a woman who had signed things that killed people. "Mr. Neegan. Sit. You'll want the tea; it's the last of a batch grown in actual Ceylon soil and it will not be replaced." She poured two cups herself. "My name is Vesper Kaine. I hold no rank you would recognise and no title I could prove. Ask me anything and I'll lie only where I must, and I'll tell you when I'm doing it. That's more courtesy than you'll get from the Consortium." Arthur sat. "Then let's start with the easy one. Am I a prisoner?" "You're an *asset*." She slid the cup toward him. "The distinction is thinner than you'd like but it is real. A prisoner is a cost. An asset is an investment, and investments are protected." She sipped. "Do you know what your survey found, Mr. Neegan? Not the number. The *meaning*." "Nine hundred metres of monazite-analogue host rock with Azra concentration averaging four point one grams per tonne across a strike length I haven't finished tracing." He said it flatly. "The meaning is that I'm rich, or dead." "The meaning," Kaine said, "is that the Sixty-One Years is over." He waited. "There have been sixty-one years of peace between the Terrestrial Compact and the Antares Combine. Not friendship — *stalemate*. Both fleets are built around fission-fusion hybrid drives that require Azra as a decay catalyst. Both sides have enough Azra to threaten and not enough to *win*. Do you understand what that means, structurally? It means every warship either side builds is a hostage. Burn your catalyst to reach the enemy and you arrive unable to leave. The peace is not held by treaty, Mr. Neegan. It is held by *scarcity*." The brass rings turned overhead. Arthur set down his cup very carefully. "And my claim," he said, "is not scarce." "Your claim, if your figures hold, contains more recoverable Azra than the sum of all catalogued deposits in the solar system." Kaine's voice did not change at all, which was somehow worse. "Whoever holds it can build a fleet that does not have to come home. Which means the stalemate ends. Which means someone will use it — not out of malice, but out of *arithmetic*. Because the moment one side believes the other might get there first, waiting becomes the only unforgivable mistake." "So you want to buy it." "No." She almost smiled. "The Consortium will offer to buy it. They'll offer you a figure with nine digits and a villa on Elysium and a seat on a board, and you'll be dead inside the year, because a seller who remembers where the vein runs is a liability and a dead first-generation settler is a paragraph in a safety report. The Compact will offer you *protection*, which means a comfortable room somewhere in the Jovian trojans where you will spend forty years describing rock strata to men who don't tell you their names." "And Antares?" "Antares," said Vesper Kaine, "offers you something none of them will. We offer to make you *necessary*." She turned a slate toward him. Arthur read it. The figure at the top was not money. "That's a lease instrument," he said slowly. "Naming me as sole assayer of record. In perpetuity. Non-transferable, non-delegable—" "Meaning no shovel goes into your ground without your certified survey. Meaning every faction in this system needs your signature, your hands, and your continued heartbeat." She leaned back. "I am not offering you safety, Mr. Neegan. I am offering you *leverage*. It is the only durable form of safety there is." Arthur thought of the diagnostic screen. Four hundredths of a gram, and a whole ship bent around it. "And if I say no?" "Then in eleven hours we dock at Deimos Transfer," Kaine said, "and you will discover how many other people have already arrived to ask you the same question. Some of them will not pour the tea."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Asimovian style and prompt requirements. The author successfully captures the classic sci-fi atmosphere with retrofuturistic elements like monospaced diagnostic displays and technical terminology, while building both intimate character moments and vast political implications - a hallmark of Asimov's approach. The worldbuilding is particularly effective, establishing the political dynamics through concrete details like the Azra catalyst bed readout and the "Sixty-One Years" of peace maintained by scarcity. The author skillfully uses Arthur's engineering background to ground the fantastic elements in believable technical detail. Vesper Kaine emerges as a compelling antagonist/ally figure with her matter-of-fact delivery of existential threats. Her dialogue feels authentic to the genre while avoiding exposition dumps through natural conversation flow. Arthur's responses show appropriate bewilderment and growing comprehension without becoming passive. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with particularly strong descriptive passages like the contrast between Arthur's utilitarian transport experience and the luxurious meeting room. The imagery of brass rings casting shadows and the Ceylon tea detail effectively establish the power dynamics at play. The chapter successfully advances the larger plot while maintaining tension. The offer of becoming "necessary" rather than protected provides a clever twist that feels earned rather than convenient. The political stakes are clearly established without overwhelming the personal story. Some minor weaknesses include occasional slightly overwrought descriptions and a few moments where the dialogue edges toward exposition, though these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The pacing is well-controlled, building from Arthur's confusion to the revelation of the stakes to Kaine's proposal. The ending maintains appropriate tension without false positivity, setting up future conflicts while resolving the immediate scene. The piece demonstrates sophisticated understanding of both genre conventions and character development. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 89.3
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations The safelight makes everything a confession. That's the thing nobody tells you about darkrooms — that red is not a color so much as a permission. Under it, Elliot's face loses all its usual anxious sharpness. His cheekbones go soft, the smudge of eyeliner he's worn since September becomes a bruise-colored suggestion, and the silver rings on his fingers turn to dull garnet as he moves the tongs through the developer. He's humming. He does this. Some tune I don't recognize, three or four notes circling back on themselves, barely more than breath. He doesn't know he's doing it. I've timed my own breathing to it twice tonight without meaning to. "That one's coming up fast," I say, because I have to say something or I'll say something else. "Mm." He tilts the tray. "I overexposed. It's going to be muddy." "It's going to be moody." "Those are different words, Dani." "Barely." He laughs — that quiet exhale through the nose, the one that always sounds slightly surprised at itself. Nineteen. He's nineteen and he laughs like someone apologizing for taking up sound. I'm twenty-five. I have opinions about lens flare and a mouth that gets me in trouble and a reputation, in this program, for being the woman who decides things. I asked out my last three partners. I chose the restaurants, the positions, the ending dates. It's not a personality, it's a load-bearing wall, and I have never once considered what's behind it. But I have been standing in this room three nights a week for a month now, not deciding anything, watching this boy hum. --- "Can I tell you something?" he says. The print is floating. He's not looking at it or me; he's looking at the fixer tray like it owes him money. "Yeah." My voice comes out too quick. I hate that. I try again, slower. "Yeah. Course." "I don't know if I'm a boy." The extractor fan hums. Somewhere down the hall a door bangs. I keep my hands very still on the edge of the counter because I know — I *know* — that if I move too fast right now I will scare something out of this room that isn't coming back. "Okay," I say. "That's not — I'm not saying I'm a girl either. I don't think." He pushes the print with the tongs, aimless. "I don't have the word. Everyone wants the word first. My roommate asked me what my pronouns were and I said 'he' because it was the fastest way to end the conversation and then I felt like I'd — lied? Not lied. Rounded down." *Rounded down.* God. He does this, too — he finds the exact phrase and then looks embarrassed by it. "You don't owe me a word," I say. "You're the first person who's said that." "I'm a very smart woman, Elliot." He looks up. In the red light his eyes are black all the way through. "You are," he says, and it's not flirting, it's so much worse than flirting, it's *sincere*, and I feel it land somewhere under my sternum like a dropped stone. --- Here's what I don't say. I don't say: I have spent my whole adult life attracted to people with edges. Butch women with jaws like architecture. Men so male they seemed load-tested. I liked knowing where the borders were so I could decide, unilaterally, to cross them. And then this. This soft-shouldered kid in a moth-eaten black cardigan and a skirt he insists is "just a long shirt," who knows more about Francesca Woodman than our professor does, who flinches when anyone raises their voice, who is standing four feet from me *unbecoming* in real time, and I want him — them — *him for now, he said he for now* — with something that has no shape I recognize. I don't know what that makes me. I've been a lesbian, then bi, then "whatever, I don't do labels," which was a cool thing to say at twenty-two and now feels like a coat that doesn't fit. If I want this, what have I been? If the borders were the point, and there are no borders, what am I even doing here? I don't say any of it. This is not my hour. My whole life I've taken the wheel and tonight the most loving thing available to me is to sit in the passenger seat with my hands in my lap. It's excruciating. It's kind of holy. --- "Do you want help pulling that?" I ask. "You're about to over-fix." "Oh — shit." He fumbles. I move without thinking, my hand over his on the tongs, and we both go completely still. His hand is cold. Darkroom cold. There's a callus on his index finger from holding pens wrong. "Sorry," I say, and don't move. "It's okay." Barely audible. "Is it?" I turn my head. He's close enough that I can see the little constellation of freckles across his nose that daylight hides. "Because I want to be really clear that I'm — I have a way of running at things. And I don't want to run at you." He swallows. I watch his throat do it. "I think," he says slowly, "I'd like to be run at. Eventually. Just — slowly." "Those are different words, Elliot." That laugh again, closer now, warm on my jaw. "Barely." We stand there with our hands stacked on a pair of tongs in a tray of chemicals, and neither of us kisses the other, and it is the most erotic eleven seconds of my entire life. --- He goes back to humming while the print washes. I lean against the counter and let it happen to me. And I think: maybe I don't need the word either. Maybe I get to be the thing that develops slowly, in the dark, in a bath of something caustic, coming up gradual and strange and not at all what I metered for. The image surfaces. It's muddy. It's gorgeous. "Told you," I say. "You said moody." "I'm always right, that's my whole thing." He hangs it up to dry, and his fingers are shaking, and he's smiling at the wall like nobody's watching. I'm watching. I'll keep watching, as long as he lets me.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated literary craft in exploring gender identity, attraction, and vulnerability through an intimate darkroom setting. The narrative successfully captures Dani's complex internal landscape as she navigates her attraction to Elliot while respecting their gender questioning journey. The writing excels in several key areas. The prose is elegant and controlled, with particularly strong metaphorical language around photography that serves the dual purpose of advancing plot and deepening thematic resonance. Lines like "The safelight makes everything a confession" and "maybe I get to be the thing that develops slowly, in the dark" demonstrate skillful integration of setting and meaning. The voice is consistently authentic to Dani's character - assertive yet introspective, with a natural rhythm that feels genuinely twenty-five and artistically inclined. Character development is nuanced and believable. Dani's internal conflict between her usual take-charge nature and her desire to give Elliot agency feels psychologically authentic. Elliot's vulnerability and tentative self-exploration is handled with sensitivity, avoiding both oversimplification and melodrama. The dialogue feels natural and serves character development effectively, particularly Elliot's "rounded down" comment which perfectly captures the complexity of gender questioning. The emotional complexity is perhaps the piece's greatest strength. Rather than rushing toward resolution, it sits comfortably in uncertainty and gradual revelation. Dani's questioning of her own identity and attraction patterns feels earned rather than forced, emerging organically from her encounter with Elliot's gender exploration. The pacing is well-controlled, building tension through small moments and careful observation rather than dramatic events. The darkroom setting is used expertly to create intimacy and metaphorical depth without feeling heavy-handed. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the metaphorical language borders on being slightly overwrought, though it generally stays within appropriate bounds. The ending, while satisfying, could perhaps have pushed slightly further into the complexity of the situation, though the restraint shown is also a strength. The piece successfully avoids common pitfalls of amateur writing about LGBTQ+ themes, treating the subject matter with appropriate gravity while maintaining literary sophistication. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma ## 8:52 a.m. — Piazza di Trevi The Vespa's front wheel stopped four inches from Ben Whitmore's left knee, and the guidebook went up like a startled pigeon. "*Ma sei cieco?*" The rider flipped up her visor. Dark eyes, a smear of engine grease along one cheekbone. "You stand in the road reading a book about the road you are standing in. This is a kind of poetry, no?" "I'm so sorry — *mi dispiace* — *scusi* — I was checking the, ah, the *aqua virgo*, the aqueduct, it's actually still feeding the fountain, which is remarkable when you consider—" "You are British." "Is it that obvious?" "You apologized four times for almost dying." She killed the engine and swung a leg over, all leather and impatience, and picked up his guidebook from the cobbles. She did not hand it back. "Nineteen ninety-eight edition. *Dio.* Half these restaurants are dead." "It was my father's." She paused, half a beat, then flipped to a dog-eared page. "And this? He circled a gelateria in Trastevere?" "He promised to take me. Never got round to it." Ben cleared his throat. "Might I have my—" "Later." She tucked it inside her jacket. "You are going nowhere important." "I have a reading room booking at the Vatican Library at eleven." "You have," said Alessandra, "a very sad life." ## 9:40 a.m. — Via del Governo Vecchio She rode like grammar was optional. Ben clung to the seat rail, dignity flapping behind him, and discovered that terror at forty kilometres an hour felt shockingly close to joy. "You have deliveries," he shouted. "Actual work." "I deliver in the order that pleases me." She slalomed around a nun. "Today you are cargo." At the second stop — a notary's office with a brass plaque — she came out with an envelope signed and a heavy crystal paperweight that Ben was quite certain had been on the reception desk when they went in. It disappeared into her jacket beside his father's guidebook. "Alessandra." "Yes, Benedetto." "That's not my—" "It is now." ## 11:15 a.m. — A rooftop above Campo de' Fiori There had been a service door. There had been a stairwell with a chain across it that she stepped over like a woman stepping over a puddle. Now there was all of Rome, rust and ochre and antenna-forests, and Ben's heart going like a moth in a jar. "This is trespassing." "This is *access*." She sat on the parapet with her boots dangling eight storeys above a fruit market. "Sit. Look. You came two thousand kilometres to read about Rome in a room with no windows." He sat. Not on the parapet. Near it. "Why me?" he said. "You could have shouted at me and driven off. That would have been the efficient version of this morning." Alessandra considered the skyline. "You looked like a man who has never once done what he wanted." "That's rather cruel." "It is, yes." She smiled without apology. "Was it wrong?" Ben found he had nothing to say, which she seemed to enjoy enormously. ## 1:30 p.m. — Trattoria, no name, no menu She ordered for both of them in Roman so fast it sounded like an argument, and possibly was. The artichokes came burnt and perfect. Ben, three glasses in, was explaining medieval water law with his hands. "Say it in Italian," she said. "*L'acqua... è... molto... antica.*" "You sound like a hostage." "I sound like a man who got a B in his GCSE." "*Sei un disastro.*" She leaned across the table and wiped oil from his chin with her thumb, casual as weather, and left him unable to remember what an aqueduct was. Then she leaned back, watching the colour climb his neck, delighted. That was the thing he was beginning to understand about her: she pushed to see what moved. The bill came. She paid it. The waiter's little brass bell from the bar did not survive the afternoon. ## 3:05 p.m. — Ponte Sisto "*Alessandra Fioravanti.*" The man was fifty-ish, linen shirt, expensive watch, a gallery owner's tan. His smile arrived a second late. "Marco." She said it the way you'd name a weather event. "Still on the bike." He looked at Ben with frank curiosity. "And you are?" "Ben. Ben Whitmore. I'm — I nearly ran into her. Or she nearly—" "Ah." Marco laughed, one syllable, not kind. "Listen to me, *inglese*. She is the best day you will have in this city. Then you go home and you notice things are gone. My cufflinks. A drawing my mother gave me. She takes little pieces, *capisci?* Not for money. For the — how do I say — for the sport." "Marco," said Alessandra pleasantly, "your fly is open." It wasn't. He checked anyway. By the time he looked up, she had Ben by the wrist and they were twenty metres gone. They walked in silence to the middle of the bridge. The Tiber slid greenly below. "Is it true?" Ben asked. "Which part?" "Any of it." She stopped. For the first time all day she looked at him without the mischief, and it was worse, somehow — direct, and tired. "I take small things from people who have too many things. I do not know why I do it. I have theories. None of them are interesting." A shrug. "You should get your book back before dark." "I'd rather," Ben said, surprising himself, "you kept it a while longer." Her mouth twitched. "*Attento.* That is almost dangerous, what you just did." ## 7:50 p.m. — Trastevere, the circled gelateria It still existed. Ben ate pistachio on a doorstep beside her while swifts screamed overhead, and thought about his reading room, unbooked now, and did not care. "I fly back Sunday," he said. "Then you have four days." Alessandra stood, pulled the guidebook from her jacket, and pressed it into his hands. Something was tucked into the Trastevere page: a paper napkin, a phone number, a small brass bell drawn in biro. "You stole a bell for me." "I stole nothing." She was already walking to the Vespa. "I liberated a bell. Come, Benedetto. There is a rooftop I have not shown you, and the gate is locked." Ben Whitmore, thirty-four, Cambridge, cardigan, looked at the sky going violet over the Janiculum, and got on the bike.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative flair in crafting a contemporary romance set in Rome. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge clearly through dialogue and action rather than exposition. Alessandra's mischievous energy and Ben's reserved academic nature are well-contrasted, and their chemistry develops believably over the course of the day. The structure works effectively, using timestamped vignettes that create momentum while allowing for character development. The dialogue feels natural and reveals personality - Alessandra's directness ("You have a very sad life") and Ben's flustered politeness come through authentically. The author handles the cultural clash well, avoiding stereotypes while highlighting genuine differences. The prose is generally elegant and economical, with strong imagery ("terror at forty kilometres an hour felt shockingly close to joy") and vivid scene-setting. The kleptomania subplot is woven in subtly as requested, manifesting through small actions rather than explicit revelation. The pacing builds nicely from the initial collision to increasingly intimate moments. However, there are some weaknesses. The transformation of Ben from cautious academic to willing rule-breaker happens quite rapidly, though the author does provide some justification through Alessandra's perceptive comment about him never doing what he wants. The Marco encounter, while serving to reveal Alessandra's past, feels slightly forced as exposition. Some moments border on being overly cute or convenient. The ending strikes an appropriate note - not overly resolved but suggesting possibility. The brass bell callback is a nice touch that ties the narrative together. Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Outpost's grav plating hums a half-step flat on Thursdays. Nobody but me notices, and I've stopped mentioning it, because the last time I did, Grubb spent four hours under the floor and came up with a wrench, a dead moth, and no explanation. So it's humming, and Yorrel and his brother are arguing about ore futures in the corner booth like they've argued for eleven years, and the Marrow twins are asleep sitting up, holding hands. Cozy. My kind of slow. Then the door sighs open and she comes in — a Vesh, tall, coat still crackling with dock static, her tentacled dreads pushed back off her face in a way that says she's been pushing them back off her face for six or seven hours straight. She doesn't scan the room like a runner. She sits down like a woman lowering something heavy she can't put down. "Vega whisky, neat," she says. "Better make that a double." "Vega's got a bite to it." "I know what Vega's got." I pour. She drinks a third of it without breathing, and I start wiping the spot in front of her — a little scarred crescent in the resin where somebody, decades before me, put out a cigarette. "Long haul?" I ask. "Nine jumps in four days." "That's not a haul, that's a crime against your spine." "My spine and I have an understanding." She sets the glass down. I wipe next to it. "You're the bartender." "Nettle. Nets, if you're staying." "Am I staying?" "You bought a double. That's a deposit." Something in her face loosens by a millimeter. "Ivane." "Ivane. First time at the Outpost?" "First time in the belt." She turns the glass a quarter-turn. "It's smaller than I expected. The station." "Everybody says that. Then they come back in a year and say it's bigger." I go over the spot again. The rag squeaks. "So what's nine jumps in four days chasing?" "Not chasing." She looks at me for the first time, properly, and her pupils are doing that Vesh thing where they widen in slow pulses, like something breathing underwater. "Being chased is different from chasing." "It is." I keep my hands moving. Rag, crescent, circle. "You want me to ask, or you want me to not ask?" "I want the second one, and I'll take the first." "That's most people." I refill her without being asked — half, not a double, because I'm not a monster. "Debt?" "Not money." "Family?" "Not exactly." "Law?" She laughs, one syllable, entirely mirthless. "Which law?" "Ah." I stop wiping for one second, then start again. "That's a specific kind of answer, Ivane." "Is it." "People who ask 'which law' have usually met more than one." Behind me, Yorrel bangs the table and shouts something about tonnage. The Marrow twins don't stir. Ivane lowers her voice under the noise, which tells me she knows how a bar works, which tells me she's been in a lot of them, which tells me more than her coat does. "I need to know something," she says. "Before I say anything else." "Go." "Does the Outpost have a syndic?" The rag stops. I make it start again. "We have a station chief. Habrit. He's asleep by twenty-two hundred and he thinks the word 'jurisdiction' is a kind of pastry." "That's not what I asked." "No," I say. "It isn't." "So?" "So the answer's complicated, and the answer costs more than a double." "I'll buy the bottle." "You couldn't afford it and I wouldn't sell it." I lean my hip on the cooler. "Look. We're four thousand souls in a rock with a bar and a chapel and one very opinionated hydroponics collective. Nobody comes here to be found. That means everybody here has a reason not to look too hard at anybody else. That's not lawlessness, it's — etiquette." "Etiquette." She says it the way you'd say a diagnosis. "It works. Ninety-nine nights out of a hundred, it works beautifully. You want to know who to be afraid of on this station? Nobody. You want to know who to be careful with? Everybody." "And you?" "I'm the one who hears things. That's worse or better depending on the night." Wipe. Wipe. "Which brings us back around. Nine jumps. Four days. Not money, not family, not law-singular." Ivane looks down into the whisky, and her dreads shift, restless, one curling briefly around her own wrist like it's comforting her. "There's a name," she says. "I'm going to say it, and I need you to not react." "I don't react. I wipe." "Sorrel Vane." I wipe. I wipe the crescent, and the resin around the crescent, and a perfectly clean patch two centimeters left of the crescent, and my hand keeps going in the same small circle while the grav plating hums its flat Thursday note and Yorrel shouts about tonnage and my whole ribcage turns into an airlock cycling. "Huh," I say. "You didn't react." "I said I wouldn't." "You went the wrong color." "That's the lighting. It's very unflattering, we've complained." I set the rag down. Then I pick it back up, because my hands need somewhere to be. "Where'd you hear that name?" "From a man on Cerc Station who said it was worth a lot of money to certain people. Then from a woman on Hemlin who said it was worth a lot of blood. Then from a manifest." She takes a slow drink. "The manifest is why I'm here." "Manifests are wrong all the time." "This one was signed." "Signatures are wrong all the time too." "Nets." She says my name gently, and that's the part that scares me. "I'm not here to collect anybody. I'm here because in eleven days a ship called the *Fair Recompense* docks at this station, and there are people aboard it who have been looking for Sorrel Vane for six years, and I would very much like to be somewhere else by then." She sets the glass down, empty. "But I thought somebody here ought to know. Etiquette." The plating hums. Somewhere down the corridor, the chapel bell rings the hour, off-key, like everything else I love. "Another double?" I ask. "Please," says Ivane. I pour two.

+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gone South The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder. That's the thing I'm thinking about at 6:40 in the morning on Canal Street, which is maybe insane, considering. Considering I have forty-one dollars. Considering my phone is at nine percent and I turned off location services in a gas station bathroom outside Meridian like some kind of fugitive, which I guess I technically am, or would be if Mom called anybody, which — she might not. That's the part that keeps circling back like a fly at a picnic. She might not. But mostly it's the strap. It slips off every eight steps or so and the bag swings down and clonks against my hip bone and I have to do this shrug-hitch move, and each time I do it I want to scream. I bought this backpack at Walmart in eighth grade. It has a small hole in the bottom corner where a mechanical pencil poked through. It is, currently, the only object in the world that belongs to me. New Orleans smells like a dumpster that someone poured a daiquiri into and then set out in the sun. I love it immediately, which I don't trust. I don't trust anything I feel right now. Two days ago I sat on the arm of the good couch — the one nobody sits on — and said the sentence I had rehearsed for eleven months, and Dad made a sound like a truck downshifting, and Mom said *this is a phase, this is that internet*, and then a lot of other things, and now here I am watching a man in a tuxedo shirt hose vomit off a sidewalk and thinking: at least this is honest. At least nobody here is pretending to be nice to me. I walk until my heels blister. That's a strategy. Then I sit on the edge of a fountain in a little square with a church and hundreds of birds and a fortune teller setting up a card table, and I eat a granola bar from my hoodie pocket, and I make myself do math. Forty-one dollars. Hostels are like thirty. There's no way I'm getting into a hostel at sixteen. The math does not go anywhere good, so I stop doing the math. "You're gonna get sunburned like that." There's a girl sitting on the other side of the fountain lip. She was not there ten seconds ago, I swear to God. Little, with a shaved-and-growing-out head, dyed some color that used to be green. Big canvas bag. Nose ring. Boots duct-taped at the toe. "I'm fine," I say. "You are extremely not fine. You are Wonder-Bread white and it's June." She scoots along the stone until she's maybe four feet away. Up close she's older than I thought. Nineteen? Twenty? Her eyeliner is yesterday's. "You got in last night." "How do you know that." "Because you're sitting in the sun in Jackson Square with your bag on your lap like a purse and you keep looking at your phone like it's gonna tell you something." She grins. Her front tooth is chipped, a neat little diagonal. "Also you smell like a truck." "I got a ride." "Yeah, everybody got a ride." She holds out a hand. "Wren." "Taylor." "Taylor." She says it back exactly how I said it, no eyebrow, no pause, no *huh*, and something in my chest lets go so fast it's almost painful, like when your foot wakes up. That's it. That's all it takes. Somebody says your name back flat and normal and you'd follow them into traffic. *Don't*, I think. *You don't know her. This is exactly how it happens. This is the after-school special.* "Come on," Wren says, standing. "I know a place does free coffee till nine if you look pathetic, and honey, you're not gonna have to act." --- The place is a folding table outside a church on Rampart. A guy named Deacon Ray — not a deacon, Wren says, that's just his name — hands me coffee in a styrofoam cup and a banana and doesn't ask me one single question, which I appreciate so much I almost cry into the banana. Wren talks the entire time. She talks the way water goes downhill. She's from Ohio, or she's from Florida, or her grandmother's from Ohio; the story changes twice in fifteen minutes and I notice and I decide not to notice. She's been here nine months. She knows which parking garage stairwell is safe and which one absolutely is not. She knows a girl who'll cut your hair for five bucks. She knows the two shelters that take under-eighteens and she says the names of them fast and low, like a warning and a gift at the same time. "You got people looking for you?" she asks. "I don't know." "That's the worst answer." "I know." She nods slowly, like I passed something. "Rule one," she says. "Don't tell anybody your last name. Rule two, don't tell anybody your last name. Rule three, if a dude offers you a couch, there's no couch." "Is that from experience?" Her face does a thing — a shutter coming down and going back up so fast you'd miss it if you weren't a person who'd spent sixteen years reading a room for weather. "I'm a wealth of experience," she says brightly, and stands up, and hitches my strap back onto my shoulder for me without asking, and it stays. --- We spend the day walking. That's what you do here, apparently: you walk, you sit, you get moved along, you walk. Around three we're on the river steps and the brown water is going by fat and slow and a tugboat sounds its horn and I think, without deciding to: *nobody in the entire world knows where I am.* It's terror. It's the purest terror I've ever felt. And underneath it, way down, something with its face turned up to the sun. "Hey," Wren says. "Don't do that." "Do what?" "That face. You're about to call somebody." "I'm not." "You are. Everybody does, day one." She's looking at the river, not me. "Wait till day four. If you still want to on day four, do it, I'll even find you a charger. But not day one. Day one you're not you yet." I don't ask who I'll be on day four. The strap slips off my shoulder again. This time I let it hang.

Wren is skillfully crafted as both helper and potential threat, with her shifting backstory and practiced street wisdom creating appropriate ambiguity. The prose style is confident and distinctive. Metaphors like "talks the way water goes downhill" and "something with its face turned up to the sun" are fresh without being overwrought. The recurring motif of the slipping backpack strap serves as both realistic detail and metaphor for Taylor's precarious situation. Dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, advancing plot, and building tension. Wren's speech patterns and the way she handles Taylor's name create immediate characterization. The conversation flows organically while conveying crucial information about street survival. The emotional complexity is well-handled. Taylor's conflicted feelings about their family, their simultaneous terror and liberation, and their desperate need for connection despite knowing the dangers all ring true. The piece avoids both excessive darkness and unearned optimism. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The morning arrived the way mornings did now: without ceremony, without a forecast, and without anybody to blame. Midas lay on his mattress — a stack of ruined encyclopaedias with a duvet over it, which meant he slept on top of all human knowledge and dreamed of sandwiches — and stared at the ceiling of the Nook. The Nook had once been a self-storage unit. It still bore the cheerful painted slogan YOUR STUFF, SAFE AND SOUND!, which had aged into a threat. "We're out of water," he said. "*Because you deserve it,*" said Chewy. Chewy sat on the shelf where Midas had put him, because Chewy could not put himself anywhere. He was a koala, or had been designed by someone who had heard a koala described over a bad telephone line. Grey plush, worn to canvas at the elbows. One glass eye, one button. Inside him, somewhere beneath the stuffing, a small stubborn cell continued to hold a charge the way a grudge holds a family together, and every so often it moved his jaw and let out something from the Before. "I don't deserve it," said Midas. "That's the thing about deserving. It stopped being load-bearing." "*Ask your doctor if it's right for you.*" "There's no doctors, Chewy." "*Now with real fruit.*" Midas swung his legs off the encyclopaedias and looked at the map. The map was drawn on the back of a laminated fire-evacuation notice, which had been a joke he'd stopped finding funny around year three. On it, in charcoal, was the Nook, the dry creek, the field of feral rhubarb, and a rectangle labelled **AQUATIC LEISURE CENTRE (PROBABLY WET)**. "Right," he said. "Here's the plan. It's a swimming pool. Swimming pools are basically enormous water containers that people used to *sit in*. Nobody's touched it because nobody thinks of it as water, they think of it as *leisure*. We go, we filter, we boil, we live another fortnight. Three hours there, three back, home before the dogs get organised." Chewy said nothing. Midas found this more unsettling than the slogans. "Say something reassuring." "*Terms and conditions apply.*" --- It took four hours to get there, because the road had opinions now. Midas walked with Chewy strapped to his chest in a baby carrier, facing outward, on the grounds that two pairs of eyes were better than one even if one pair was a button. Chewy's function, as far as Midas had ever determined, was to occasionally speak, thereby reminding Midas that language existed and was not a symptom. The Aquatic Leisure Centre had lost its roof but kept its dignity. Faded lane markers. A high-dive board pointing at the sky like an accusation. And in the deep end: water. Green, thick, spectacular water. Water you could have hidden a submarine in and not noticed until it surfaced. "That," said Midas, "is beautiful." "*Dive into flavour.*" "Don't." He got out the bucket, the rope, the four collapsible jerrycans, and the coffee filter he had been washing and reusing for eleven months and had come to regard as a colleague. He knelt on the tiles. He lowered the bucket. The bucket came up full, which was good, and containing a fish, which was interesting, and then the tiles came up too, which was neither. There is a specific silence that occurs in the half-second after ceramic tile decides it is no longer in a professional relationship with concrete. Midas experienced this silence, then the pool, then a great deal of the pool. He surfaced in a bloom of algae, and the first thing he thought was not *I am drowning* but *the jerrycans*, and the second thing he thought was *Chewy*, because Chewy was strapped to him and Chewy was going down like a small grey anchor of sentimental value. He got them both to the shallow end by a method he later described as "arguing with the water until it agreed." Then he lay on the sloping floor with a bear on his chest, coughing up something that had been an ecosystem. "*Refreshingly different,*" said Chewy, waterlogged, an octave lower. "I hate you," said Midas, with feeling, "and if you power down I will grieve for a week." The jerrycans had all floated, which was the single competent act of the day. He filled them. He lashed them to the frame he'd made out of a shopping trolley and a child's bicycle. He looked at the sun, which was doing that low orange thing it did when it wanted you to worry, and he began to walk home with ninety kilos of murky future behind him. The dogs found him at the rhubarb. They were not, in fairness, malicious. They were simply a committee that had reached consensus. Midas counted six and stopped counting, because after six the number stops being information and becomes weather. What he did next he would tell differently on different nights. What actually happened was that he pushed the trolley over, seized a jerrycan, and ran, and the dogs — being dogs — pursued the interesting rolling thing rather than the boring shouting thing, and Midas went the long way round through the collapsed footbridge, and lost a shoe, and gained a shin, in the sense that his shin became something he was now aware of at all times. Somewhere in there Chewy shouted "*UNBEATABLE PRICES! EVERYTHING MUST GO!*" directly into a labrador's face, and the labrador, confronted for the first time in its life with advertising, sat down. --- He came home in stages. He came home as a limp, and then as a crawl, and then, over the last two hundred metres, as a man dragging one jerrycan and holding a koala by the ear, saying things to it that he would not have said to a person. Twenty litres. Ninety went out, twenty came back. A shoe gone, a filter gone, a shin ruined, dignity long since written off as an operating cost. He set the jerrycan down inside the Nook. He propped Chewy on the shelf, dripping, staining the wall a hopeful green. "Twenty litres," Midas said. "Twelve days. That's not nothing." Chewy's jaw worked. Water ran out of him. "*Worth every penny.*" Midas looked at the ceiling. YOUR STUFF, SAFE AND SOUND. "Yeah," he said. "All right. Yeah." And he slept on top of all human knowledge, and dreamed, once again, of sandwiches.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, philosophical observations wrapped in humor, and the ability to find profound meaning in mundane situations. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic world that feels both bleak and oddly cozy, much like Pratchett's approach to existential themes. The characterization is particularly effective. Midas emerges as a believable survivor - competent enough to have lasted this long, but prone to the kind of mishaps that make for engaging storytelling. His relationship with Chewy is well-developed, creating genuine emotional investment despite (or perhaps because of) the koala's limited functionality. The dialogue between them, while one-sided in terms of intentional communication, creates a compelling dynamic. The prose style successfully mimics Pratchett's voice with clever observations like "mornings arrived without ceremony, without a forecast, and without anybody to blame" and "he slept on top of all human knowledge and dreamed of sandwiches." The author demonstrates skill in balancing humor with genuine pathos, particularly in moments where Midas's isolation becomes apparent. The plot structure adheres well to the prompt's requirements, moving from planning through execution to failure and return. The mission's failure feels organic rather than forced, arising naturally from the degraded infrastructure and changed world dynamics. The encounter with the dogs is particularly well-handled, avoiding both excessive drama and unrealistic resolution. However, some elements feel slightly underdeveloped. The world-building, while atmospheric, could benefit from more specific details about the collapse. Certain comedic beats, while in the right spirit, occasionally feel like they're trying too hard to achieve Pratchett's effortless wit. The ending, while appropriate, doesn't quite achieve the perfect balance of hope and resignation that characterizes Pratchett's best work. The technical execution is generally strong, with good pacing and natural sentence flow. The imagery is vivid without being overwrought, and the author shows restraint in not over-explaining the world or characters' motivations. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door didn't so much ring as panic. "Shut it—sorry—shutting it—" A man's back pressed against the glass, arms spread like he was holding off a flood. Outside, the rain fell on Stryd y Bont in a fine grey mizzle and, some distance off, someone shouted a name. Nerys Pritchard did not look up from the ledger. "You're dripping on the mat." "That's what mats are for, historically." "That mat's from my mother. Wipe your feet." He wiped his feet. Then he turned, and she saw the face — the one from the side of the bus shelter in Aberystwyth, forty feet of jawline advertising a spy franchise — and she thought, *oh, for God's sake*, and wrote *3 x Mabinogion (schools)* in the column marked ORDERS. "Is there a back door?" he asked. "There's a back door." "Brilliant. Where?" "At the back." A pause. He laughed — a real one, surprised out of him, too loud for the shop. "Right. Yes. Fair." He pushed wet dark hair off his forehead and gave her the smile. She had seen it in a cinema in Carmarthen and had thought, at the time, that it was probably illegal in some countries. Up close it was worse, because it came with a flicker of expectation, like a man putting a coin in a slot machine and waiting for the lights. The lights did not come on. "You don't know who I am," he said, delighted, wrongly. "Cai Morwood," said Nerys. "You were the Welsh one in the submarine film. You said *bore da* to a Russian for some reason." "That was a directorial choice." "It was a bad one." He put a hand to his chest. "I've been shot at by seven men in Kyiv, and it hurt less." "There's a shelf of your autobiography by the window. Signed ones didn't move any faster than the unsigned, if you're wondering." "I wasn't." "You were." He opened his mouth, closed it. Out on the street, two figures in waterproofs jogged past with long lenses held under their coats like poached salmon. Cai flattened himself behind the bay of local history and watched them go with an expression she hadn't seen on the bus shelter: tired, and a bit hunted, and about nine years older. "They've been on me since Cardiff," he said. "There's a — there's a thing. A story. My agent says ride it out somewhere charming and rural." "Congratulations. You've found rural." "You're not going to ask what the story is?" "No." "Everyone asks." "I'm not everyone. I'm at work." She turned a page. "Tea's a pound in the tin. It's builders'. There's no oat milk, there's no wifi password, and if you touch the maps in the drawer without asking, I'll set the dog on you." "You don't have a dog." "I'll get one." He laughed again, and this time he didn't check to see whether she was watching him do it. He wandered. He picked things up: a foxed copy of *Cwm Rhondda* hymnals, a mildewed Ordnance Survey of Snowdonia, a jar of pencils. Then he stopped, and went very still, in the way people go still in a church or a hide. "Is that a Coward?" Nerys looked up properly for the first time. "It's a Coward." "*Birds of the British Isles and Their Eggs*. Volume two. That's —" He had it open, one hand under the spine like it was a baby's head. "God, my grandfather had these. In Machynlleth. He'd have me out at five in the morning with a Thermos of tea so strong it was structural, and we'd sit in a ditch and freeze and he'd whisper Latin at me." "What did he get you on?" "Everything. Pied flycatcher. Redstart. He was mad for a dipper." Cai looked up. "You?" "Choughs," said Nerys, and heard herself say it too fast. "There's a pair on the headland past Cwm Bach. Been there four years. They nest in an old lead adit and they do this thing when the wind comes up off the sea, they just — throw themselves off. Sideways. Fold up and drop, for no reason at all except it's Tuesday." "Showing off." "Yes." She shut the ledger. "I don't hold it against them. Birds can be vain. They've earned it." "And men can't?" "Men have less impressive plumage." He grinned down at the plate — the eggs laid out in rows, hand-tinted, faintly obscene in their perfection. "How far's the headland?" "Forty minutes if you walk it. Longer if you're being photographed." "And you go, do you? Regularly?" "Wednesday afternoons. I shut at one." A beat. "I'm not asking you." "I know." "I'm genuinely not." "I know," he said. "That's very slightly the problem." Nerys put the pencil down. The rain shifted against the window; somewhere upstairs a floorboard settled. She was aware, distantly and with irritation, of the heat in her own face, and she thought: *forty-one years old, Nerys, and blushing in your own shop, in front of a man who has publicly described himself as a rascal in three separate magazines.* "You do that a lot?" she said. "Do what?" "Turn it up. Like a dial." He considered denying it. She watched him consider it. Then he set the Coward down on the counter, very carefully, squared it to the edge, and said, "Yes. Since I was about fourteen. It's exhausting, actually. I don't know how to be in a room where someone hasn't decided I'm marvellous." "Try it. It's free." "It's not, though. It costs a lot." He looked at her. "How much for the book?" "Twenty-two." "It's worth ninety." "Not to me it isn't. It's been on that shelf since 2019, and I want the space." "Liar," said Cai Morwood, softly, and put down two tens and a five, and did not ask for the change, and did not ask for anything else, which was, she thought afterwards, quite the cleverest thing he could have done. At the door he paused. "Cwm Bach. Past the headland." "Wednesdays," said Nerys, to the ledger. "I shut at one."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated craft in multiple areas. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters with authentic voices - Nerys's dry, no-nonsense Welsh pragmatism contrasts beautifully with Cai's practiced charm that gradually reveals genuine vulnerability. The dialogue crackles with wit and subtext, particularly in exchanges like "You don't have a dog" / "I'll get one" and the entire sequence about the Coward bird book. The Welsh setting feels authentic and lived-in, with specific details like "Stryd y Bont," "mizzle," and local references that ground the scene without feeling forced. The author handles the romance trope cleverly - the immune-to-charm dynamic is executed with genuine chemistry rather than mere contrivance. Character development is particularly strong. Cai's admission "I don't know how to be in a room where someone hasn't decided I'm marvellous" feels earned rather than exposition-heavy, emerging naturally from his interactions with Nerys's resistance. Nerys's internal acknowledgment of being "blushing in your own shop" shows her own vulnerability beneath the prickly exterior. The prose style is confident and distinctive, with memorable phrases like "the bell over the door didn't so much ring as panic" and "tea so strong it was structural." The pacing builds tension effectively through small moments - the shared interest in birds becomes a genuine connection point that feels organic rather than manufactured. However, the piece occasionally veers toward being overly clever, particularly in some of Nerys's more cutting responses. The ending, while satisfying, relies somewhat heavily on the "mysterious stranger leaves money and walks away" romance convention. Some descriptions, while vivid, border on precious ("hand-tinted, faintly obscene in their perfection"). The emotional complexity is well-handled - both characters maintain their defenses while revealing genuine attraction and vulnerability. The scene fulfills its function within the larger romance framework while standing alone as an engaging encounter. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave without protest. That was the first wrongness — Aya had expected the groan of swollen oak, the shriek of a hinge that had not seen oil since the old queen's reign. Instead it swung like a butler's arm, inward and gracious, and the underhold breathed out at them: whale-oil smoke, wet stone, the iron tang of the deep cisterns below. The second wrongness was the light. Every lamp in the vault had been lit. Not the guttering half-dark of thieves, but a bright, brazen, accounting-house glare, brass reflectors polished and angled so that the room held no shadow at all — and shadow was where Aya did her work. The third wrongness stood at the far end of the chamber with her gloved hands folded on the head of a cane, in front of the reliquary plinth where the scythan artifact should have been, and was not. "Mind the step," said Ilsabet Vray. "Katra always forgets the step." Katra swore, low and vicious. Simeon said nothing at all, and in the silence his pocket watch went on ticking, absurdly loud, tick, tick, tick, a clockwork heart counting out what remained of the night. They came from the pillars — six of them, then eight, harpoon-men in oilskins with the guild's whale-tail brand burnt into their collars, and the long brass-throated lances that could punch through a bull sperm whale's skull at forty feet. Two of them carried something worse: bell-mouthed censers on chains, already smoking, and Aya knew that smell. Saltpetre, bone-ash, and cold iron filings. Warding smoke. Someone had told them. *Someone told them.* She reached for the immateria anyway — reached the way one reaches for a step in the dark, that instinctive dreadful confidence — and felt her mother's gift meet the smoke and *slide*, like a knife off wet glass. The other side was there. It simply could not hear her. "Arrested," Aya said. Her voice came out steady. She was proud of that, later, when there was a later. "The Crownsmen took you at four this morning. Bettan watched them put the irons on." "Bettan watched me put on a very good performance," Ilsabet said. "And then he ran off and told nine people, which is precisely nine more than I needed. A guild is a body, girl. Now and again a body must be bled to see where the corruption pools." She tilted her head. "You came so *quickly*. Not even a decent interval of mourning." "You were going to hang." "And you were going to inherit." Ilsabet's cane tapped once on the flags. "Take the masks." It was not a fight. Aya had a knife in her boot and a summoner's tongue in her head and neither was worth a farthing against eight harpoons in a lit room. Katra went for it regardless — of course she did — and was put down with the flat of a lance across the shoulders, folded neat as laundry, wheezing on the stones. Simeon simply raised his long thin hands and let them take his arms, and his watch ticked on against the ribs of the man who held him. A fist closed in Aya's collar. A thumb hooked under the lacquered edge of her mask — the beaked plague-doctor thing she'd bought in the Fishmarket for eleven pence, because it was ugly and common and no one would ever look twice at it. It came away with a small wet sound, like a scab. The lamplight was very bright. She had not felt so naked since her mother's scaffold, standing in the crowd, holding her governess's hand and being told not to look. Somebody in the ring of harpoon-men laughed — a short, startled bark, immediately swallowed. "Well," said Ilsabet Vray, and for the first time something moved in her face. "Well, well. Aya *Corvinel*. Old Rannoch's daughter. Which makes you—" she came closer, close enough that Aya could smell the pastilles she chewed for her chest — "the witch's whelp." *There it is.* Aya kept her chin up. It was the only thing she had left to keep up. *Not thief. Not rival. Witch's whelp. Twenty-two years of Latin and lattice-work and the fencing master and the pianoforte, and I am still the thing they hanged my mother for.* "Immateria," Ilsabet said, tasting it. "I knew someone in this house was calling them. Three men dead in the Bittern Street job with their eyes gone soft in their heads. I told myself it was gas. I *wanted* it to be gas." She rapped the cane against the nearest censer, and the smoke coughed. "Men understand brass. They understand oil, and steel, and a debt. They do not understand *you*, and neither do I, and what I cannot understand I put in the sea." "Then you'll be putting four thousand crowns in the sea with me," Aya said. Tick. Tick. Tick. "Go on." "My father is Rannoch Corvinel of Hallowmere. He sits on the Harbour Board, he owns nine bottoms out of the Morska whaling fleet, and he has precisely one living child." Aya's mouth was dry as ash. She spoke through it. "Kill me and you have a corpse and a scandal. Keep me and you have a lever on every excise seal, every berth manifest, every customs man from the Groyne to the Narrows. He'll pay. He'll pay again. He will pay until he dies of it." And there — beneath the words, arriving with the awful slowness of a ship coming out of fog — the rest of it. *He will pay, and then he will know. Everyone will know. The Corvinel girl, masked, in the Morska guild, calling out of the immateria like her mother before her. There is no road back from this room. There is no morning where I take breakfast in the east parlour and complain about the marmalade.* *Mother. Is this how it felt, when they read the charge?* "You'd sell your father," Ilsabet said. "I'd sell my father's *purse*." Aya swallowed. "It's the only part of him I ever had access to." The old woman studied her for a long moment. Behind her, the empty plinth. Somewhere below, water moved. "Irons," Ilsabet said at last. "All three. And keep the smoke on her — thick, mind. If it thins, I'll know, because we'll all be dead." She turned away. "Bring me pen and paper. It seems I'm writing to an aristocrat." Tick, said Simeon's watch. Tick. Tick.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric worldbuilding within the "whalepunk" fantasy setting. The author successfully establishes the Victorian-gothic tone through specific details like whale-oil lamps, brass reflectors, harpoon-men, and the industrial maritime setting. The opening sequence of "wrongnesses" creates effective tension and immediately signals the trap awaiting the protagonists. The dialogue feels authentic to the period and characters, particularly Ilsabet's measured, calculating speech patterns and Aya's desperate but intelligent negotiation attempts. The author handles the power dynamics well, showing Aya's quick thinking even in defeat. The revelation of Aya's identity as "the witch's whelp" carries appropriate weight and connects meaningfully to the broader worldbuilding around magic being feared and outlawed. Character motivations remain consistent throughout - Ilsabet's methodical approach to rooting out threats, Aya's aristocratic background informing her negotiation strategy, and the clear class tensions. The piece effectively shows rather than tells, particularly in revealing character relationships and the magical system through action and dialogue rather than exposition. However, the piece has some weaknesses. While atmospheric, some descriptions veer toward purple prose ("like a knife off wet glass," "arriving with the awful slowness of a ship coming out of fog"). The pacing occasionally slows with overly elaborate metaphors. Katra and Simeon remain somewhat underdeveloped, serving more as plot devices than fully realized characters. The ending, while logical, feels somewhat predictable once the trap is revealed. The emotional complexity is strong, particularly Aya's internal struggle with her inevitable exposure and the parallel to her mother's fate. The author successfully avoids overwrought melodrama while maintaining gothic atmosphere. The technical execution is generally solid with natural sentence flow and engaging prose.
