+ Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 89.5
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**THE COURT OF THE DREAMING, IN SESSION** The gallery was standing room only, which was unfortunate, as roughly a third of those present had no legs. Dream of the Endless sat above it all in a chair carved from one long, uninterrupted scream. He had been listening for eleven minutes. He appeared to have been listening for a century. "Call the petitioner," he said. The bailiff — a thing of teeth and municipal patience — unrolled a scroll and boomed: "**FURST LOAVE.**" "First Love," corrected a small voice. "**THE COURT RECOGNIZES FURST LOAVE.**" He came forward: a plump, pink-cheeked entity in a waistcoat the colour of a peach bruise, clutching a portfolio to his chest. He bowed three times, which was two more than necessary, and one of them nearly toppled him. "My lord. Thank you. I've brought materials." "You have brought a great many materials." "Swatches, mostly." First Love opened the portfolio. Meadow light spilled out across the courtroom floor, warm and slightly buttery. Several nightmares in the third row hissed and put up parasols. "This is the field, my lord. Wildflowers. Cornflower, ox-eye, a little clover for the smell. Eleven months of work. The bees are *individually voiced*." "Come to the injury." "Yes. Yes." He dabbed his forehead with a handkerchief embroidered with two initials inside a heart. "The dream belongs to Maximilian, aged thirteen, of a town whose name I have promised not to say aloud because he is embarrassed by it. The dream ran nine times without incident. The construction is delicate. He lies in the flowers. *She* lies in the flowers. There is conversation of no consequence whatsoever — this is essential — and then, at the crucial moment, they lean in, and—" "And?" "And nothing, my lord. That's the *art*. Nothing happens, and he wakes up feeling like he's been hollowed out and refilled with warm bathwater and he doesn't know why. That is a *formative experience*. He will chase that feeling for fifty years. He will marry badly twice because of it." First Love's chin trembled with professional pride. "It's some of my best work." "And the tenth night." First Love closed the portfolio. "On the tenth night, the respondent moved in." "**CALL,**" said the bailiff, consulting the scroll, "**MOORE-AH. MOAR-HAG. THE MOR—**" It stopped. It tried again. "**MRS. MOORE.**" "Mora," said Mora, from the defendant's box, where she had been all along, filing a nail. "It's not hard. It's two sounds." She was — the court noted, in the way courts note things they will later deny noticing — extremely difficult to look at directly, and impossible to look away from. Something about the arrangement of her. She wore the light badly, on purpose. "You have entered a constructed dreamscape not your own," said Dream. "I have." "You have altered its terms." "Improved them, arguably." "Describe the alteration." Mora shrugged with one shoulder. "The girl gets on top of him. That was already there — that's his, that's not mine, I want that on the record. Adolescent boy, he's the one who put her up there. I just… continue the scene past where *he* stops." She nodded at First Love. "She leans down. Her hair goes long and wet. Her weight comes on all at once, so his ribs learn something new about arithmetic. And then I sit, and I eat, and he lies there wide awake and unable to move a finger, and he cannot decide, for a full three minutes, whether he is having the worst experience of his life." The gallery murmured appreciatively. Somewhere a nightmare said "*that's* craft," and was shushed. "He *screams*," said First Love. "He screams *afterwards*," said Mora. "In the moment he's very quiet. Very attentive. Best-behaved boy I've had in a decade." "You are feeding upon a minor," said Dream. "I'm feeding on *breath*. Breath is breath. And I'd like the court to consider" — she set down the nail file — "that a girl's gotta eat too, you know." There was a pause of the specific quality that occurs when a legal system is being asked to accommodate an appetite. "That is your defence." "That's the whole of it, yeah. I could dress it up. I could talk about ancestral grazing rights, my grandmother had a *lease* on the entire Carpathian basin, we ate chests from the Danube to—" "Do not." "Fine." She folded her arms. "Then it's: a girl's gotta eat." Dream looked at First Love. "You object." "I object *strenuously*, my lord. This is a *first love*. It is supposed to be tender and stupid and end in nothing. It is not supposed to *straddle him and drain his lungs*." First Love's voice cracked upward. "He's started *anticipating* it. Do you understand? Last night he went to bed *early*." Mora examined her nails again. "He is *thirteen*," First Love wailed. "He will be forty before he understands what happened to him. He will have a *type*." "He'll have a *rich inner life*," said Mora. "**ORDER,**" suggested the bailiff, hopefully. Dream of the Endless said nothing for some time. He was, technically, thinking about jurisdiction. He was, in a small and secret chamber behind that, thinking about how tedious it was to be the only adult in a house of nine billion sleepers, and how rarely he was permitted to enjoy himself. "I find," he said at last, "that the dreamscape was made by the petitioner and remains his." First Love clasped his hands. "I find also that the respondent's need is genuine, and that need is older than architecture." Mora inclined her head. "Therefore." Dream let the word settle. "The petitioner retains title. The respondent retains access — on nine nights of ten, she may not enter. On the tenth, she may." "That's — my lord, that's *rewarding* her—" "She will not be told which night." Dream's mouth did something that was almost certainly not a smile. "Nor will you. Nor will the boy." The court went very quiet. "He will lie in the flowers," Dream said, "and he will not know. Every time. Forever. Until he outgrows the dream, which he will do very late." Mora began, slowly, to laugh. "Anticipation," said Dream, rising, "is a shared meal. Learn to share it. Court is adjourned." "**COURT IS A DOOR, JOURNEYED,**" boomed the bailiff. Nobody corrected it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional craft in executing a complex prompt that demanded a delicate balance of dark fantasy, comedy, and courtroom drama. The author successfully creates a vivid Court of the Dreaming that feels authentically Gaiman-esque while maintaining its own distinct voice. The characterizations are particularly strong. Dream's weary irritation comes through perfectly in lines like "He had been listening for eleven minutes. He appeared to have been listening for a century." First Love is endearingly bumbling yet passionate about his craft, while Mora is confidently predatory with just the right amount of casual menace. The dialogue crackles with personality - Mora's dismissive "a girl's gotta eat" and First Love's horrified "He will have a *type*" are pitch-perfect character moments. The comedy works on multiple levels without undermining the darker elements. The bailiff's malapropisms ("FURST LOAVE," "COURT IS A DOOR, JOURNEYED") provide consistent levity, while deeper humor emerges from the absurdity of bureaucratizing dream invasion. The line "Anticipation is a shared meal. Learn to share it" is both funny and genuinely unsettling. The prose is economical yet evocative. Descriptions like "a chair carved from one long, uninterrupted scream" and "wore the light badly, on purpose" create vivid imagery without excess. The author follows the instruction to use descriptives sparingly while still establishing a rich atmosphere. The resolution is particularly clever - Dream's Solomonic judgment that neither party knows which night Mora can enter transforms the boy's experience into perpetual anticipation. This feels both true to Dream's character and creates a genuinely dark twist that serves the story's themes. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the comedy risks overshadowing the darker elements, and some dialogue tags could be more varied. However, these are minimal concerns in an otherwise expertly executed piece that fully delivers on its ambitious prompt. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The moon hangs low and red over the Carpathian foothills, and somewhere beyond the treeline a pack of wolves howls—not in chorus, but in ragged, staggered voices, as though they cannot agree on what they are mourning. Yennefer of Vengerberg does not look up. She kneels in the wet loam of a battlefield three days cold, palms flat against the earth, drawing what she needs from the residue of violence. Two hundred men died here. Their terror still clings to the soil like grease, and terror, properly rendered, is fuel. "You're stealing from the dead." The voice comes from directly behind her. There was no one there. She is certain there was no one there—she warded a forty-pace circle before she began, and nothing crossed it. She does not startle. She finishes the sigil, stands, and turns with the unhurried patience of a woman brushing dirt from her skirts. He is tall. Absurdly tall, and dressed absurdly too: a red coat the color of arterial spray, a wide-brimmed hat, small round spectacles tinted orange, behind which something moves that is not quite an eye. He smiles, and the smile has too many teeth arranged in too many rows. "They aren't using it," she says. "No." He tilts his head. "They aren't." The wolves howl again, closer, out of rhythm. He does not glance toward them. Neither does she. It has become, in the space of four seconds, a contest. "You walked through my wards," Yennefer says. "I walked around them. Your circle is beautiful. Very precise. It excludes the living, the dead, and everything in between." The teeth widen. "I am not in between. I am *outside*, madam. There's a difference, and it's the entire architecture of my existence." "How philosophical for a corpse." "How impertinent for a meal." She laughs. It's not performance—she is genuinely delighted, and that seems to interest him more than any scream could. "You've misidentified me. It happens. Provincial creature." "You smell of lilac," Alucard says, "and gooseberries, and about four hundred grams of iron, and a lie you told yourself so long ago you've forgotten it was a lie." He breathes in, slow, theatrical. "The body you're wearing isn't the one you were born with." The night goes very quiet. Even the wolves pause. Yennefer's face does not change. But the air around her cools by five degrees, and frost climbs the dead grass in a widening ring. "Careful," she says. "Ah." He sounds almost tender. "There it is." "There's what?" "The weakness. Everyone has one. Yours is that you built a masterpiece and you still hate the foundation." He steps forward, into the frost, and his boots leave no prints. "I've eaten kings, sorceress. I've eaten men who thought they were gods. Do you know what they all tasted of, at the last? Regret. Every single one. Sour as vinegar." "And what do you taste of?" That stops him. Only for an instant—but she sees it, and she files it away like a coin under a floorboard. "You'd have to bite me to find out," he says. "I'd rather not. I've no idea where you've been." Alucard laughs, and it is an awful sound, low and layered, as though several throats are producing it at slightly different times. The wolves answer him. He raises a gloved hand toward the moon in something like a salute. "Let me see it," he says. "The magic. Not the parlor trick with the frost. The real thing." "Why?" "Because I'm bored, and boredom in a thing like me is a public health concern." She considers. She is centuries old and she knows exactly what he is doing—he is establishing terms, converting her power into a performance she gives at his request. It is what she would do. So she gives him nothing. She simply turns and begins walking east, toward the road. He is in front of her before her second step lands. "Rude," he says. "You're standing in my way." "I'm standing everywhere. It's a talent." His form fractures at the edges; shadow pours from beneath the red coat, and for a moment the field is full of eyes, hundreds of them, blinking out of the darkness at various heights, and the howling of the wolves becomes the howling of something with far more mouths. "Beg." "No." "Beg, and I'll make it interesting." Yennefer sighs the sigh of a woman dealing with a drunk at a diplomatic function—and opens her hand. The sigil she drew in the loam ignites. Not with fire. With *absence*: a column of screaming null that punches upward through the shadow-mass, and every eye in it goes out at once, like candles in a wind. The pressure drops. Something enormous makes a sound of genuine surprise. When the light dies, Alucard is on one knee in the mud, his hat gone, half his face missing, and he is *laughing*—the laugh of a man who has just been handed a gift he did not expect. The flesh crawls back over the bone. Muscle knits. The eye reassembles itself last, and it is looking at her with an expression she has seen exactly twice before in her long life, both times on men who were about to become extremely inconvenient. "Again," he breathes. "No." She retrieves his hat from the mud, considers it, and drops it. "You'd only enjoy it, and I don't reward beggars either." He rises. Nine feet of him, then seven, then six-and-a-half, folding himself back into the shape of a man because the shape of a man is more frightening when you know it's a choice. "The bird of Hermes is my name," he says softly, "eating my wings to make me tame." "How lovely. Does it rhyme in the original?" "You could stay." He is not smiling now. "There's very little in this world that can wound me, and less that can bore me, and you have managed the first and refused the second in under ten minutes." Yennefer walks past him. This time he lets her. "I'm not sweet," she says over her shoulder, "and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving, and I'm certainly not a diversion for something that can't die properly. Find your own way to end, monster." "I intend to." His voice follows her down the road, unhurried, patient as geology. "Sleep well, sorceress. I'll be dreaming of your foundations." The wolves howl, out of time, out of tune, and the red moon watches them both go.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated craft in multiple areas. The author successfully captures both characters' essential natures while creating a compelling dynamic between them. Alucard's predatory arrogance and philosophical menace come through clearly, as does Yennefer's calculated coldness and refusal to be intimidated. The dialogue crackles with tension and wit, particularly exchanges like "How philosophical for a corpse" / "How impertinent for a meal." The atmospheric opening with the discordant wolf howls and blood moon establishes an appropriately gothic tone that sustains throughout. The prose strikes an effective balance between literary sophistication and accessibility, with memorable phrases like "boredom in a thing like me is a public health concern" and "patient as geology." The power dynamic shifts convincingly as requested - Alucard initially seems dominant, Yennefer refuses to play his games, she demonstrates her magical prowess by actually wounding him, and he becomes genuinely intrigued rather than merely predatory. Neither character shows weakness first; instead they circle each other with mutual wariness and grudging respect. The magical system feels grounded and consequential. Yennefer's spell that creates "absence" rather than fire is both creative and fitting for her character. The description of Alucard's regeneration is visceral without being gratuitous. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose edges toward purple ("column of screaming null"), though this generally serves the gothic atmosphere. The ending, while thematically appropriate, feels slightly abrupt given the buildup of tension between the characters. The piece successfully integrates both characters' signature quotes naturally into the dialogue. The medieval European setting is established through subtle details rather than heavy exposition. The 1000-word length is used efficiently to develop both character and conflict. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. Model Output:
**Prison Strings** The rumor goes like this: the cameras in Green Dolphin Street Prison die when *she* walks past. Not all at once — one at a time, a wave of grey static rolling down the corridor like something crawling under the skin of the building, then snapping back to clarity behind her. The guards blame the wiring. The wiring is fine. Jolyne Cujoh has been in enough places where the rules bend to know when someone is bending them. She watches from the yard fence, elbows hooked through chain-link, hair in two buns going frizzy in the Florida heat. The new arrival crosses the concrete in a black suit that doesn't have a single crease in it, which is impressive, because it's ninety-six degrees and everyone else in this place is sweating through their orange. Auburn hair. Eyes with rings in them, like someone dropped a stone into two ponds and froze the ripples. Behind her walk four inmates. Not with her. *Behind* her. Evenly spaced. Same pace. The big one from C-Block, the one who broke a guard's jaw last month, is walking like a golden retriever heeling. "Special investigator," someone says. "From overseas. Here about the, y'know. The weird stuff." "Yeah," Jolyne says. "I bet she is." --- The interview room has a table bolted to the floor and a camera in the corner. The camera's light is off. "Jolyne Cujoh." The woman smiles. It is a very good smile. Jolyne has seen better ones on used-car lots. "Thank you for agreeing to speak with me." "Didn't agree to shit. Two guards dragged me." "I know. I'm sorry about that." Makima folds her hands. "You've been through a great deal, haven't you? Framed. Abandoned by the system. Your father—" a delicate pause, weighted like a hook, "—arrived too late, didn't he." Jolyne's jaw tightens a half-millimeter. Stone Free stirs under her skin, threads humming. *She's fishing. Don't bite.* "That's a real specific thing for an investigator to know," Jolyne says. "I read your file." "Ain't in my file." The smile doesn't change. That's the thing that gets Jolyne — it doesn't *change*, not by a degree, not by a twitch. A real person's face is a little ocean, always moving. This one is a photograph of an ocean. "You have an ability," Makima says. "String. You can unravel yourself, can't you? Become thread, and reweave. It's beautiful, honestly. Most abilities are so blunt. Fire. Strength. Yours is *architecture*." She tilts her head, and the ringed eyes catch the fluorescent light in a way eyes shouldn't. "Tell me. When you unravel — is it still you? Or is it a thousand small things pretending to be one big thing?" "Wow," Jolyne says. "You practice that in the mirror?" "Sometimes." Something about the honesty of it makes the back of Jolyne's neck go cold. --- The problem, Jolyne realizes over the next three days, is that Makima never gives an order. She *asks*. Gently. And people do it, and then they explain to Jolyne — sincerely, eyes wet, hands shaking — why it was their own idea. Gwess trades away half her contraband and calls it a favor. A guard opens a door and can't remember doing it. Hermes says, unprompted, that maybe Jolyne should stop making trouble, and then stops mid-sentence and looks like she's going to throw up. That's the moment Jolyne stops being suspicious and starts being *scared*. Because Hermes doesn't say that. Not ever. Jolyne runs a string that night — one filament, thinner than a hair, threaded under her cell door, down the corridor, up the wall, wound around the frame of the camera outside Administration. She feels the vibration when Makima passes. She feels the camera *stop*. And she feels the string go slack, like something reached up and cut it without touching it. Then, along the remaining thread, coming *back* toward her hand: pressure. A gentle tug. Like a leash being tested from the other end. Jolyne yanks her arm back so hard she cracks her elbow on the bunk. "Okay," she breathes into the dark. "Okay. Yeah. Fuck you too." --- They meet on the fourth day, out by the laundry, in the blind spot Jolyne mapped and Makima walked into like she'd been invited. "You cut my string," Jolyne says. "You put a string on me." "You're doing something to my friends." "I'm asking them questions." Makima's hands are in her pockets. Four inmates stand behind her, arms slack, faces empty. "They're happy to answer. People *want* to be useful, Jolyne. It's the kindest thing about them." She looks at the ones behind her with an expression that is almost fond. "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." "They ain't dogs." "They chose collars. I only held the other end." "*Nobody chose shit,*" Jolyne snarls, and Stone Free explodes out of her, fist cocked— —and stops. Not held. Not blocked. *Considered.* Jolyne feels her own arm, her own Stand, her own self, hanging in the air like a coat on a hook, while something enormous and patient looks at her from a great height and decides whether she is worth the trouble. Her father's voice, cold and flat in the back of her skull: *Panic is how you lose.* So Jolyne doesn't panic. She *unravels*. Not her fist — her *whole arm*, all at once, five hundred strands blowing apart in the humid air, and the pressure closes on nothing, on empty space, on a shape that isn't a shape anymore. You can't put a collar on a thousand small things pretending to be one big thing. The strings whip out, loop the four blank-eyed inmates, and *haul* them back and down and away, out of the blind spot, into the camera's cone of light — into the record, into witnesses, into a world where someone will notice. Makima watches it happen with genuine, unhurried interest. "Ah," she says. "Architecture." Jolyne reweaves, arm reassembling strand by burning strand, and grins with all her teeth. "Yeah. Also, sweetheart? If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney." She spits on the concrete. "You want to run a theme park in here, you'd better bring the *mouse.*" Makima considers her for a long moment. Then she smiles — the same smile, unchanged, a photograph of an ocean — and turns, and walks away. Down the corridor, one by one, the cameras go dark.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and character understanding. The author successfully captures both characters' essences - Jolyne's hot-headed defiance and street-smart attitude, and Makima's chilling manipulative nature masked by false pleasantness. The supernatural prison setting is well-established and atmospheric. The prose style is notably sophisticated, with evocative imagery like "eyes with rings in them, like someone dropped a stone into two ponds and froze the ripples" and "a real person's face is a little ocean, always moving." The writing maintains consistent third-person present tense throughout and creates genuine tension through the escalating psychological battle. Character voices are authentic - Jolyne's profanity and defiance feel natural, while Makima's soft-spoken menace is chilling. The dialogue serves multiple purposes, revealing character while advancing plot. The author effectively shows rather than tells, particularly in demonstrating Makima's control powers through the behavior of other inmates. The pacing builds effectively from initial suspicion to direct confrontation. The climactic scene where Jolyne uses her string powers creatively to escape Makima's control is both visually striking and true to her adaptive nature. The ending maintains appropriate darkness - this isn't a victory, just a temporary standoff. Some minor weaknesses include occasional overwrought metaphors and a few instances where the prose becomes slightly purple. The piece could have explored the emotional complexity of the situation more deeply, particularly Jolyne's fear and isolation. However, these are relatively minor issues in an otherwise well-executed piece that successfully fulfills the prompt's requirements while maintaining narrative tension throughout. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 88.7
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**ITEM #:** SCP-████ (PROVISIONAL) **OBJECT CLASS:** PENDING **ADDENDUM ████-1: PERSONAL ACCOUNT OF DR. NOAH ARENDT, RESEARCH DIVISION, SITE-19** *Submitted at the request of the Site-19 Ethics Committee and the Department of Temporal Anomalies. The following is transcribed from Dr. Arendt's handwritten submission, retained in its original form per DoTA request.* --- I found the first one on a Tuesday. I remember because I'd been running the Tuesday battery on SCP-████-B, the cognitive suite, and I'd gotten back to my office at 16:40 with a coffee I didn't want. The note was centered on my desk blotter, folded once. My handwriting. Not an approximation of my handwriting — *mine*, including the way I cross a lowercase t with a leftward hook, which I have never seen another human being do. > *Noah. The breach starts in Sub-4, not Sub-2. They will tell you Sub-2. It starts at the seal behind the emergency shower, the one nobody logs. You have eleven days. Do not sign the requisition. — N.A.* I filed it. I did the correct thing. I want that on the record because of what comes later. Security review found nothing. Corridor 4-C camera showed my office door, closed, undisturbed, for the entire ninety-four minutes I was away — except for a single frame-drop at 16:22:07, during which the feed desynchronized and resynchronized without dropping the timestamp. Technical Services logged it as a compression artifact. It was the only artifact in fourteen months of that camera's operation. The second note appeared six days later. Same frame-drop, 09:14:51, two minutes before I returned from the mess. > *You signed it. I told you not to sign it. Cross-check the pressure differentials yourself, don't let Kovac do it, Kovac isn't cleared anymore after what happens. Eleven days was wrong. It's four. It was always four. I keep doing this and the number keeps moving.* Dr. Kovac was, at that time, cleared. Dr. Kovac had been cleared for nine years. I had signed a requisition — a routine order for replacement gasket assemblies — the previous afternoon, before I read the note, which is either meaningless or the entire point. The Department of Temporal Anomalies opened a file. I was cooperative. I was, I think, glad. **ADDENDUM ████-2: INVESTIGATIVE SUMMARY (ABRIDGED)** Three hypotheses were pursued concurrently. **H1 — Genuine retrocausal transmission.** Handwriting analysis returned a match to Dr. Arendt at a confidence interval described by the examining specialist as "uncomfortable." Paper stock matched Site-19 requisition lot 8841. Ink matched the pen in Dr. Arendt's own breast pocket, to the batch. Chronometric sweeps of Dr. Arendt's office detected no Kant-counter deviation, no localized entropy inversion, no measurable temporal gradient of any kind. DoTA noted, however, that *information* transmission leaves a substantially fainter signature than mass transmission, and that absence of evidence at their instrumental sensitivity was "not informative." **H2 — Psychological manipulation by a contained entity.** Dr. Arendt's primary assignment was SCP-████, a Euclid-class entity with demonstrated capacity for suggestion at range through indirect channels. Its containment log showed no anomalous activity. Its containment log had also, on two prior occasions, been demonstrated to be an unreliable document. The entity, when interviewed, declined to answer questions and asked twice about Dr. Arendt's sleep. **H3 — Endogenous dissociative episode with confabulated physical evidence.** Dr. Arendt would, under this hypothesis, be writing the notes himself in a fugue state. This accounted elegantly for the handwriting, the paper, and the ink. It accounted poorly for the camera. The camera was the problem. It was always the camera. --- They put me under observation. I asked them to. I slept in a monitored room with my hands on the outside of the blanket and I wore a wrist actigraph and I did not leave my bed, and at 03:31 the room camera dropped four frames, and there was a note on the floor by the door. > *they moved the shower. the shower is on the other wall now and nobody remembers, ask them, ask them where the emergency shower in 4-C is and watch their faces. I have written this 40 times. or 4. you are not the first one I have written to and you are not going to be the last one either, that's the thing they don't tell you about a loop, it isn't a circle, it's a spiral going DOWN, and every time I come back there's less of me to send. Sub-4. SUB-4. don't let them show you the schematic, the schematic is from after* The emergency shower in Corridor 4-C is on the north wall. It has always been on the north wall. I checked the schematic. I checked it and I felt the floor of my own mind flex under me, because I was certain — physically certain, the way you're certain your hand is your hand — that I had walked past that shower on the *south* wall every morning for four years. That was the day I stopped being able to tell the difference between remembering and being told. Here is what I want the Committee to understand. If this is temporal, then I am watching a man I will become dissolve in real time and I am the only one who can save him and I am doing nothing. If this is the entity, then something has reached inside my head with a gloved hand and is arranging the furniture, and every act of diligence I perform is a lever it is pulling. If it is neither — if it is only my own brain coming apart in an interesting shape — then the kindest thing anyone can do is take my keycard. I have not been able to choose between these for nineteen days. I have run out of tests. The camera glitches. The camera *always* glitches, exactly, at the moment, and no artifact in this Site has ever been that punctual. The last note came this morning. It was not folded. It was very short and the letters were very large. > *stop looking for the breach* > *you are how it gets out* **ADDENDUM ████-3:** Dr. Arendt was reassigned pending evaluation and voluntarily surrendered Level 3 credentials at 11:20 on ██/██/20██. At 11:20:00, all seventeen cameras in Corridor 4-C dropped four frames simultaneously. Requisition 8841 has been recalled. The gasket assemblies were never delivered. No one has been able to locate the shipment.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP report demonstrates exceptional understanding of the Foundation universe's clinical documentation style while delivering a psychologically complex narrative about temporal anomalies and deteriorating certainty. The author masterfully employs the SCP format's bureaucratic structure to create mounting dread through procedural language. The piece excels in its authentic voice - Dr. Arendt's account feels genuinely like a researcher's clinical yet increasingly desperate documentation. The progression from methodical scientific observation to existential terror is expertly paced. The handwriting analysis details, camera frame-drops, and bureaucratic procedures all feel authentic to the SCP universe while serving the narrative tension. The central conceit - notes from a future self warning of a containment breach - is executed with sophisticated ambiguity. The three competing hypotheses (temporal anomaly, entity manipulation, psychological breakdown) create genuine uncertainty that mirrors the protagonist's deteriorating mental state. The detail about the emergency shower's location is particularly effective, showing how reality itself becomes unreliable. The prose maintains clinical precision while building psychological horror. Phrases like "I felt the floor of my own mind flex under me" and "every act of diligence I perform is a lever it is pulling" demonstrate elegant writing that serves both character and atmosphere. The bureaucratic addenda structure allows for multiple perspectives while maintaining narrative cohesion. The ending is appropriately dark and unresolved, fitting both the SCP format and the story's themes. The final detail about the missing gasket shipment provides a chilling concrete consequence to the abstract temporal horror. Minor weaknesses include some exposition that could be more seamlessly integrated, and the middle section occasionally slows the pacing. However, these are minimal issues in an otherwise expertly crafted piece that fully realizes its ambitious concept within strict format constraints. **Item #:** SCP-████ ("The Recursive Archive") **Object Class:** Euclid (Pending Reclassification) **Special Containment Procedures:** All identified instances of SCP-████-A (hereafter "doorways") are to be sealed with reinforced steel plating and monitored by remote camera. Structures containing doorways are to be acquired through Foundation front companies and listed as condemned. Exploration of SCP-████ is currently suspended by order of the Site-19 Ethics Liaison pending review of Incident ████-K. Personnel are reminded that removal of documentation from SCP-████ requires Level 4 authorization. Personnel are further reminded that this restriction was added to this document on ██/██/████ by an editor whose credentials cannot be verified. **Description:** SCP-████ is a spatially anomalous structure accessible through 47 confirmed instances of SCP-████-A: unmarked doors of uniform dimension (203 cm × 91 cm), constructed of an unidentified grey composite material with no visible hinges, handles, or seams. Doorways manifest exclusively in structures abandoned for a minimum of eleven years. Distribution appears global and non-clustered. In total darkness, a faint amber glow is observable escaping the edges of each doorway. This glow is not detectable by photographic media and does not illuminate surrounding surfaces. Its source is undetermined; ambient light behind the door, when measured from within SCP-████, is 0.0 lux. Beyond each doorway is a single continuous interior space designated SCP-████. Surveys indicate a volume exceeding 400 cubic kilometers arranged in nested hexagonal galleries. Gallery floors intersect at angles that cannot be reconciled with any consistent geometry; exploration teams have repeatedly descended staircases and arrived at galleries above their point of origin. Shelving is continuous, unbroken, and contains an estimated 10⁹ documents in 340 identified scripts, of which 12 remain untranslated. The archive is climate-controlled. Maintenance apparatus of unknown design operates in the walls. **Recovered Document Excerpts:** > *[Ledger 4-A-1129, translated from a Semitic-adjacent script, carbon dating inconclusive]* > > "...the fourteenth year since the Opening. The Concordance maintains six of the original ninety-one facilities. Of the Directorate, none remain who remember the vote. We continue the work because the work is what remains. There is no longer a world to secure. There is only the securing." > *[Bound volume, Gallery 88, printed in modern English on paper manufactured to no known standard]* > > "PRELIMINARY POST-EVENT SURVEY — CONCORDANCE FOR THE PRESERVATION OF SEQUENCE > > Estimated surviving population: 0.0004% of pre-Event baseline. Estimated surviving *continuity*: unquantifiable. > > Cause of Event: breach at Facility ██, subject designation withheld per Directorate Order 5. Duration of Event: not measurable by any surviving instrument. Recommendation: begin the archive. Begin it before we forget that we were the ones who did this." The recurring term "Concordance for the Preservation of Sequence" appears in over 60,000 recovered documents. Organizational charts, procedural manuals, and object classification taxonomies attributed to the Concordance are functionally identical to Foundation equivalents, differing primarily in nomenclature and in the presence of a seventh classification tier for which no definition survives. Of greater concern are Gallery 91's personnel files. These number approximately 40,000 and are formatted as Foundation employment records. Cross-referencing has confirmed 312 exact matches to currently employed Foundation staff, including matching fingerprint records, dental radiography, and childhood medical history. All 312 files bear intake dates between 1340 and 1690 CE. All 312 files are marked, in a hand that varies between documents, with the single word **RETAINED**. **Exploration Log ████-7 (Abridged):** MTF Zeta-9 ("Dust Readers") entered via doorway instance 12 (former grain elevator, ███████, Kazakhstan). **0:41** — Team descends to Gallery 88. Agent Vhalis reports the amber glow, previously described as emanating from the doorway, is now behind them and moving. **1:17** — Team observes six bipedal entities in Gallery 90. Entities wear sealed encapsulating suits of a pale grey material consistent with Foundation Class-IV hazmat design, though with no insignia and no visible faceplate. Entities are engaged in the systematic removal of shelved documents into wheeled containers. **1:19** — Team Leader Ostrow calls out in English, then Russian. Entities cease activity simultaneously. All six turn to face the team. **1:20** — Entities abandon their containers and depart at speed through a gallery aperture. Agent Vhalis pursues nine meters and returns, reporting that the aperture "goes down for a very long way and there's nothing making noise in it." **1:24** — Abandoned containers are found to hold 4,100 documents, all pertaining to the identity, cause, and containment history of the object responsible for the Event. All 4,100 documents have had their central paragraphs excised with mechanical precision. Removed material was not recovered. **1:52** — Gallery 91. Team locates Ostrow's own personnel file, intake date 1502 CE. Ostrow declines to open it. Ostrow's file is subsequently found to be missing from Gallery 91 on all later expeditions. **2:30** — Gallery 91-B. Team recovers a visitor's ledger, leather-bound, maintained in ink. Entries are dated. Signatures are legible. **Addendum ████.1 — The Visitor's Ledger:** The ledger contains 1,904 entries spanning 1611 to the present. The final eleven entries fall within the last six years. Handwriting analysis has matched four of these entries to sitting members of the O5 Council with confidence exceeding 99.1%. A fifth entry matches the hand of O5-█, who is recorded as deceased in 1998. None of the eleven visits appear in Overwatch travel logs, authorization records, or site access manifests. Each of the eleven entries is accompanied, in the "PURPOSE OF VISIT" column, by the same two words: **"Routine verification."** **Addendum ████.2:** On ██/██/████, all doorway instances simultaneously ceased to open. Remote cameras confirm the doors remain in place. Under blackout conditions, the amber glow persists at the edges of all 47 instances. Fourteen hours after sealing, Gallery 91's inventory manifest — recovered during Exploration ████-7 and held in secure storage at Site-19 — was found to have been amended. Three hundred twelve entries had been struck through. A three hundred thirteenth line had been added. It has not yet been filled in.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the SCP Foundation format and delivers a compelling narrative that fulfills most of the prompt requirements. The piece successfully creates an architecturally impossible archive accessed through mysterious doors, incorporates the recursive element of Foundation personnel discovering their own organization under a different name, and includes exploration logs with hazmat-suited entities removing documents. The writing maintains the clinical, bureaucratic tone characteristic of SCP documentation while building genuine tension and mystery. The concept of the "Concordance for the Preservation of Sequence" as a predecessor organization is well-executed, and the discovery that current Foundation staff have centuries-old personnel files marked "RETAINED" creates an effective sense of cosmic horror and temporal displacement. The exploration log is particularly strong, showing rather than telling through specific timestamps and observed behaviors. The entities' synchronized response to being discovered and their systematic document removal creates palpable tension. The detail about Ostrow's personnel file disappearing after he declines to open it is a masterful touch that implies agency within the archive itself. The recovered documents feel authentic and provide crucial worldbuilding without over-explaining. The progression from the ledger entries describing a post-apocalyptic scenario to the revelation of O5 Council unauthorized visits builds effectively toward the climax. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The ending, while atmospheric, feels somewhat abrupt and could benefit from more development of the implications. The character development is necessarily limited by the SCP format, though this is more a constraint of the genre than a failing. Some technical details about the doors and archive could be more vividly described to enhance the imagery. The prose is generally clean and professional, avoiding purple prose while maintaining engagement. The piece successfully balances exposition with narrative momentum, and the recursive elements create genuine unease about the Foundation's nature and history. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Offworlder ## Chapter Four: The Grey Hour The briefings had said: *Two lineages, mutually hostile, held in equilibrium by the Concordat.* They had said it in that flat voice the Ekumen's analysts use when they have never smelled a place. I went out at the grey hour, when the official functions had dissolved into liqueurs and the Concordat's protocol officers were counting each other rather than me. My coat was local, bought secondhand through a servant who did not ask why. I had studied how the Hemani walk — the slight forward lean of a people bred for the high thin valleys, the ribcage deep as a barrel — and I could not imitate it, but I could keep my head down. The Lower Market at Ashenmoor runs along an old flood channel, stalls built into the stone revetments, and it does not close because the light does not truly go. Grey day, grey dusk, then the long violet interval they call the walk-between. Lamps of burning fat, smelling of rancid butter and something sweeter. The fabrics were the first contradiction. They hung in bolts from crossbeams, handwoven, the weft slubbed and irregular in a way that on Terra would have marked them as artisanal luxury, and here marked them as ordinary. But the colors. There was a blue that did not exist. I mean this precisely: it sat in a region of the spectrum my eye kept trying to file as green, and failing, and trying again as violet, and failing, so that looking at it was like listening to a word in a language you almost know. Beside it a red with a granular depth, as if the pigment were suspended in the fiber rather than bonded to it. I learned later they come from the *sunnel* lichens of the scree slopes, and that the dyers' guild is one of the oldest institutions on the planet, older than the Concordat, older than the schism. The second contradiction was the woman selling them. She was Hemani, unmistakably — the barrel chest, the wide flat nostrils, the extra fold at the inner eye. Her assistant, who was cutting cloth to length with a bone-handled shears and arguing with her about the price of a bolt, was Vaset. Long-limbed, narrow, the tapered fingers, the pale hair growing in that characteristic double crown. Two subspecies, the briefings said. Mutually hostile. They were arguing the way you argue with your sister's husband. With a comfortable, practiced contempt that took forty years to build. I bought two arm-lengths of the impossible blue because I had to say something, and my accent gave me away instantly, and the woman looked at me for a long moment and then charged me the ordinary price. That was the third contradiction, and the one that stayed with me. I walked for three hours. I saw a shrine where offerings of both lineages were stacked in separate but adjacent alcoves, and the separation was clearly ritual rather than sentimental, and the same old man swept both. I saw a crèche where the children were mixed and the caretakers were all Vaset, which meant something about labor and status that no briefing had mentioned. I saw four hybrid individuals, which the briefings said were rare to the point of nonexistence, and I saw them in three hours, in one district, at the grey hour, which suggested to me that they were not rare but merely not counted. Then I went back to my quarters and Command was waiting in the light-field, and I was reprimanded. I will not transcribe it. Aksel is a good officer and he was frightened, which made him thorough. *Unsanctioned departure. Unverified environment. You are not an ethnographer, Envoy, you are an instrument of the Ekumen and instruments do not wander.* I said yes. I said I understood. I said, when he had run down, that the briefings were wrong, and he said, tiredly, that of course they were wrong, they were assembled from Concordat documents, and whose documents did I imagine those were? Then he said: You will approach the Minister of Science. I said: The Minister of Science is not a scientist. He said: No. That is why you will approach him. Go and be underestimated. It is the only advantage you have. --- Minister Oren Halvarrek received me in a room with no chairs, which is a technique, and offered me tea in a cup too hot to hold, which is another. He was Vaset, elderly, and had the stillness of a man who has outlived four governments by never once being interesting at the wrong moment. "You walked in the Lower Market," he said. "Yes." "You did not deny it. Good. Denial wastes an hour." He drank his tea, apparently without pain. "What did you learn?" "That your census undercounts." Nothing moved in his face. "Which category?" "The one you don't have a word for. Or rather — you have several words, all of them insults, which is a kind of category." "*Marrow-crossed*," he said. "That is the polite one. Continue." "I think your Concordat is not an equilibrium between two hostile lineages. I think it is a mechanism for maintaining the fiction that there are only two lineages, because the alternative is arithmetic that no one in this building wants to do." He set down the cup. "The Ekumen sends children," he said, "and the children say true things loudly, and then they are surprised when the true thing becomes a weapon in a hand they did not choose. Do you know what happens if your arithmetic is done publicly, Envoy? Not in ninety years. In nine months." "Tell me." "Ah," he said, and for the first time he sounded almost pleased. "*Tell me.* Not *I know.*" He walked to the window, where the violet interval was thickening over the roofs. "You bought cloth. What color?" "The blue that isn't." "*Sunnel-second-wash.* My mother's guild." He did not turn around. "Every dyer on this world is of mixed marrow. Every one, for six generations. It is the guild's only entrance requirement, and it is unwritten, and it is why the guild is old and the Concordat is not. You have been inside the thing you came to discover and you thought you were buying a scarf." I stood with the scalding cup and said nothing, which was the first genuinely diplomatic act of my career. "Come back on the ninth day," said the Minister of Science. "Bring the cloth. And, Envoy — walk. Every night, walk. When they stop you, use my name." "Will that protect me?" "No," he said. "It will inform me."

## Chapter Nine: Terminator Sequence The mushrooms came up through the tile cracks again overnight, which meant Wren didn't have to burn lamp oil to find the centrifuge. They were *Panellus stipticus* crossed with something—she'd never known what, the splice predated her tenancy—and they threw a cold green light about as bright as a dying phone screen. Twelve years of fruiting bodies pushing up through the fractured epoxy floor of what had been Bay 4 of a Verdanta Agricultural Solutions regional testing facility. The company was gone. The mushrooms remained. There was a lesson in that, and Wren had stopped trying to learn it. She stepped between them barefoot, because boots crushed the caps and the caps were her only free light, and knelt at the bench. The thermocycler was three machines wearing one machine's skin. The original Verdanta unit had died in the second winter—Peltier elements cooked, control board corroded to lace. What remained was the aluminum block, drilled out and re-tapped, sitting on a bed of salvaged CPU coolers pulled from the server farm two towns over. Heating came from nichrome wire wound by hand. Temperature control came from a thermistor and a microcontroller Wren had flashed with firmware she'd written on paper first, longhand, because there was no debugger, only failure. The whole assembly was clamped in a vise bolted to a workbench that had once been a door. It cycled. That was the miracle. Ninety-four degrees, fifty-eight, seventy-two, and again, thirty-five times, four hours, and if the power held it made copies of things that were dying. Everything was dying. That was the design. --- Verdanta's crops had been beautiful. Wren had seen the archival footage: wheat that yielded four times conventional, tomatoes that didn't bruise, maize engineered to fix its own nitrogen. All of it carrying what the patent filings called a Genetic Use Restriction Technology and everyone else called a terminator. Seeds sterile by design. Buy again next year, every year, forever. Forever had lasted until the year the shipping stopped. Now the world ate from a genome with a built-in expiration date. Wren's work—the whole of it, the thing that consumed her—was theft. Not from Verdanta, who no longer existed to be robbed, but from entropy. Somewhere in the terminator cassette was a repressor, and the repressor could be knocked out, and if you knocked it out cleanly the seed would set, and if you knocked it out sloppily you got a plant that grew eleven centimeters and fell over. She had done a lot of eleven-centimeter plants. --- The contract came in wrapped in wax paper, which was how you knew someone had money. The courier was a girl of maybe fifteen with a walleye and a shotgun she clearly couldn't fire. She wouldn't come inside past the mushrooms. Wren read the paper in the doorway. *Rye. Cold-tolerant. Fertile F2. Six kilos viable seed. Delivery in forty days.* Under it, the payment: two hundred liters of diesel, a working dehumidifier, and—this was the part that made Wren's hands go cold—*four grams lyophilized Taq polymerase, sealed, cold-chain intact.* Four grams. She had been running her reactions on Taq she cultured herself out of a hot spring outflow forty kilometers north, harvesting *Thermus* from a mat of orange slime, purifying with a heat step and prayer. It worked maybe six times in ten. Four grams of real, sealed, factory enzyme was two years of certainty. "Who's asking?" Wren said. The girl shrugged. "Man said you'd know it was serious by the enzyme." Which was true, and which meant whoever it was had read her, had known exactly what would move her, and that was its own warning. Cold-tolerant fertile rye, in a world where every rye line north of the old border carried Verdanta's Frostmark cassette, meant somebody intended to feed a lot of people, or control the feeding of a lot of people, and there was no third option. Wren thought about the settlement. Eighty-one souls, down from ninety-four in the spring. Thought about diesel for the well pumps. "Tell him yes," she said. --- The Frostmark line was seven years dead in her freezer, which ran on a compressor scavenged from a dairy chiller and a bank of lead-acid cells that she equalized by hand every eighth day. Seven years at negative eighteen with three unlogged thaw events. The DNA came out of the tube like wet ash. She ran it on a gel—agarose from boiled seaweed, poured into a mold she'd 3D-printed back when there was still filament—and stained it with the mushrooms' own extract, which fluoresced under a UV LED just enough to see. The lane was a smear. No bands. Fragmentation down to a few hundred base pairs, maybe less. Which meant she couldn't amplify the cassette whole. She'd have to walk it. Overlapping primers, thirty-base windows, assemble the fragments back together in vitro like reconstructing a smashed plate from powder. Forty days. Maybe two hundred reactions. Maybe more. She sat down on the floor among the glowing caps and put her head in her hands and felt the tremor start in her left arm. --- The tremor was from the anti-parasitic. Three years ago the settlement had gotten liver flukes from the north reservoir, and there had been no praziquantel and no prospect of any, so Wren had done the thing you did: gone into Verdanta's abandoned therapeutic library, found a viral vector encoding an anti-helminthic peptide, and injected herself first. Because that was the rule. You went first. It had worked. The flukes died. Twelve other

Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone, and Arthur Neegan, who had spent eleven years listening to the pumps and scrubbers of Mars, found the sound almost homely. Almost. The difference was that the scrubbers in Sector Nine had been his to repair. This one belonged to someone else, and so, for the moment, did he. They had come at 0640 that morning, six of them, in matte-grey pressure suits with a stylized starburst at the shoulder—Antares Diplomatic Corps, the insignia said, in a script so tasteful it might have been embroidered by a duchess. The man in charge had removed his helmet at the airlock and apologized for the hour. He had been very polite. He had also declined, twice, to explain what would happen if Arthur said no, and that omission had been the most informative part of the conversation. Now Arthur sat strapped into a couch of real leather—real, he was fairly sure; nobody bothered faking that particular smell—and watched Mars shrink in the viewport from a world into an ornament. The rust-colored disc turned slowly, showing the long scar of the Tharsis leases, the sun-catching glint of the Nyx smelters. Somewhere down in that ochre haze was a plot of ground four hundred meters on a side, registered to A. Neegan, Colonial Freeholder, Class Three, and beneath it a vein of azra that the geological survey had estimated—conservatively, the man from Kolat Mining had said, sweating—at nine hundred thousand metric tons. Nine hundred thousand tons of a metal that made uranium impatient. "You're doing the arithmetic," said a voice. Arthur turned. A woman had come into the compartment without his hearing it, which suggested either very good boots or very good training. She was perhaps sixty, silver-haired, dressed in a plain charcoal tunic with no insignia at all, which on a ship where everyone else wore starbursts was itself a kind of rank. "I'm doing the arithmetic," Arthur admitted. "Don't. It's the wrong arithmetic." She settled into the couch opposite and folded her hands. "Everyone begins by multiplying tons by price per gram. It is a comforting sum because it has an answer. My name is Councilor Vasquez-Ohl. I represent certain interests in the Antares Combine." "Diplomatic Corps." "The Corps is a department of the Combine. The Combine is a chartered trading company with the right to raise its own security forces, negotiate its own treaties, and—" she smiled faintly, "—apologize at six in the morning. You may consider the word 'diplomatic' to be decorative." "I'd worked that out." "Good. Then we can skip a stage." She touched the arm of her couch and the compartment lights dimmed; a holo-tank in the deck woke and threw up a slowly rotating schematic of the inner system, Sol a hard white bead at its center. "Mr. Neegan, what do you know about azra?" "I'm a mining engineer. I know it accelerates decay. Point-source catalysis, inverse-square falloff, no reaction mass consumed—" "You know what it does. I asked what you know." The schematic bloomed; threads of light sprang from Mars, out past the belt, out to the ragged edge where the interstellar shipping lanes began. "Twenty-two years ago, a survey drone found the first gram of it in a Martian regolith sample. Today the entire fusion economy of six systems is being rebuilt around it. A pile that took thirty years to breed plutonium now takes eleven days. A starship that needed four hundred tons of reaction mass to reach Alpha Centauri in a human lifetime now needs forty. Do you understand what that means?" "Cheaper freight." "It means the end of distance as a political fact." She let that sit. "For four centuries, Mr. Neegan, distance has done the work of law. Colonies could not be conquered because they could not be reached in time. Fleets could not be massed because fleets could not be fueled. Azra dissolves that. And every polity in human space understands it, which is why there are now nineteen separate claims of sovereignty over the Martian crust and why three of them are backed by warships." Arthur said, slowly, "And my four hundred meters." "Your four hundred meters is currently the single richest confirmed deposit in human possession. Which is why you are on this ship, and not at the bottom of a fissure with your suit seals mysteriously fatigued." She said it without any change of tone at all. "I want to be understood as being on your side, insofar as anyone is." "That's a careful sentence." "I'm a careful woman." The holo faded. "Here is the offer. The Combine will purchase your freehold outright—not the ore, the title—for one hundred and twenty million credits, paid into a Cerean escrow beyond the reach of Martian colonial courts, of Kolat Mining, and of the Terran Revenue Board. You will receive Combine citizenship, which carries with it the protection of the Combine's security forces. You will also receive a technical directorship at the site, because frankly you know the geology better than anyone we could hire, and because a man with a title feels less like a man who has been robbed." Arthur was quiet a moment. Below the deck, the pumps hummed on. "You've told me what I get," he said. "You haven't told me what happens if I decline." "No," Vasquez-Ohl agreed. "I haven't." "Then let me tell you what I've worked out, and you tell me where I'm wrong." He leaned forward. "You didn't send six armed men to my door because you were worried I'd refuse. You sent them because someone else was coming, and you wanted to arrive first. There are, what, three parties bidding? Four?" Something flickered across her face that might have been approval. "Seven," she said. "And one of them is not bidding." "Meaning?" "Meaning that one of them has concluded that a deposit nobody controls is preferable to a deposit controlled by a rival, and that four hundred meters of Martian crust can be rendered permanently unrecoverable with a fission charge of remarkably modest size." She rose. "You have until we dock at Deimos Transfer to decide, Mr. Neegan. I would use the time. Once you are aboard the station, the conversation will no longer be private, and I cannot promise the next party to make you an offer will bother with the leather couch." She left. Arthur sat looking at the small rust-colored ornament in the viewport, and did the arithmetic again, and got a different answer.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Asimovian style and prompt requirements. The author successfully captures the classic sci-fi atmosphere with retrofuturistic elements like leather couches on spaceships, diplomatic corps with decorative titles, and the political complexity typical of Asimov's work. The world-building effectively balances intimate details (Arthur's specific plot dimensions, the sound of air scrubbers) with grand political implications (the dissolution of distance as a political fact). The dialogue carries the narrative effectively, revealing character motivations and plot stakes through conversation rather than exposition dumps. Vasquez-Ohl emerges as a nuanced character - polite yet threatening, informative yet withholding crucial details. Her careful phrasing ("insofar as anyone is") and strategic omissions create tension and reveal her diplomatic training. Arthur's characterization feels authentic for a mining engineer thrust into galactic politics. His practical mindset shows through his focus on "doing the arithmetic" and his methodical analysis of the situation. The progression from his initial confusion to growing understanding feels earned. The prose maintains elegance without becoming overwrought. Phrases like "Mars shrink in the viewport from a world into an ornament" and "a metal that made uranium impatient" demonstrate creative imagery that serves the narrative. The technical details feel researched and plausible within the sci-fi framework. The political intrigue builds effectively, with hints at larger conflicts (nineteen sovereignty claims, warships, seven bidding parties) while maintaining focus on Arthur's immediate predicament. The escalating stakes from economic opportunity to personal survival create genuine tension. Some minor weaknesses include occasional exposition that borders on telling rather than showing, particularly in Vasquez-Ohl's explanation of azra's political implications. However, this serves the Asimovian tradition of characters discussing complex ideas, so it doesn't significantly detract from the piece. The ending maintains appropriate tension without false resolution, leaving Arthur (and readers) with a genuine dilemma and uncertain future. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations The safelight makes everything a confession. That's what I'm thinking at eleven forty on a Tuesday, elbow-deep in stop bath, watching Elliot's hands move through the red glow like they belong to someone underwater. He has good hands. Long, and always a little ink-stained, and tonight there's black polish chipping off three of his nails, which means he painted them at least four days ago and hasn't fixed them, which means something, though I couldn't tell you what. I've been reading him like this all semester. Cataloguing. It's a bad habit and I'm not sorry. "You're doing the thing," he says. "What thing." "The thing where you stare at me and then pretend you were looking at the enlarger." "The enlarger's very interesting." "It's off, Dani." I laugh, and he does too, that small quick laugh he has, like he's letting it out of a jar. He goes back to the negatives. Contact sheet number four. We've got fourteen images that work and we need twenty, and the professor wants them mounted by Friday, and neither of us has mentioned that we could have finished this project two nights ago if we ever actually worked instead of talking. Here's the thing about me: I take charge. I asked out my first girlfriend at sixteen by handing her a note that said *yes or no, circle one.* I've never waited for anybody. My friends call me a bulldozer with a nice haircut and they're not wrong. And here I am, twenty-five years old, standing three feet from a nineteen-year-old boy in a mesh shirt and a thrifted funeral coat, and I am doing *nothing*, on purpose, for the first time in my life, and it's killing me. Because two weeks ago in this room he said: *Can I tell you something weird?* And I said sure, because I say sure to everything. And he said, very fast, to the developer tray: *I don't think I'm a boy. Or — I don't know. I don't know if that's the right sentence. I've been trying out sentences.* Trying out sentences. God. I think about that phrase constantly. I think about it when I'm brushing my teeth. Tonight he's quieter than usual, and I know that's the tell now, so I wait. I load paper into the easel. I wait through two prints and a fixer change and finally he says: "I tried a different name. In my head. Not out loud." "Yeah?" "It felt like wearing someone else's coat." He tilts a print with the tongs. "Which — I like wearing other people's coats. So maybe that's fine. Maybe that's the whole point." "That's the best thing anybody's said in this building all year." "Don't." He's smiling though. The red light does something to his face; it flattens all the anxiety out of it and leaves just the bones. "You're going to make me self-conscious." "You're always self-conscious." "I'm *aware* of myself. It's different." A pause. "Is it different?" "I have no idea. I've never been aware of myself in my life." He laughs so hard he drops the tongs, and I bend to get them, and my shoulder brushes his hip, and something goes through me like a struck match — and here's the confusing part, the part I've been chewing on for weeks like gum that lost its flavour but I can't spit out. I have a type. I have a *loud* type. Butch women with forearms. Men who look like they could change a tire while insulting you. Definition. Edges. I like knowing what I'm holding. And Elliot has no edges. Elliot is a soft-focus photograph of a person in the middle of becoming, and I want him — them — *him*, he still says him, I asked, I made myself ask instead of guessing — I want him so badly it's embarrassing, and I don't know what that makes me. I don't know if my type was ever a type or just a costume I liked. Maybe I'm the one trying out sentences. "Dani." He's looking at me now. "You went somewhere." "I'm thinking about how I'd photograph you." "You have. Ninety times." "Badly. I've been photographing you badly." I lean back against the counter. "I keep shooting you like you're finished. Like it's a portrait. It's not a portrait, it's a — long exposure. Something moving." He doesn't say anything for a second. Then, quiet: "That's a nice thing to say. I don't know what to do with it." "You don't have to do anything with it." "You usually want people to do things." "I know." My voice comes out rougher than I intend. "I'm working on it." And this is when I turn to reach for the paper and my elbow catches the box — the whole open box, fifty sheets of Ilford, the good stuff, twenty-two dollars I don't have — and it goes off the shelf, and the lid goes one way and the paper goes another, fanning out across the wet floor under the not-safe glow of the print viewer that has been on this entire time because *I* turned it on. We both just watch it happen. Slow. Terrible. Fifty sheets fogging to grey. "Oh my God," I say. "That's — okay. That's okay." "That's forty minutes of work and all our paper." "Dani." He's crouching, gathering, and he's *laughing*, that jar-laugh but bigger, and he holds up a ruined sheet like evidence. "Look. It's ruined. It's completely ruined and nothing happened." "What?" "Nothing bad happened." He looks up at me from the floor, and the grey paper catches the red and his eyes are enormous. "I keep waiting for the thing where it ruins everything. And it's just — paper." I crouch down too. Close. Our knees. "I want to kiss you," I say, "and I've decided not to ask you in a way that makes it hard to say no, so I'm just putting it out there on the floor with the paper, and you can leave it there." He is very still. Then he reaches over and takes my hand, ink-stained fingers, chipped polish, and holds it like something he's checking the weight of. "Not tonight," he says. "But keep the sentence. I want to try it on later." "Okay," I say. And I mean it. That's the part that undoes me — I mean it, completely, and I sit down on the wet floor beside him in the red light, holding his hand, ruined paper everywhere, no project, no plan, nothing finished. Long exposure. Something moving.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The narrative successfully captures Dani's voice as an assertive yet introspective character navigating unfamiliar emotional territory. The author skillfully uses the darkroom setting both literally and metaphorically, with the red light creating an intimate confessional atmosphere that serves the story's themes of identity exploration and vulnerability.
