+ Coming of age: Lost & Found in Osaka — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Lost & Found in Osaka** The chord hit her from half a block away — a bent, screaming note that cut through the arcade's electronic burble like a knife through plastic wrap. Mika stopped walking. Her plastic bag of secondhand patch cables swung against her knee. She knew that melody. Everyone knew that melody, but almost nobody played it *like that* — the busker had taken the theme and dragged it somewhere dirtier, slower, letting the notes sag before snapping them back into place. Mika drifted closer, stopping just outside the ring of watchers, half-hidden behind a vending machine. The busker was maybe eighteen, nineteen. Short bleached hair with three centimeters of black roots. A denim jacket with the sleeves hacked off at the shoulder seams, worn over nothing but a tank top, in October. Her amp was a battered little cube taped to a hand truck. The last note rang out. Six or seven people clapped. Two of them dropped coins in the open guitar case and fled into the arcade. Mika clapped too, once, then stopped, aware of her own hands. "Hey." The busker was looking directly at her. "You. Vending machine girl." Mika's throat closed. "You've been standing there for like three songs." "I — sorry. I'll —" "No, no, no." The busker waved a hand. "That's a compliment. Everyone else looks at their phone the whole time and then walks off. You were *listening*. There's a difference. I can feel it, like—" she wiggled her fingers at her own temple, "—psychic radar." "I. Um." Mika stared at the pavement. "Your, um. The tuning. It's down a whole step. Right?" The busker's eyebrows went up. "D standard. Not — not drop D, because the fifth string was still, um, a fourth, when you did the — the run in the bridge, so." Mika's voice was getting quieter and faster at the same time. "Sorry. That's a weird thing to say." "That is an *extremely* weird thing to say." The busker grinned, wide, all teeth. "Do it again." "...What?" "Say another weird thing. That was great. Nobody's ever noticed the tuning. Guys come up to me all the time to explain my own pedals to me, but nobody's ever—" She held out a hand. "Rina." Mika looked at the hand for a beat too long before shaking it. "Mika." "Mika. You play?" "Not — not guitar." "What, then?" "Synths." A pause. "Synthesizers." "Like, keyboards?" "Sort of." Mika shifted her bag. "More like — I build sounds. The keyboard part is kind of, um, incidental." "Okay, *incidental*," Rina said, delighted. "Explain." "It's — there's an oscillator, that's the raw sound, and then you shape it, with filters and envelopes, so you can make it, like." Mika's hands came up without her permission, sculpting air. "Make it breathe. Or hit. Or fall apart slowly. And a lot of the old anime stuff, the eighties stuff, is all — that's a DX7, that's a Juno, and people think it's cheesy but it's actually really precise, they knew exactly what they were doing, and—" She stopped. Her ears were hot. "Sorry." "Why do you keep apologizing?" "I don't know." Rina crouched to loosen her strap. "So what's in the bag?" "Cables. There's a shop on the third floor of that building, the one with the broken sign, and they have a bin of old patch cables for eighty yen each, and most of them are dead but if you test them—" "You test them in the store?" "They have a tester on the counter. The old man lets me." Mika's mouth twitched. "He calls me *ojōsan* and complains about the price of solder." "Mika." Rina stood up, guitar swinging around to her back. "Mika, Mika, Mika. You are the coolest person I have talked to all week and I've talked to like ninety people." "That's not—" "Have you eaten?" Mika blinked. "Have I—" "Eaten. Food. There's a kaiten place two streets over, past the maid café with the sad flyers guy. Hundred and ten yen a plate, the salmon's decent, the tamago's *incredible* and I will fight anyone who says otherwise." Rina was already stacking her coins into the pocket of her jacket. "Come on. I made four thousand yen today, I'm basically a corporation." "I don't — you don't have to—" "I'm not *doing you a favor*, I'm hungry and I hate eating alone. That's a selfish request. You can say no." Mika opened her mouth to say no, because that was what her mouth did. "...The tamago's really good?" "It's *transcendent.*" "Okay." "Yes!" Rina thumped the top of her amp. "Okay, help me with the hand truck, the wheel sticks—" She got one strum out — just checking the tuning, thumb across the strings — when the sky detonated. *Whump. Whump-whump.* Both of them looked up. Above the arcade's neon crown, between the buildings, a chrysanthemum of gold light unfolded and drooped, then another, then three at once, green and white, close enough that the sound arrived late and enormous and swallowed everything: the arcade, the crane games, the guitar, all of it flattened under the noise. The crowd on the street had stopped moving. Fifty phones went up in unison. Rina's hand was still resting on the strings, silenced. "Riverside festival," she shouted over the booms. "I forgot it was tonight." "You're being drowned out," Mika shouted back. "Yeah." Rina didn't look upset about it. Gold light slid across her face, then green. "Can't compete with that. Nobody can. That's basically God's amp stack." Mika laughed — a real one, surprising herself, a short ugly honk of a sound. Rina turned to look at her, eyebrows up. "Oh, *that's* your laugh." "Shut up." "No, I like it. It's honest." Another *whump*; the vending machine buzzed in sympathy against Mika's shoulder. Rina finally lifted her hand off the strings. "Okay. God's playing the closing number, we're not gonna beat it. Sushi?" "Sushi," Mika said. They pushed the hand truck up the street, wheel squeaking, while the light kept changing colors on the pavement in front of them.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character development within the slice-of-life genre. The author successfully creates two distinct voices through dialogue and internal narration - Mika's hesitant, knowledge-rich speech patterns contrasted with Rina's confident, playful tone. The setting of Den Den Town is rendered authentically with specific details like the cable shop and pricing that ground the scene in reality. The character work is particularly strong. Mika's social anxiety and passion for synthesizers feel genuine, manifesting through her apologetic speech patterns, technical knowledge dumps, and physical reactions like her "throat closing" and "ears getting hot." Rina's characterization as an outgoing busker is well-executed through her direct approach, casual profanity, and ability to read social situations while remaining genuinely interested in others. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with natural interruptions, overlapping thoughts, and realistic speech patterns. The author avoids exposition dumps by weaving background information into character interactions organically. Mika's technical explanation about tuning and synthesizers feels authentic to her character while revealing her expertise. The prose style is clean and evocative without being overwrought. Descriptions like "a bent, screaming note that cut through the arcade's electronic burble like a knife through plastic wrap" create vivid imagery without purple prose excess. The fireworks sequence provides effective environmental storytelling and a natural transition point. The pacing builds naturally from initial observation through awkward first contact to easier conversation, culminating in the invitation to eat together. The transformation feels earned rather than forced - Rina's genuine interest in Mika's knowledge provides believable motivation for connection, while Mika's gradual opening up tracks realistically with finding someone who appreciates her expertise. Some minor weaknesses include occasional over-reliance on character tags in dialogue and a few moments where the prose becomes slightly self-conscious. The ending, while satisfying, could have pushed the emotional complexity slightly further. However, these are minor issues in an otherwise well-crafted piece that successfully captures the awkward beauty of unexpected human connection. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: Six Minutes The watch came in a box with no return address, and Mom said that meant I shouldn't wear it. "It was probably Aunt Deb," I said. "She forgot the card. She always forgets the card." That was three weeks ago. Now it's Tuesday, and I'm standing in the boys' bathroom at Fairmont Middle with my sleeve pushed up, staring at the little silver dial on the watch face — the one that isn't a dial at all, but a spiral, tightening in on itself like water going down a drain. Here's what the watch does. You press the crown twice. You feel a cold pinch, like someone pressing an ice cube to the back of your neck. And then the world hiccups, and you're six minutes in the past. Six minutes. Every time. Not five, not ten. Six. I found out by accident. I'd dropped my tray in the cafeteria — spaghetti day, of course — and I was mashing buttons on the watch in pure humiliated panic, and then *hiccup*, and I was standing in the lunch line again with the tray in my hands, and Marcus Ruiz was telling me the same joke about his brother's driving test, word for word, and nobody was laughing at me, because it hadn't happened yet. I didn't drop the tray that time. After that I used it for everything. Pop quiz on the Louisiana Purchase? Take it, fail it, rewind, look up the answers, take it again. Say something stupid to Priya Chandrasekhar by the water fountain? Rewind. Say something less stupid. Rewind again. Say something almost charming. I used it eleven times last Thursday alone. --- The changes started small enough that I could explain them away. My jeans got short. Mom said I was growing, and she said it happy, the way parents do, like growing is a trick you're performing for them. My voice cracked in the middle of reading aloud in English, and Dylan Foss made a noise like a goose, and I *didn't* rewind that one, because I was too busy touching my throat and feeling something there that hadn't been there in September. Then my shoes stopped fitting. Then there was hair on my legs — actual hair, dark and coarse, not the soft fuzz I'd had — and a smell coming off me in gym class that made me want to crawl out of my own skin. Then, last Friday, Mr. Petrosian handed back our essays and said, "Nice work, Mr. Ayala," and then paused with the paper still in his hand and squinted at me and said, "How old are you again?" "Thirteen," I said. He looked at me for four full seconds. "Huh," he said. --- So that's why I'm in the bathroom now, with the lights buzzing and the third stall door hanging crooked, looking at myself in the long scratched mirror over the sinks. My jaw is wrong. That's the only way I can put it. My jaw is heavier. There's a shadow along it, a real shadow, the kind Dad has to shave off. My shoulders have gone wide and bony inside my hoodie and my hoodie used to be big on me. My eyes look tired in a way that thirteen-year-old eyes are not supposed to look. And then the mirror flickers. Not the lights. The *mirror*. Like a TV switching channels for a half-second — and for that half-second the face looking back at me isn't mine. It's a man's face. Thirty, maybe. Thirty-five. Lines at the corners of the eyes. Gray coming in at the temples like frost on a window. And that man's mouth is moving, saying something, and even though there's no sound I can read it, because he says it slowly, like he knows I have to catch it: *STOP.* Then it's just me again. Just a kid with a jaw that doesn't belong to him, breathing too fast in a bathroom that smells like bleach. I looked at the watch. The spiral had gotten tighter. --- I would have stopped. I swear I would have. But then came fifth period, and the fire alarm, and Ms. Whitlock's classroom door, and the thing I did. Here's what happened the first time, the *real* time: the alarm went off and everybody shoved into the hallway, and in the crush somebody knocked Priya's backpack off her shoulder, and she bent down to grab it, and the crowd went over her like a wave over a rock. She got a broken wrist and a black eye and she cried, and I stood there frozen with my hands in my pockets like a coward. Six minutes. That's all it took to fix it. I rewound. The alarm went off. I got to her first, I grabbed her arm, I pulled her sideways into the doorway of the science lab and held her there while the hallway emptied. "What are you *doing*?" she said. "Saving you," I said, and my voice came out low and strange, a stranger's voice, and she looked up at me and her face did something I didn't understand — a flicker of not-recognizing. And out in the stairwell, someone screamed. Because Priya was supposed to be there. She was supposed to fall right there, at the top of the stairs, and stop the crowd for eleven seconds, and in those eleven seconds Coach Berrigan was supposed to come up from the gym and get the doors open at the bottom. She wasn't there. The crowd didn't stop. The doors didn't open. I'm not going to write down what I saw at the bottom of those stairs. I can't. Every time I try, my hand shakes so hard the pen tears the paper. Eleven kids. That's what they said on the news. *Eleven.* --- So now it's midnight and I'm sitting on the edge of the bathtub in my own house with the door locked, and my hands look like a grown man's hands, veined and knuckly, and there's a real beard coming in now, three days of it, in one day. The spiral on the watch face is almost closed. I don't know how many are left. Maybe one. Maybe a hundred. Maybe if I press it enough times I go all the way back to the fire alarm and let her fall, and eleven kids get to grow up, and I don't. I press the crown once. I look up at the mirror. And the man is there, waiting for me, and he's crying, and he nods.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Goosebumps-style teen horror prompt, effectively capturing the voice of a middle schooler discovering supernatural consequences to his actions. The author successfully incorporates all required elements: the smart watch's time-rewinding ability, physical aging effects, changing social treatment, timeline disruption with tragic consequences, and the setup for a final reversal. The narrative structure is well-crafted, using short sections to build tension and reveal information gradually. The protagonist's voice feels authentic for a thirteen-year-old, with natural dialogue and age-appropriate observations. The writing maintains consistent tone throughout, balancing the supernatural elements with believable middle school scenarios. The imagery is particularly effective, especially the mirror scenes with the older version of himself and the watch's spiral "tightening in on itself like water going down a drain." The physical transformation details feel earned and disturbing in an age-appropriate way. The author shows restraint in not explicitly describing the stairwell tragedy, which maintains the Goosebumps tone while acknowledging serious consequences. The emotional complexity is notable - the protagonist's initial delight in fixing embarrassing moments gradually transforms into horror as he realizes the true cost. The ending with the crying older self creates a haunting image that fits the genre perfectly. Some minor weaknesses include occasional telling rather than showing (particularly in explaining the watch's mechanics) and a few moments where the prose becomes slightly overwrought. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The piece successfully creates genuine tension and dread while maintaining the accessible style appropriate for the target audience. The story feels complete despite being a single chapter, with clear stakes and a compelling cliffhanger that would drive readers to continue. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The shooting gallery's canvas backdrop had been painted to resemble a forest, though whoever painted it had never seen one. The trees were the wrong green, too blue, like something dreamed rather than remembered, and among them tin ducks rattled along their track with a sound like coins poured into a hat. Evelyn stood where the boardwalk's planks had warped, one hand on the rail, and did not go closer. Twenty feet off, a fortune teller's booth leaned into the dusk. Its shutters had been folded back to reveal charts hung on nails: a great flayed hand, palm out, mapped like a country. MOUNT OF VENUS. THE GIRDLE OF SATURN. LINE OF LIFE — and beneath the printed words some previous proprietor had inked a warning in a cramped hand she couldn't read from here. The paper had gone the color of weak tea. Nobody sat inside. She was aware of herself as if from above. A young woman in a linen dress the color of butter, gloves she had not needed, standing very still in a place designed against stillness. *His locks.* There it was again — that phrase, surfacing like something in a bathtub she'd rather not identify. She had read it in a poem once, a bad poem, and now it had attached itself to a man she had spoken to for eleven minutes on a Tuesday. "You came." He was on her left, which was wrong; she'd been watching the stairs. "I was passing," she said. "Along a boardwalk you'd have to take a train and a trolley to pass." "I like the ocean." "You can't see the ocean from here." He tipped his head. Behind him the gallery lights came up all at once and threw his shadow long across the planks. "You can see the gallery, and the fortune teller, and the frozen custard. The ocean's around the other side." "Then I like the sound of it." "That I'll allow." He was not smiling, exactly. It was something adjacent to a smile that had decided not to commit. "You're a careful liar. Careful liars are the interesting kind. The reckless ones only tell you what they wish were true." "And what do the careful ones tell you?" "What they're afraid of." A gull screamed. Somewhere down the boards a barker promised the eighth wonder of the world for one thin dime. "I don't know your name," she said. "No." "That's not an answer." "It's a fact. Facts are more use." He turned toward the fortune teller's booth, and she found she had turned with him, which she resented, though she couldn't have said whom she resented. "Do you believe in palmistry?" "I believe people pay for it." "That's not the same question, but it's a better one." He stopped before the flayed-hand chart. In the buzzing light his curls were less black than she remembered — there was a wine color in them, near the temple. "My grandmother read hands. On a kitchen table in Bay Ridge, for neighbors, for nothing. She'd hold your palm and go quiet, and everyone thought that was the mystery. It wasn't. She was listening to your breath. When she got near the thing you didn't want said, you'd stop breathing. She'd feel it in your wrist." "That's a confidence trick." "It's attention. Most people can't tell the difference. That's why the trick works." He glanced at her, quick and unhurried both. "Give me your hand." "No." "Good." The word landed oddly. She waited for him to press — she had prepared, on the trolley, several graceful refusals, and had privately looked forward to using them — and he did not press, and the prepared refusals sat in her mouth like unspent coins. "Good?" she said. "You've been told a hundred times to be agreeable. It's a relief to hear you decline something." He put his hands in his pockets. "Also, if you'd given it to me, I'd have known you were in more trouble than you are." "And what trouble am I in?" "The ordinary kind. You told someone you were going to the pictures." Her chin came up. "I told my sister I was meeting a friend from the typing pool." "Which is worse. Pictures can be checked and forgiven. A friend from the typing pool has a name and can be found, and when she's found and says she never saw you, your sister will understand you thought it through. That's the part that frightens them. Not the lie. The planning." "You've a low opinion of me." "I have a high opinion of you," he said. "That should worry you more." Down the boardwalk a rifle cracked, then again, then a tin duck went over with a clang, and a girl shrieked with pleasure, and the carousel organ started up two hundred yards away, all in the same three seconds, and for those three seconds Evelyn did not breathe. He didn't touch her wrist. He didn't need to. She saw him note it, and file it, the way a man notes a card that has fallen face up. *Leave.* The thought arrived clean and reasonable, in her mother's voice, and she examined it as one examines a dress in a shop window while walking past. *There is still time and no one has been unkind to you and nothing has happened at all.* Nothing had happened at all. That was the trouble. She had come to Coney Island twice now to have nothing happen, and both times had gone home unable to sleep. "You could tell me your name," she said. "It's not a very great secret to give away." "It isn't. That's why I'll keep it a while." He nodded at the shooting gallery, at the blue-green forest that nobody had ever walked in. "Eight shots for a nickel. If you hit five, they give you a paper rose. If you hit eight, the man gets nervous and asks where you learned." "And where did you learn?" "See — you assume I hit eight." "Didn't you?" "Yes." He took a nickel from his pocket and turned it over once between two fingers, thoughtfully, like a man deciding something that had already been decided. "Come and shoot. You'll want your gloves off." She looked at the fortune teller's booth, at the great open palm with its inked warning she still could not read, and at the empty chair behind the curtain where nobody sat to tell her anything. Then she began, one finger at a time, to take off her gloves.

+ Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
They ate dinner at the long pine table that JT's grandfather had built, back before the road came in, when everything had to be hauled up the last two miles on a sledge. The table had a groove worn into it near the head, where four generations of elbows had rested. JT sat with his thumb in that groove and pushed his beans around his plate and waited for someone to say something about the clearing. Nobody did. Mike ate like a man who hadn't seen food in a week. Their father sat with his hands around a coffee mug he wasn't drinking from, looking at the window over the sink. It was full dark outside, so there was nothing to see there but the kitchen reflected back—the three of them, small and yellow-lit, floating out among the trees. "Good day," Mike said finally. "Seen fresh sign all along that ridge." "Mm," their father said. "Bet we could push up past the beaver flowage tomorrow. Get above them." "Mm." JT set his fork down. His heart was going the way it did before a math test, a stupid rabbit-flutter he was ashamed of. "Dad." His father's eyes came around. They were ordinary eyes, brown and tired, threaded red at the corners the way they always got up here. Nothing in them at all. That was the thing JT would think about later, lying in the loft listening to the stove tick: there was nothing in them, and that was worse than if there'd been something. "There was a buck in that clearing," JT said. The refrigerator hummed. Mike stopped chewing. "Big one," JT said. "You were right up next to it. You had your hand out." His father took a sip of the cold coffee and made a face and got up and poured it in the sink. He ran the tap a while. Over the water he said, "You want to get your boots oiled tonight. They're drying out on you. That's why you were falling behind." "Dad—" "Because you get a crack in the welt and that's it, that's your week. Your feet'll be soup." He shut off the tap. "There's the neatsfoot under the bench." Mike was looking at JT with an expression JT couldn't read, or maybe with no expression, which by then was starting to feel like the same thing. Mike was nineteen and had a way of going flat and adult when their father was in the room, like a dog that lies down when the bigger dog walks past. "You remember it though," JT said. "Right? You had to have—" "I remember walking up on a lot of nothing," their father said, pleasantly, and that was the awful part, the pleasantness. "I remember standing there a minute. Country like that plays hell with your eyes. Light comes down through the spruce, you'll see anything you want." "You weren't looking at light. You were touching—" "JT." Just his name, level, no heat in it. The way you'd set a glass down on a table. Their father went to the door and took his coat off the peg and went out onto the porch, and JT heard the deck boards take his weight, one, two, and then stop, and then not creak again for a long time. Mike scraped his plate. "Why do you do that." "Do what?" "Poke at him." Mike put his plate in the sink. "He hasn't been right since Mom. You know that. You don't have to keep sticking your finger in it." "You were there too," JT said. "You had the same face on him. Like you were listening to something." Mike stood at the sink with his back to him. The window over the sink still had the kitchen in it, and in the window Mike's face hung there, and for a second—one second, and JT would take it back later, would file it under tired, under wanting it to be true—for a second Mike's face in the glass wasn't looking at the dishes. It was looking out past them, out into the trees, and it was smiling. "Eat your beans," Mike said. --- JT lay in the loft with the sleeping bag pulled to his chin. The lodge made its noises. It had always made them and he had always liked them, the way a house you know settles into itself at night like a big animal getting comfortable, but now every one of them had a question mark on the end. Around two he heard the porch door. He knew he wasn't going to look, and then he was at the little gable window with his palms on the cold glass, and he did look. His father was standing in the yard in his long johns and unlaced boots. No coat. It couldn't have been much above twenty degrees; JT could see the man's breath going up in slow plumes, could see the pale of him against the black wall of spruce at the edge of the mown grass. He was facing the woods. His arms hung at his sides. He wasn't moving. Not shivering, not rubbing his arms, not doing any of the thousand small things a cold body does without being asked. Just standing, and looking, and breathing. And out at the tree line, low down where the spruce boughs made a dark skirt over the ground, there was a shape. JT told himself it was a shape. It was about the height of a truck hood and it was the wrong color for anything, a color like wet slate, and it was breathing too, and their breath went up together into the yard light in one column, in and out, in and out, matched like a metronome. JT's own breath fogged the glass. He wiped it with his sleeve and the yard was empty except for his father, who was walking back toward the porch, unhurried, and who stopped at the bottom step and tilted his head up—not toward the window, not exactly, just up—and stood that way for a five-count. Then the door, and the boots coming off, and the creak of the springs downstairs. In the morning there'd be frost on the grass, and JT would go out before either of them and find two long lines of it melted away, running from the tree line to the porch and back, like something enormous had gone over the ground and taken the cold with it. He'd stand there in his oiled boots with the coffee going bitter in his mouth and decide, for the fourth time that week, not to say anything.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Stephen King-inspired surreal horror style requested. The author successfully maintains JT's perspective as an unreliable narrator caught between reality and something more sinister, building tension through psychological ambiguity rather than overt supernatural elements. The dialogue feels authentic and serves multiple purposes - revealing character dynamics, building tension, and showing rather than telling the family's dysfunction. The father's deflection ("Country like that plays hell with your eyes") and Mike's protective dismissal ("Why do you do that") ring true to how families navigate around trauma and denial. Character actions remain believable throughout. JT's desperate need to validate his experience, his father's evasive responses, and Mike's protective stance all feel psychologically authentic. The midnight scene with the father standing in the cold creates genuine unease without crossing into implausibility. The prose demonstrates considerable skill in balancing concrete details with atmospheric dread. Phrases like "the kitchen reflected back—the three of them, small and yellow-lit, floating out among the trees" create vivid imagery while reinforcing themes of isolation and displacement. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality. The piece builds tension effectively toward the midnight encounter, which serves as a strong payoff. The ambiguous shape at the tree line and the synchronized breathing create genuine horror through suggestion rather than explicit revelation. The ending with the melted frost lines provides a haunting physical trace that validates JT's experience while maintaining uncertainty. The emotional complexity is well-handled, particularly in how grief (the mother's death) intersects with the supernatural elements. The family dynamics feel lived-in and authentic, with each character responding to trauma differently. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly overwrought, and a few instances where the metaphors feel forced. The pacing occasionally slows during exposition, though this doesn't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 89.3
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Hell is Other Demons The ash began at six, as it always did, drifting down over the Nine Circles like the world's least enthusiastic snow. Lucifer Morningstar stood at the window of his study and watched it settle on the roofs of the Administrative Quarter, and thought, as he did most mornings, that he really ought to do something about the drainage. Instead he made toast. He had learned to make toast in 1963, after Lilith had said something cutting about his inability to feed himself, and it had become, over the intervening decades, a small monument to spite. He ate it standing up, over the sink, dropping crumbs into the disposal, which screamed faintly. Everything in the palace screamed faintly. It was a design choice he had come to regret in the way one regrets a tattoo. At eight he took the morning briefing. "The Lake of Fire is down to a simmer," said Beleth, who had a clipboard and the manner of a man who had once been enthusiastic about something. "Thermal output's off forty percent. The damned have started calling it the Jacuzzi." "Fix it." "We'd need to divert from the Wailing Aqueduct." "Then divert." "The wailing will stop." Lucifer considered this. Somewhere below, five hundred thousand souls were being punished for sins that had, in most cases, involved insurance fraud. "Let it stop for a week," he said. "It'll be worse when it starts again. Anticipation is half of suffering. Write that down." Beleth wrote it down. He had four hundred pages of things Lucifer had told him to write down, and had begun to suspect that this was his own personal damnation, which it was. At ten, Lucifer signed the transfers. Nine thousand souls redistributed between circles on appeal, each one a small essay in human self-justification. *I only embezzled to help my mother. I only strangled him a little.* He signed them all with the same pen, a Parker 51 that a man in Cleveland had traded his soul for, in 1949, along with a cure for his son's polio. The son had lived to eighty-one. Lucifer had liked that deal. It was the only pen he used. At eleven, Lilith let herself in. She didn't knock. She had never knocked, not in six thousand years, not even during the period when they were legally—by the peculiar and byzantine standards of infernal law—divorced. She came through the east door with ash in her hair and a paper bag in her hand, and set the bag on his desk without comment. Lucifer did not look up. "You have a key." "I've always had a key." "I changed the locks." "I know," said Lilith. "I liked the new ones. They bite." He looked in the bag. Two pomegranates and a bottle of something Greek. He did not thank her. Thanking her would have been a concession, and they were nine weeks into the current cessation of hostilities, and concessions were how these things began, and how they began was how they ended, and he had promised himself— "You're thin," she said. "I'm incorporeal." "You're thin *conceptually*." She sat on the edge of his desk, displacing a stack of transfer orders, and looked at him with the specific patience of a woman who had watched him do this before. "You haven't been eating. You've been eating *toast*." "I like toast." "You *loathe* toast. You make toast at me." She picked up a transfer order, read it, made a face. "Who approved the Jacuzzi?" "It's a thermal fluctuation." "It's a *hot tub*, Lucifer, they're playing cards in it—" and then she stopped, because she had come here for other reasons, and they both knew it, and knowing it made the air in the room feel crowded. They ate the pomegranates in silence, over a tray, seed by seed, spitting the pips into a bowl that had once held the eye of a saint. Outside, the ash came down. It came down on the Bureau of Ironic Retribution and the long grey queues outside Processing and the eighteen thousand acres of parking lot that served no vehicles and never had, and which was, according to internal surveys, the single most despair-inducing structure in the realm. "I've taken a lease in Dis," Lilith said. "Fourth Circle. Two floors and a courtyard." "Congratulations." "It's a *lease*, Lucifer. Eleven months." "Then congratulations for eleven months." She threw a pomegranate seed at his head. He let it hit him. It was, in its way, the most affectionate thing that had happened to him since March. At two, they had the first argument, which was about the aqueduct and was not about the aqueduct. At three, they had the second, which was about whether he had ever, in six millennia, asked her a single question about herself, and this one had teeth, and he lost it, badly, and stood at the window with his hands behind his back and said nothing for eleven minutes while she smoked. At half past three she said, "The ash used to be white." "It was never white." "It was. When we started. It came down white and you said it was—" She stopped. "Snow," said Lucifer. "I said it was snow. I hadn't seen snow. I was going from descriptions." "You were showing off." "I was very young." "You were *four thousand and six*." "I was young for my age." She laughed. It was not a large laugh. It got out before she could stop it, and she looked annoyed about it, and he turned from the window and saw her being annoyed about it, and something in his chest performed a manoeuvre that he would have denied under any form of questioning, including the ones he had invented. At six she left. She took the empty bag and left the bottle, which was a message, and he understood it, and hated that he understood it. At seven, Beleth returned with the diversion order. Lucifer read it. Then he took his Parker 51 and struck out the aqueduct clause, and wrote in the margin: *Leave the wailing. Take it from the parking lot lights.* "The lot will be dark, my lord." "Yes," said Lucifer Morningstar, Prince of the Power of the Air, and set down his pen, and looked at the bottle on his desk for a long moment. "Let them find their own way out." The ash kept falling. It was not white. It never had been.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the prompt's requirements, successfully merging the mundane bureaucracy of running Hell with intimate relationship dynamics. The author captures a distinctly Gaiman-esque voice through understated irony and matter-of-fact treatment of the fantastical. The characterization is particularly strong. Lucifer emerges as a figure both cosmic and petty, making toast out of spite while managing the eternal punishment of souls. His relationship with Lilith feels lived-in and authentic, with their dialogue carrying the weight of millennia together. The detail about the Parker 51 pen and its origin story exemplifies the author's skill at weaving meaningful backstory into mundane objects. The prose maintains excellent restraint, avoiding the temptation toward overwrought description that often plagues fantasy writing. Lines like "Everything in the palace screamed faintly. It was a design choice he had come to regret in the way one regrets a tattoo" demonstrate the perfect balance of dark humor and relatable frustration. The structure effectively uses the "day in the life" format, with time stamps creating rhythm while the narrative builds emotional tension. The bureaucratic elements (thermal output reports, transfer orders, the Jacuzzi complaint) provide excellent comic relief while reinforcing the absurdist premise. The ending achieves genuine poignancy without sentimentality. Lucifer's decision to darken the parking lot rather than stop the wailing suggests character growth through small acts of mercy, while the final image of ash that "was not white. It never had been" provides thematic closure about lost innocence and the impossibility of return. Minor weaknesses include some dialogue that occasionally feels slightly constructed rather than completely natural, and a few moments where the pacing could be tighter. However, these are minimal concerns in an otherwise accomplished piece that successfully fulfills all prompt requirements while maintaining literary quality throughout. Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
The morning came the way it always came in the ludus: with the smell of piss and barley. I woke before the horn, as I always did, and lay listening. Above me in the bunk, Castus ground his teeth in his sleep like a mill wheel. Beyond the cell door, out in the yard, the water-carrier's cart squealed on its ungreased axle, and somewhere past the walls the whole city was clearing its throat — bakers' shutters banging up, a mule train coming down from the Esquiline, a woman screaming at a man in Greek about a debt. Rome never slept. It only rolled over and complained. I had been three years in the school of Vatia and I could still tell you the hour by the sounds. That was survival, of a sort. In the mines, they told me, a man loses track of days and then of himself. Here I knew every noise, every shift in the air, the way I had once known the wind coming off the Rhodope hills before the rain. The horn went. We shuffled out. Barley porridge in wooden bowls, thick enough to stand a spoon in, with a splash of vinegar-wine and a fistful of ash-bread. They fed us like cattle because we were cattle: valuable, insured, entered in a ledger. The doctor came twice a month to pinch our flesh and look at our tongues. I ate slowly, sitting with my back to the wall in the arcade where the sun did not yet reach, and watched the new ones. Six of them, bought at the market by the Tiber the week before. Dacians, mostly, from Trajan's wars — men with long moustaches and eyes like shuttered windows. One boy could not have been sixteen. He held his bowl in both hands and stared at the sand of the practice yard as though it were a river he had to cross. "He'll last a month," Castus said, sitting down beside me and spitting a stone out of his bread. "He'll last as long as they let him." Castus laughed. He was a Gaul with a nose that had been broken so many times it lay almost flat against his cheek, and he had killed eleven men in the arena and wept over exactly one of them. "You're in a philosopher's mood, Thracian." "I'm in no mood at all. It's too early for moods." That was a lie. I had woken with a mood in me like a stone in a boot, and it had a shape: a rumour, which had come into the ludus the way all rumours came, through the mouths of the water-carriers and the whores who serviced the guards. There would be games in Maius. Not municipal games, not some magistrate's little offering of six pairs and a bear. Games from the palace. A hundred and twenty pairs, they said, to honour the Emperor's new forum, and the aediles had been squeezing the schools for a month. Vatia would sell us by the dozen. He would weep as he did it, our lanista, that fat pious fraud, and he would weep about the price and not the men. And in the Senate they would praise the Emperor's generosity to the people, and the people would praise it too, because bread and blood were the only two things Rome gave freely, and a man who eats another's bread learns to applaud on cue. I had learned that. There is nothing so obedient as a full belly. After the meal came the drills. Two hours at the palus — the wooden post, that patient enemy — with a practice blade of weighted wood, twice the heft of steel, until the shoulder burned and the sweat ran into the eyes and Marcus the trainer walked among us with his vine-staff, cracking it across a thigh here, a spine there, roaring that we struck like women drawing water. Then, because the aedile's man was coming to view the stock, they gave us our own weapons for an hour. They brought mine wrapped in oiled cloth, and I took it and I felt what I always felt: a small treacherous joy. A sica. The curved blade, a forearm long, bending inward like the crescent of a young moon, honed on the inside of the curve so that it did not stab but *drew* — a blade for reaching around a shield, for taking the back of a knee, the hollow of an armpit, the soft places a straight sword can never find. My people had carried such knives before Rome ever heard of us. My father had used one to gut fish and slaughter goats and once, when I was six, to open the throat of a Roman surveyor who came to measure our fields for tax. I remember the surveyor's wax tablets lying in the dust with the numbers still on them, and I remember thinking that the numbers had not gone away. They gave me the curved blade because I was Thracian and the crowd expected it. They dressed me in the small greaves and the crested helmet with the griffin, and they called me by a name I had not been born with, and they made of my grandfather's knife a costume. That was the thing about Rome. It did not only take your country. It took your country's things and sold them back to you as spectacle, and taught you to be proud of the performance. And I *was* proud. That was the poison of it. When I held the sica my hand knew things my mind had never taught it, and I felt, for the length of that hour, less like a beast in a ledger and more like a man with a lineage. The Romans had given me back my hands. They charged the earth for it. I went through the forms slowly in the corner of the yard, the sand hot now through my sandals, cicadas starting up in the dead fig tree by the wall, the stink of the tannery three streets over drifting in on the wind with the smell of hot dust and rosemary from someone's kitchen. Across the yard the Dacian boy was being shown how to hold a shield. He held it too high. They all did, at first. I turned the blade so it caught the light, and thought about Maius, and about the price of a Thracian in a good year, and I found I could not decide whether I was afraid.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and historical authenticity. The author successfully creates an immersive Roman setting through carefully chosen sensory details - the smell of "piss and barley," the squealing cart wheels, the sounds of the awakening city. The first-person narration from the gladiator's perspective feels authentic and grounded, avoiding romanticization while maintaining emotional depth. The characterization is particularly strong. The protagonist emerges as a complex figure - neither purely victim nor hero, but a man caught between survival and identity. His relationship with his Thracian heritage, embodied in the sica blade, creates compelling internal tension. The observation that Rome "took your country's things and sold them back to you as spectacle" demonstrates sophisticated understanding of cultural appropriation and imperial dynamics. The prose style is controlled and evocative without becoming overwrought. Phrases like "Rome never slept. It only rolled over and complained" show wit and personality. The writing maintains consistent voice throughout, with the narrator's philosophical bent feeling earned rather than imposed. The piece effectively incorporates period-appropriate social and political commentary - the bread and circuses dynamic, the treatment of conquered peoples, the commodification of human life. These themes emerge naturally from the character's observations rather than feeling didactic. However, the piece has some structural weaknesses. While it successfully creates atmosphere and character, the narrative feels somewhat static. The day progresses predictably through routine activities without significant dramatic tension or revelation. The ending, while thematically appropriate, lacks punch and feels somewhat inconclusive even for a slice-of-life piece. The dialogue, though limited, feels natural and serves character development well. The interaction with Castus efficiently establishes their relationship and the protagonist's worldview. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 89.3
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Skerryvane Lighthouse, by Oban — 3rd February 1911** Dear Mother, Landed Tuesday, wet through to the vest. The relief boat couldnae get in close so they swung me off on a rope like a bag of meal, and my box after me, and the boatman shouting that if I dropped my boots into the sea I'd be walking home. Fine welcome. There's the two of us here forbye the Principal, a Mr Corrie from Peterhead who has said eleven words to me in four days, and nine of them concerned paraffin. The other is a lad younger than me called Ewart who whistles. I would rather he did not. The tower is ninety-one steps and I ken every one of them already. The light is a fine thing, I'll grant it. When she's lit and turning you can stand in the room with her and feel the whole tower breathing. Tell Mrs Dunnet I got her scarf and it's earning its keep. Your son, Donald --- **14 Rose Vennel, Greenock — 19th February** My dear Donnie, Well and I hope you thanked the woman properly and not just through me, for she knitted it while her hands were bad. There is not much doing here. Your uncle Hughie has taken a notion he is dying, which he takes every winter about now, and by Easter he'll be dancing. The yard is slow. Mrs Nairn's boy went to Canada and she has been that proud and that greeting about it in the one breath that you cannot tell which she is at. Do not fret about the man Corrie. Some men are only quiet, and quiet is not the same as thinking ill of you. Your father went three days once without a word to me and it turned out he had lost a wager and was ashamed. Eat. You will not, so I am saying it. Your loving Mother --- **Skerryvane — 8th May** Dear Mother, I'll tell you a queer thing about this place. There is nothing to look at but water and yet you look at it the whole day. There's no a tree. I hadnae known I liked trees. Corrie has begun to speak. He speaks of currents, and of a keeper at Ailsa who went strange, and he tells the story like a man handing over a warning wrapped in a story so he does not have to say the warning out loud. I am not going strange. I am polishing brass and I am reading the almanac backwards for want of anything else with print on it. Send books. Any books. I read the label off a tin of syrup twice. Donald --- **Greenock — 2nd June** Dear Donnie, There is a parcel coming with three books in it from the Mission and one of them is about bees which I could not help, it was what they had. I have put in your father's snuff mull as well. I ken you never took snuff and neither did he much after the yard, but I want you to have it and I want it out of the press where I keep coming on it. You will mind the dent in the lid, that was from the plate that came down on him at Cartsdyke, and he used to say the box took the blow that was meant for his ribs and he owed it a debt. The lid has that bit of shell set into it — mother-of-pearl he called it, he cut it off an oyster shell a Whitby man gave him and he filed it to fit with his own hands and it took him a fortnight of evenings and he was insufferable about it. It goes green and pink when the light is on it sideways. The hinge is mended with copper wire because he broke it dropping it off the tram and would not let the man in Cathcart Street touch it, he said his own botch was worth more than another man's mend. Hold it in the dark and you'll ken which way is up by the shell. Your Mother --- **Skerryvane — 21st June** Dear Mother, It came. I had it out in the light room the whole watch and you're right, it takes the beam and gives it back green. I'm keeping it in my breast pocket, which is daft for a man who never takes snuff. But the weight of it is a company. Corrie saw it and asked, and I told him about the plate at Cartsdyke, and he told me about his own father, who was a cooper, and that was the longest either of us has talked since I came. I am better, Mother. I willnae say I'm happy but I've stopped counting the days till relief, which is the same thing sideways. Donald --- **Greenock — 4th November** Dear Donnie, Do not be coming home in December, the fares are wicked and you have only just got your good name up with the Board. I am fine. Mrs Dunnet is in and out. My chest is only the usual and the doctor is a young man who likes to be seen to be doing something. Write me the ordinary things. What you had to your tea. Whether the lad still whistles. Your Mother --- **Skerryvane — 26th January 1912** Dear Mother, Your writing has gone away from you. I've your last three here on the table and I've set them side by side like a man reading a chart and I do not like the course. I have asked Corrie for my leave and he has given it without one question, which frightened me more than a refusal. I am on the relief boat the 14th. Do not argue with me by post, you'll only win. Your son, Donald --- **Greenock — 3rd February** Donnie. Come. I am not able to be proud about it any longer. Mother --- **Skerryvane — 9th April 1912** Dear Mother, I ken. But I've the paper and the pen and the habit, and I'd rather write to you than not. I was in time. That's the thing I want set down. Nine days, and you knew me every one of them, and on the Thursday you asked me what I'd had to my tea and I lied and said mutton. You wanted the mull to stay with me and it has. I've it in my pocket the now. Corrie is retiring in the autumn and they've said the Principal's post is mine, which you'd have told the whole vennel inside the hour. I light her at dusk and she turns all night and can be seen eleven miles. I did not tell you that when I was low, because I was too busy being lonely to notice it was worth telling. Somebody out on that black water sees my light and kens where the rocks are. That's the work. That's a decent thing for a man to be doing. I'll not go strange, Mother. I've a green and pink bit of shell in my pocket that tells me which way is up in the dark. Your loving son, Donald
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary narrative successfully fulfills the prompt requirements while delivering a genuinely moving story. The piece spans over a year, following Donald's journey from initial isolation at Skerryvane Lighthouse to finding meaning in his work after his mother's death. The Scottish working-class voice is authentically rendered without falling into caricature. Donald's dialect feels natural and consistent - "couldnae," "forbye," "willnae" - while his mother's voice is slightly more refined but still distinctly Scottish. The author demonstrates skill in differentiating the two voices while maintaining believable familial intimacy. The gradual plot revelation is expertly handled. Early letters establish Donald's isolation and his mother's supportive nature. The introduction of his father's snuff mull serves as both a tangible connection to family and a symbolic anchor. The mother's declining handwriting and increasingly brief letters subtly signal her deteriorating health without explicit statement - a masterful example of showing rather than telling. Character development is nuanced and believable. Donald's transformation from a lonely, counting-days keeper to someone who finds purpose in his work feels earned through the specific details: his growing relationship with Corrie, his appreciation for the lighthouse's function, and ultimately his mother's death forcing him to find meaning independently. The prose is elegant and restrained, avoiding purple language while still being evocative. Phrases like "the whole tower breathing" and "green and pink bit of shell that tells me which way is up in the dark" are poetic without being overwrought. The writing captures the rhythm of Scottish speech naturally. The emotional complexity is particularly strong. The story deals with isolation, duty, family bonds, and grief without sentimentality. The final letter achieves genuine pathos - Donald's continued writing to his deceased mother feels psychologically authentic rather than merely sentimental. The ending strikes an appropriate balance. While there's a note of acceptance and purpose, it's tempered by loss and the reality of continued solitude. Donald's realization about his work's importance feels organic rather than forced optimism. Minor weaknesses include some predictable elements - the declining mother, the gruff colleague who warms up - but these are handled with enough specificity and skill to transcend cliché. The pacing is well-controlled, with each letter advancing both plot and character development efficiently. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 77.5
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The WiFi password is taped to the counter. Laminated, even, which means someone thought about it, made a decision, and committed. "GuestPass2019!" — and there it is, the exclamation point, that little apologetic gesture toward complexity requirements, the digital equivalent of putting a bow on a brick. 2019 means they haven't rotated it in six years. Six years of guest traffic on what I'd bet money is the same flat network as the POS terminal, because the same person who laminated that card is the person who set up the router, and that person used the default admin credentials, and I know that the way I know the sun is up. Don't. You are not doing this. You are here for a human being. Her name is Priya and she's four minutes late and I have already mapped three ways into this restaurant's infrastructure and one way into the walk-in cooler, because the back door is propped with a milk crate for the smokers, and the smokers are the vulnerability in every physical security model ever devised. People want to be comfortable more than they want to be safe. That's not cynicism. That's just the load-bearing fact of my entire former career. There. Coming through the door. Green corduroy jacket, and she's scanning the room left-to-right, which is normal, most people go left-to-right — "Hi. Sorry. The bus." She sits. She has ink on the side of her hand, left-handed, and a lanyard shoved half in her pocket like she's embarrassed by it. Be present. Be a person. People are not attack surfaces, they are people, and Dr. Ostrowski says the compulsion is a coping mechanism for a childhood in which information was the only currency I could control, and I paid her one hundred and ninety dollars an hour to tell me that so I should probably take it seriously. "How was the bus?" "Aggressively a bus." Good. That's good. That's a joke with structure — setup, subversion, confident brevity. She's not nervous. Or she performs not-nervous, which is functionally the same until it isn't. Twenty minutes in and something extraordinary happens, which is that I stop counting exits. She mentions, sidelong, apologetically, in the way people mention the thing they actually care about, that she'd spent Saturday at a Commander night. And I say *Commander* out loud in a tone that startles us both, and then the table becomes a different table entirely. She plays a Yuriko deck. Of course she does. Ninjutsu, unblockable, information asymmetry as a win condition — the girl plays *reconnaissance as a lifestyle* and doesn't seem to know it about herself. I tell her my deck is Kess and she laughs and says "so you're the reason people leave," and I say yes, and it's the most seen I've felt in maybe a year. We argue about whether Thassa's Oracle should have been banned earlier. We argue *well*. She interrupts me twice and both times she's right, and both times she circles back to let
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical writing ability and a clear understanding of the hacker mindset prompt. The author successfully establishes the protagonist's compulsive vulnerability-scanning behavior through concrete, believable observations about WiFi passwords, physical security gaps, and system weaknesses. The internal monologue feels authentic to someone with deep technical knowledge trying to suppress their professional instincts in a social setting. The characterization is nuanced and psychologically credible. The protagonist's struggle between their analytical nature and desire for human connection creates genuine internal tension. The mention of therapy sessions with Dr. Ostrowski adds depth and suggests realistic self-awareness about their behavioral patterns. The transition from security-focused observations to genuine engagement over Magic: The Gathering feels organic and well-earned. The prose style is confident and distinctive, with sharp, observational details that reveal character efficiently. Lines like "People want to be comfortable more than they want to be safe" and the description of the exclamation point as "the digital equivalent of putting a bow on a brick" demonstrate wit and insight. The voice remains consistently analytical yet increasingly warm as the connection develops. However, the piece has significant structural issues. Most critically, it cuts off mid-sentence just as it reaches the central conflict mentioned in the prompt - the phone unlock pattern observation and subsequent fallout. This leaves the narrative incomplete, missing the key dramatic moment and resolution that would demonstrate the protagonist's ability to navigate social consequences of their compulsive behavior. The Magic: The Gathering section, while well-written and character-revealing, consumes considerable word count without advancing toward the promised central conflict. The pacing feels slightly uneven as a result. Additionally, some technical observations, while accurate, occasionally slow the narrative momentum. The dialogue that appears is natural and character-appropriate, particularly the Magic discussion. The emotional engagement builds effectively through the shared interest discovery, though the incomplete nature prevents full assessment of the piece's emotional arc. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 91.3
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The lab table is cold under my forearms, and I've arranged my pencils parallel to the edge, which I know looks obsessive, so I nudge one out of alignment to seem casual. That's the kind of thing I do. I stage my own casualness like a set designer. Mr. Okonkwo says, "Elena, you're with Danny." Four words. Two names. And now there is a boy sitting down eighteen inches to my left, unzipping a backpack, and my entire nervous system has become a smoke alarm with a dying battery. *Okay. Opening line.* Option one: "So do you want to do the ramp or the pendulum?" Direct. Task-oriented. Boring, though. The kind of question a substitute teacher asks. But safe. Safety is worth something. Safety is worth a lot, actually, given the alternative, which is Option two: something funny. But funny requires timing, and timing requires that I not rehearse, and I have already rehearsed, which means when I say it, it will come out with the flat over-practiced cadence of a school announcement, and he will do that thing people do — the half-second lag before the polite laugh — and I will hear that lag for the rest of the year, at night, in the dark, playing on a loop like a song I hate. He's getting out a pen. It's chewed at the top. Something about that undoes me a little. Someone who chews pens is a person with a nervous system too, probably, theoretically. Option three: comment on the room. "It smells like a swimming pool in here." Except it doesn't — it's ammonia, they mopped, and the fumes are sitting low over the tables like weather. Actually the smell is aggressive enough that if I *don't* mention it that's almost stranger, because we're both sitting in it, breathing it, our eyes both faintly stinging, and to say nothing is to pretend we're not sharing an experience, and isn't that what a normal person would do — acknowledge the shared experience — Ammonia. NH₃. Nitrogen with its three hydrogens, that lopsided little pyramid with the lone pair on top, which is why it's polar, which is why it's a base, which is why it gets into your sinuses like it has an appointment there. Trigonal pyramidal. My brain is doing this instead of speaking. My brain is a very impressive machine that has been installed in the wrong vehicle. "You okay?" he says. Oh no. I have made a face. I made a face at the smell, or at the molecular geometry of the smell, and he saw it, and now there's an opening — an actual naturally occurring conversational opening, gift-wrapped — and I have to fill it in under one second or the silence becomes a thing with a name. "The mop," I say. *The mop.* Two words. I said "the mop" like a caveman identifying a threat. There were forty better versions of that sentence sitting right there in my mouth and I reached past all of them and grabbed the mop. But he laughs. Not the lag-laugh. A real short one, out the nose. "Yeah, it's brutal. My eyes are watering. I look like I'm crying about physics." *Say something. He gave you a joke, you have to give one back, that's the exchange rate, that's how this works.* "Reasonable response to physics," I say. And he laughs again and I feel something in my chest go warm and then immediately I feel the second thing, which is the fear, because now the bar is set at *funny* and I have to keep clearing it for the next forty minutes and I only had the one. Inventory check: Am I slouching? Slightly. Is that better or worse? Worse if it reads as bored, better if it reads as relaxed. Are my hands doing anything? My hands are picking at the sticker residue on the table, which is fidgeting, which is a tell, so I stop, but stopping makes them just *lie there* like two dead things, so I pick up a pencil to give them a job. Am I looking at him too much? I looked at him for what felt like nine seconds when he said "brutal." Recalibrate. Look at the worksheet. But not the whole time, because then I'm the girl who won't make eye contact, and that's its own diagnosis. He's reading the instructions out loud, sort of half-mumbling them, and I already read them last night because I read ahead, always, so I know that question four is going to trip us up, and I could just — say that. "Question four is worded badly, they mean the *net* force." Helpful. True. Also: proof that I read ahead, which is proof that I am the kind of person who reads ahead, and there is a specific flavor of girl-who-reads-ahead that I have spent two years trying not to be legible as, not because I'm ashamed of it exactly but because it gets you a category and categories are hard to climb out of. But he'll figure out question four eventually and then I'll have withheld information to seem cooler, which is a worse crime, morally, and also strategically, because being useful is honestly the only asset I have here. I am not funny on demand. I am not good at hair. I can, however, explain net force. "Question four's a trap," I say. "They mean net." He looks over. "Wait, really?" "Yeah. It says 'the force' but there's two." "Okay, that's — yeah, okay, I would've gotten that wrong." He writes something. Then: "You're good at this stuff." Four words this time. *You're good at this stuff.* And here is the terrible part, the part I could never explain to anyone: I don't get to just enjoy it. I get about a quarter of a second of pure gold and then the analysis starts. Did he mean *good at this stuff* as in impressive, or as in *good at this stuff and therefore a resource*? Is this the beginning of something or the beginning of him copying my answers? Should I deflect? If I say "not really" that's fishing. If I say "thanks" that's arrogant. If I say nothing — "Thanks," I say. My voice comes out smaller than I built it. The ammonia shifts, thins, and for a second I can smell his laundry detergent instead, something clean and green, and I think: I will remember this table. This exact table, this stinging air, the chewed pen, the eighteen inches. He slides the worksheet toward me so we're both looking at it. Our elbows are maybe two inches apart now. Two inches. I could move mine one inch closer and it would be nothing, it would be plausible, it would be an accident of geometry. I don't. I sit perfectly still and I explain net force in a completely normal voice, and inside, very quietly, I am screaming with joy.

Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned.
