Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Four minutes. She said seven, and she's never late, so she'll be here at 6:58, which means I have four minutes to decide who I'm going to be. The green shirt says *I didn't try.* The black one says *I tried and this is the best I could do,* which is worse. I put the green one on. I take it off. I put it on again. Three days. Three days of one-word replies and that thing she does where she reacts to a message with a little heart instead of answering it, which is the emotional equivalent of patting a dog on the head on your way out the door. And I know — I *know* — she started the new job, I know her mother's in and out of the hospital, I know all of this because she told me, at length, on the phone, and I said *take all the time you need,* like an adult, like a person with a spine and a life. But here's what she's actually thinking. She's thinking: that was a mistake. Not a cruel thought, she isn't cruel, that's the awful part — she'll be *kind* about it. She'll sit down and put both hands around her glass and do the little inhale, and say, *I've been thinking about us,* and I already know exactly how I'll answer. I'll say: *You don't have to do the speech. I know the speech. I could give the speech.* Cool. Almost bored. And she'll say something like *don't do that, don't get defensive,* and I'll say *this isn't defensive, this is me saving you fifteen minutes,* and she'll get that hurt look, the one that means I've been Too Much again, and then I'll be the villain in a story where I was the one being left. I catch myself in the hallway mirror on the way past. Shoulders up around my ears like I'm bracing for a slap. Hands doing the thing. *Look at you.* I turn away before I have to keep looking. That's a thought spiral. I can name it. I read the book, I did the worksheets, I can say the words *catastrophizing* and *emotional reasoning* in a calm therapist voice. Naming it does approximately nothing. It's like identifying the species of a bear that is currently in your kitchen. And anyway — anyway — it isn't *irrational.* That's what nobody gets. It's not paranoia if she actually got quiet. Something changed after that night. Something must have. She saw me without the packaging and did the math. The buzzer. — She's holding flowers. Grocery-store flowers, the wet paper cone, the orange ones I like, and she's out of breath from the stairs and she says "Hi, hi, sorry, I *ran*," and she kisses me in the doorway before she's even inside, before she's put her bag down, and something in my chest unclenches so fast it hurts, like blood coming back into a foot. *See. SEE.* She got flowers. She remembered the orange ones. Nobody buys flowers for the person they're about to leave — well. Actually. That's exactly when people buy flowers. Guilt-flowers are a genre. They're practically the flagship product of the flower industry. No. Stop. Look at her face. "I've missed you," she says, into my shoulder. "This week has been *insane*." I say something normal. I put the flowers in the good jug. My hands are steady, which feels like a lie my body is telling on my behalf. She talks about her mother, the discharge paperwork, the sister who won't help. She's grey under the eyes. And I'm listening, I *am* listening, and simultaneously I am running the tape underneath: *she's building a case. She's establishing that she's been busy so that later, when she says the thing, I can't accuse her of pulling away.* And even as I think it I know how obscene it is, to sit across from someone describing their mother in a hospital gown and to be auditing them for evidence against me. She reaches over and puts her hand on my knee mid-sentence. Not looking at me. Just — puts it there, absently, the way you'd touch your own pocket to check your keys are still in it. Oh. That's the thing that gets through. Not the flowers, not the kiss. The absentmindedness of it. You don't perform absentmindedness. That's the hand of someone who thinks I'm *hers*, who isn't thinking about it at all, and I want to take that gesture and swallow it whole, I want it laminated, I want to live inside the four seconds of it. Four seconds is about how long it lasts. Because then: unless it's habit. Unless it's the muscle memory of an affection that's already over, the way you keep walking to the old bus stop for a week after they move the route. "You're quiet," she says. Here it is. This is the door opening. And I have a choice, and I can feel both options in my mouth at once — the true one, which is *I have been convinced for three days that you're done with me and I have written both of our lines,* and the safe one, which is a shrug and a *long week.* "Long week," I say. She looks at me. She has this way of looking that goes on one beat past comfortable. "Is it about me being rubbish at texting?" And I laugh, because what else, and I say "No," and she says "Because I *was*," and she says: "I kept opening your messages when I had thirty seconds and no brain and then I felt bad about not answering properly and then I didn't answer at all. Which is the stupidest possible system." There it is. The exact, mundane, unglamorous truth. Handed over freely, unprompted, before I even had to ask. She *noticed*. She thought about how it might land for me. She came here with an explanation in her pocket like she'd brought a spare key. And I feel it — the flood, the relief, so enormous it's nauseating, and underneath it a hot little wire of shame, because I built a whole courtroom this afternoon and put her in the dock and she showed up with *flowers*. *So you were wrong. So you're always wrong. So you'll be wrong again next Tuesday and you still won't believe it.* "That's okay," I say. "Honestly, I barely noticed." And I hear myself say it — the small, petty, protective lie, the door pulled two inches closed — and I watch something flicker across her face, some tiny recalibration, and I think: *don't, take it back, tell her,* and I think: *good. Now she knows I don't need it.* She squeezes my knee again anyway. I don't know how long I get to keep this. I don't know how to want it without also, quietly, beginning to grieve it. She's here. She's *here*, right now, warm hand, tired eyes, orange flowers in the good jug — and some part of me is already rehearsing the day she isn't, because if I get the lines right in advance, maybe it won't be able to kill me.

+ Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 87.2
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Debt The temple had lost its roof three generations ago. What remained was a rectangle of packed earth thirty feet on a side, bounded by four walls of gray stone, the southern one collapsed into a ramp of rubble that served as the entrance. Above, the night hung open and moonless. Someone had wedged oil lamps into the wall niches where statues once sat, and the light they threw was orange and unsteady, so that the shadows of the men crowding the perimeter swayed like water. Sixty spectators, maybe seventy. They stood on the rubble, on the low remains of the altar platform at the north end, on each other's shoulders. Coins changed hands in the dark. Two knots of men had formed—one clustered west, one east—and the air between them tasted of insult. Kurosawa Shin stood at the north end with his back to the ruined altar. Twenty-four years old, tall for it, his shoulders squared as if being measured. Around his left bicep he wore the red-and-black armband of Jigen-ryū, tied tight enough to press a ridge into the muscle. His feet were bare on the cold earth. He had bound his hands with strips of cloth and nothing else. He was not warming up. He simply stood, breathing low into his belly, watching the man at the far end of the yard with the flat attention of someone appraising livestock. Fifty feet south, Lin Baoshan crouched on his heels at the base of the rubble ramp, rolling his shoulders in slow circles until the joints popped. He was shorter, thicker through the chest, and his arms hung long and loose as rope. His armband—the same red and black, the pattern reversed—was frayed at one edge. He had earned it in an alley behind a rice broker's warehouse, which he considered a better provenance than any dojo. He spat, stood, and shook his hands out at the wrists until the fingers flapped. No referee. No bow. A man on the altar struck a broken tile with a stone, once. Shin closed the distance in four steps and attacked on the fourth. It was the Jigen-ryū opening: no feint, no measuring, everything committed forward at once. His right fist drove out from beneath his own jaw in a rising line toward Lin's throat, the whole mass of him behind it, back foot scraping a furrow in the dirt. The west knot of spectators roared. Lin was not there. He had stepped left—not back, *left*, a short crossing shuffle that took him off the line by eighteen inches—and Shin's fist passed his ear close enough to move his hair. Lin's left arm came over the top like a dropped chain, the hand loose, and the back of it slapped across Shin's right eyebrow. Shin's head snapped sideways. The sound of it carried to the walls. He recovered before Lin could follow. That was the thing about Jigen-ryū—it did not know how to be hurt, only how to answer. Shin pivoted on his front foot, squared, and threw a horizontal elbow at the place Lin's temple had been. Lin was already circling, and Shin's elbow cut empty air. Lin's circling was clockwise from Shin's perspective, always toward Shin's right, always toward the arm that had just extended and had not yet come home. Shin adjusted. He stopped chasing and instead cut the circle, stepping diagonally to intercept. It worked. Lin came around into him and Shin caught him with a straight left to the sternum that folded Lin at the waist and drove him back four feet onto the flagstones near the eastern wall. The east knot went silent. The west howled. Lin came up wheezing and grinning, which was the worst thing he could have done to Shin's composure. Shin came in again, and this time he did not stop. Three strikes in under a second: right cross, left hook, right vertical fist, each thrown from a full hip rotation, each meant to end things. The first Lin absorbed on his shoulder. The second he ducked under. The third caught him high on the cheekbone and split the skin. But ducking the second had put Lin low and inside, and Piguaquan lives inside. Coming up out of the crouch, Lin's right arm whipped from below—not a punch but a *swing*, the arm relaxed until the last instant, the palm arriving like the end of a flail—and struck Shin under the floating ribs on the right side. Shin's breath left him in a bark. He tried to step back and Lin stepped with him, staying glued to his right flank, and the left arm came over in the same overhand chopping arc as before, this time onto the side of Shin's neck. Then the right again, backhanded, across the mouth. Then the left, and the sound was wet. Three feet from the eastern wall, Shin's heel found rubble and he stumbled. Lin drove a low kick into the outside of his lead thigh and Shin went down onto one knee. The crowd surged. Someone was screaming a number—odds, a debt, it didn't matter. Lin came in to finish and Shin threw his forearm up blind. It caught Lin's descending arm at the elbow, and in the half-instant that bought him, Shin exploded upward from the knee. This was the thing his master had drilled into him for eleven years: rise as a strike. His crown caught Lin under the chin. Lin went backward, fully off his feet, and landed flat on the stones with his arms wide. Shin stood over him, bleeding from mouth and eyebrow, ribs grinding, and raised his fist for the killing blow to the throat. Lin's leg swept his ankle out from under him. Shin fell hard on his shoulder and Lin rolled onto him and put his elbow twice into Shin's jaw, and then a third time, and Shin's hands, which had been reaching for Lin's collar, opened and did not close again. Lin got up in stages. He walked to the center of the yard, turned once so both sides could see, and then sat down in the dirt because his legs would not hold him. The east knot came over the rubble like a wave. The west did not move at all. And on the ramp, in the dark, two old men who had each forbidden this stood ten feet apart and did not look at one another, and understood that nothing had been settled, and that it never would be.

The author successfully creates a vivid, atmospheric setting in the ruined temple with effective environmental details like the missing roof, oil lamps in statue niches, and the specific dimensions that ground the reader spatially. The fight choreography is exceptionally well-handled, meeting the prompt's demanding requirement for "absolute physical coherence." Each movement is clearly tracked - from Shin's four-step approach and Lin's eighteen-inch sidestep to the specific positioning near walls and the final ground sequence. The author demonstrates genuine understanding of both martial arts styles, with Jigen-ryū's explosive directness contrasting effectively against Piguaquan's circular, evasive nature. Character differentiation is achieved efficiently through physical description, fighting style, and brief backstory elements. The class tension between the elite samurai tradition and the street-fighter background adds meaningful subtext without becoming heavy-handed. The characterizations feel authentic to their respective martial traditions. The prose style is notably restrained and precise, avoiding flowery language while maintaining strong imagery. Sentences like "His crown caught Lin under the chin" and "Lin went backward, fully off his feet" demonstrate clean, impactful writing. The pacing builds effectively through the fight sequence, with shorter sentences during intense exchanges. The ending provides satisfying resolution while acknowledging the deeper, unresolvable nature of the generational conflict. The image of the two masters standing apart, understanding "nothing had been settled," adds appropriate weight and complexity. Minor weaknesses include some repetitive sentence structures and a few moments where the clinical precision of the fight description slightly distances the reader from the emotional stakes. The piece also relies heavily on physical action rather than exploring the psychological dimensions of the conflict, though this may be appropriate for the genre and length constraints. Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Breaking Formation The studio is thirty feet by fifty, mirrors on the north wall, barre along the south, and four speakers bolted into the ceiling corners so the beat hits you from every diagonal at once, one notch past comfortable. Back home we ran a single blown-out JBL on a milk crate outside Marcus's bodega and I could still hear my own breathing. Here I can't hear anything but the click track, and the click track does not breathe. I'm in the third row, second from the left. Eleven other trainees. We stand in a 3-4-4 wedge, and I've been told—twice—that my position is 1.2 meters behind Yerin and 1.2 meters to the right of Junho, and that the distance is not approximate. Instructor Baek Sunwoo enters at count zero of nothing. She doesn't announce herself. She walks to the northwest corner, where she can see both the mirror and the raw bodies at the same time, and she raises two fingers. The track drops. Sixteen counts of intro: right arm punches to the ceiling on the one, retracts to a 90-degree elbow at the sternum on the two, left mirrors it on the three-four. It's a *point* choreography, all hard angles, all *stop*. Every limb is supposed to arrive at its destination and die there. Twelve bodies freezing into the same silhouette so the camera reads one animal with twenty-four arms. My arm punches up on the one. On the two it retracts—and my wrist rolls. Just a little. A ripple runs shoulder to fingertip, the way it's rolled ten thousand times on concrete, because in my body a stop isn't a stop, it's a *catch*, it's the loose slack you leave so the next move can steal momentum from the last one. Waving. It's *waving*. It's what I do. "Stop." Music cuts. Twelve bodies hold. My arm is the only crooked line in the mirror and I can see it from here, second row from the back, that soft curve where everyone else has a hinge. She walks the diagonal from the northwest corner, past the front row, past Yerin, and stops at 45 centimeters from my right shoulder. She doesn't look at my face. She looks at my elbow. "What is this." "It's—" My Korean is nine months old and lives mostly in my mouth like a stone. "Um. Habit. Buseo—" "English is fine." Her English is better than mine. Of course it is. Her English cost money. "This," she taps the outside of my forearm with one knuckle, "is beautiful. And it is late. You arrive on the two-and. Everyone else arrives on the two. You understand what that makes you?" "Late." "It makes you *visible*." She says it like a diagnosis. "Again. From the top." --- By the fortieth run my shirt has stopped being a shirt and started being weather. We're on the chorus block now, the one that killed three trainees last month, and it goes: Count 1—drop to a right-knee lunge, left leg extended west, torso square to the mirror. Count 2—snap the head 90 degrees stage-left. Count 3-4—rise on the ball of the right foot, quarter-turn clockwise, arms crossing at the wrists in front of the pelvis. Count 5—arms fly open to a T. Count 6-7-8—three lateral chest pops, traveling one step east on each, so all twelve of us slide across the floor like beads on the same wire. The lunge I can do. The lunge is just a freeze, and freezes I've held on cardboard in November. It's counts 6-7-8 that break me. Chest pops with lateral travel means isolating the ribcage while the feet run a clean, even, metronomic slide, and my feet don't slide even, my feet *play*. On seven my right foot drags a little Brazilian scuff and my hips answer it, and suddenly I'm doing something that would get me hollered at back home, and here it means the line bends. Twelve beads on a wire and one bead has gone rogue and now the whole wire looks broken. "Stop." Silence. Air conditioning. Somebody's swallow. She's in front of the mirror now, at the north wall, addressing my reflection instead of me, which is somehow worse. "You have something they don't have," she says, and the whole room stiffens because praise from her comes wrapped in a blade. "You have *weight*. Your movement has consequence. Everything they do, they do because I told them. Everything you do, you do because something happened to you." She turns around. "And it is worthless here. Do you know why?" I know why. I've known why since the first day, when I walked into a lobby with a marble floor and eleven kids whose sneakers cost more than my flight, and I understood in one breath that this building is a factory that makes a product, and the product is *sameness that photographs well*. "Because you can't sell twelve of me," I say. Her mouth does something that isn't a smile. "Because you cannot yet *choose*. You don't move that way. You move that way because you don't know how not to. That is not style. That is a limp." She lifts her chin. "Style is when you can do it correctly and refuse." --- She restarts the track. I take the lunge on one, and here is the moment, right here, at count 5 with my arms opening to a T and the beat coming at me from four ceiling corners like walls closing: I can let my body do what it wants and be honest and be gone by Friday, or I can bolt every joint shut and stop being the thing that got me on the plane. Counts 6-7-8. I nail them. Ribcage isolated—pop, pop, pop—feet flat, even, dead metronomic, no scuff, no hip, three clean steps east, and I land shoulder-to-shoulder in a line so straight it hurts, and I *feel* my body flinch like something got taken from it. Then, on the final held pose—count 8-and, the one-beat freeze before the bridge, the beat that belongs to nobody—I let my wrist roll. One inch. A ripple down to two fingers. Late on purpose. Music runs on. Nobody stops it. In the mirror, from the northwest corner, Instructor Baek is watching me. And she nods once, hard, like a hammer setting a nail.

Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.

**THE COURT OF THE DREAMING** *In the Matter of Dreamscape 44,891-B ("The Wildflower Field")* The courtroom had no walls, only the suggestion of them. A single hourglass the height of three men stood behind the bench, dripping sand that shimmered as it fell and made a sound like distant applause. When it emptied, the session would end. It had been dripping for four hundred years and was not yet half done. Dream of the Endless sat very still, which was how he sat when he was annoyed. "Read the complaint." Lucien, who had been pressed into service as clerk because Merv had refused on the grounds that he was a pumpkin, not a paralegal, adjusted his spectacles. "The petitioner, styling itself First Love, alleges unlawful entry, structural alteration, and predatory feeding within a registered recurring dreamscape belonging to one Maximilian Kovar, aged thirteen, of Bratislava." "And the respondent?" A shape uncoiled from the shadows beneath the gallery. It resolved, more or less, into a woman — pale as a drowned moon, black hair to her ankles, a smile with too much confidence in it. "Mora," she said. "No surname. Nightmare spirit, freelance." "Freelance," Dream repeated. "Independent contractor." "Sit down." She did not sit so much as arrange herself, draping across the respondent's bench like spilled ink. First Love stepped forward. He was a plump, rosy-cheeked entity in a waistcoat two sizes too tight, holding a bundle of documents tied with ribbon. His ears were scarlet. His ears were always scarlet. "My lord," he began, and immediately dropped the documents. The court waited while he gathered them. "My lord. Dreamscape 44,891-B represents four years of work. *Four years.* The field is Slovakian wildflower, seasonally accurate — cornflower, poppy, wild chamomile. The light is late afternoon, angled at eleven degrees for maximum melancholy. The girl is a composite: her name is Zuzana, but her laugh belongs to a cousin the boy met once at a funeral, which produces a very specific ache—" "You may skip the artistry." "...Yes. Well. The dream culminates in an almost-kiss. *Almost.* The boy wakes flushed, unsure what happened, and spends the day looking at his desk. That's the *point*. That's the *whole point*. He carries that not-knowing for sixty years. On his deathbed he thinks about the eleven degrees." "And now?" First Love's voice cracked. "Now she *sits on him.*" Mora raised a hand. "In fairness—" "You *sit on him* and *drink his breath.*" "In fairness, so did the girl. Sitting-wise. That was already in the script." "She sat *playfully*. It was a moment of *charged tumbling*—" "And I refined it." Dream's fingers tightened very slightly on the arm of his chair. Somewhere in the outer Dreaming, a thousand sleepers turned over at once. "Respondent will state her case." Mora sat up. To her credit, she did not appear frightened, which either meant she was brave or had not been paying attention. "Look. I've been working the Carpathians for eleven hundred years. Chest-sitting, breath-drinking, the standard package. Sleep paralysis, terror, the whole thing. But people don't sleep in villages anymore, they sleep in apartments with white noise machines and little pills. My catchment area has collapsed. Do you know how hard it is to find a boy who *isn't* medicated?" "This does not address the trespass." "I'm getting there. So I'm walking the borderlands, starving, and I find this — this *pastry* of a dream. Unlocked. No wards, no seals, no nothing." She pointed at First Love. "He didn't even put a *lock* on it." "It's a *field*," said First Love, wounded. "You don't lock a *field*." "And I'm not saying I broke anything. I'm saying I *inherited* an opportunity. The boy's already lying flat on his back with his heart pounding and a woman climbing on top of him. Ninety percent of my work was *done*. I just added the teeth." "You added teeth." "Some teeth. And the neck extends now, which I'll admit is a choice." Dream said nothing for eleven seconds. The sand fell. "You do not deny feeding." "A girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Mora shrugged. "He's not dead. He's not even thin. Kid had two rolls at breakfast." "He's *ruined*," said First Love. "He looked at Zuzana Vargová in the corridor on Tuesday and he *flinched*." "He looked, though." "He *flinched.*" "He looked *for a long time.*" Dream raised one finger and the argument stopped as though guillotined. He regarded the pair of them: the trembling confectioner and the smiling predator. Somewhere further down his docket were three genuine incursions from the Nightmare Wing, an unresolved boundary matter with the Fashion Thing, and a raven who wished to discuss his contract. Instead, this. He was tempted — and he noted the temptation with the mild interest of a man observing weather — to give the field to Mora entirely, and to let First Love build his eleven-degree light somewhere the boy would never sleep. To see what a man became if his first love had fangs and sat on his ribs. It would be *interesting*. Some of his best subjects had been made that way. But Dream was, among other things, a functionary. "Judgment," he said. Lucien lifted his pen. "Dreamscape 44,891-B remains the property of the petitioner. Title is not transferred by improvement. However—" First Love's face fell open with relief and then closed again with dread. "However, the respondent's alterations are not without merit. Dreams that are only pleasant are not remembered. They are merely enjoyed." Mora grinned. "Therefore. The respondent is granted a tenancy. One night in seven. On that night she may sit, and she may feed, and she may extend the neck." "Six degrees," said Mora immediately. "Eleven," said Dream. "The light is not negotiable." "Fine." "Further: the petitioner will install wards on all remaining properties within a year, at his own expense, and will cease describing his work as *artistry* in these chambers. And the respondent will register. There will be a form." Mora's grin faltered. "A form." "Several forms." "I'd rather starve." "That option remains available." The hourglass dripped. Dream rose, and the courtroom rose with him, and the walls stopped suggesting themselves. "Also," he said, without turning, "the boy is to be permitted one kiss. In sixty years. At the funeral." First Love began, quietly, to weep. "Court is adjourned."

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional craft in executing a complex prompt that demanded a delicate balance of dark fantasy, comedy, and courtroom drama. The author successfully captures the voice and tone of Neil Gaiman's Sandman universe while creating an original scenario that feels authentic to that world. The characterization is particularly strong. Dream's barely contained irritation comes through in subtle details like his stillness when annoyed and the image of "a thousand sleepers turned over at once" when his fingers tighten. Mora is rendered as confidently amoral rather than evil, with her practical "a girl's gotta eat" defense feeling genuinely character-driven. First Love's earnest, flustered nature creates genuine pathos beneath the comedy. The dialogue crackles with wit and authenticity. Exchanges like Mora's "Independent contractor" response to Dream's flat "Freelance" repetition demonstrate excellent comedic timing. The legal proceedings feel both fantastical and grounded in recognizable courtroom dynamics. The prose style is admirably restrained, following the instruction to use descriptives sparingly while still creating vivid imagery. Lines like "She did not sit so much as arrange herself, draping across the respondent's bench like spilled ink" are economical yet evocative. The dark comedy emerges naturally from the situation rather than feeling forced. The bureaucratic elements (forms, registration requirements) provide humor while serving the world-building. The resolution is particularly clever, giving both parties partial victory while maintaining Dream's character as someone who finds mortal concerns tedious yet is bound by cosmic duty. The ending strikes an appropriately bittersweet note with First Love weeping and the revelation about the funeral kiss, avoiding both saccharine positivity and grimdark excess. The piece maintains narrative momentum throughout without meandering, and the 1000-word constraint is used effectively to create a complete, satisfying story. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the comedy could be more understated, and some dialogue exchanges that, while good, don't quite reach the heights of the best moments. However, these are minor quibbles with what is overall an accomplished piece of writing. Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. Model Output:
# Blood Moon A broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates, hinting at a hurried departure. Yennefer steps over it, her boots finding the mud that the fleeing peasants churned into soup. Nothing moves. The doors hang open like slack mouths. Somewhere a shutter knocks against a wall in the wind, patient as a heartbeat. She smells it before she sees anything: blood, gone cold and sweet, and beneath it something worse. Not rot. *Absence.* A hole in the world where a thing should be. "You may as well come out," she says, to the empty street. "You've been watching me since the treeline." Laughter answers her — everywhere at once, from the eaves and the well and the dark inside a doorway, as though the village itself has developed a sense of humor. He unfolds from the shadow of the church wall. Red coat like arterial spray. A ridiculous hat. Small orange lenses that catch the light of the low moon and hold it, unwilling to give it back. "Since the treeline," Alucard agrees. "You walk like a woman who owns the ground. I wanted to see how long it would last." "Longer than your village, apparently." Yennefer doesn't look away from him, but she counts: three exits behind her, a stone wall to her left she could bring down, the well with its water she could freeze or boil. She has never in her life entered a room without doing arithmetic. "Did you eat them?" "Some. Something else ate some. That's why I came." He tips his head, and the movement is wrong — too fluid, as if his neck has more joints than a neck ought to. "A brood of children playing at damnation. They hid in a cellar and shrieked when I opened the door. Pathetic. Vampires who fear the dark are an insult to the dark." "And you are — what? Its representative?" "Its favorite son." He smiles, and there are far too many teeth. "You smell of lilac." "You smell of a charnel house." "Yes." Delighted. As though she's complimented his tailoring. She lifts her hand — an idle gesture, unhurried, and a sphere of blue-white light kindles above her palm, throwing the street into hard relief. Every wall leaps back. Every shadow flees. Alucard's shadow does not flee. It spreads. "Interesting," she says. "Very," he says. They circle. Neither of them decides to; it simply happens, the way two blades find each other's measure. Yennefer keeps the light burning because it costs her almost nothing and because she wants him to believe it costs her almost nothing. Alucard walks with his hands empty and open, which she recognizes for what it is: not trust. Advertising. *I don't need them.* "You're not a witcher," he says. "They stink of onions and self-pity." "I'm a sorceress." "I've known sorcerers. Little men with little books, bargaining with things they couldn't pronounce. Vlad's court was full of them." His grin widens. "They screamed in Latin. It's not a beautiful language for screaming." "How long ago?" "Long enough that the language has changed and I haven't." She stops. So does he, six paces off, and the six paces feel like a decision they've made together. "Centuries," she says. "You want me to be impressed." "I want you to be *honest.*" The lenses tilt. "You're old. I can hear it. Your blood doesn't move like a young woman's. It's patient. Cold at the edges. You've had a very long time to learn to lie with your face." Something in Yennefer's chest closes like a fist. She lets nothing reach her expression — she has practiced that face in mirrors older than most kingdoms — but he laughs anyway, low and pleased, and she understands that he heard the fist close. That he hears everything. That she is standing in front of a creature who reads her by the traffic in her veins. So she does the only thing that has ever worked for her. She steps *toward* him. "Then hear this," she says. "I have been unmade and remade. I chose what I am, down to the bone, and it hurt more than anything you could do to me. You think you frighten me because you're a monster." She is close enough now to see the seams where his face is only *pretending*. "I've been a monster. I simply had better taste in the shape." For a moment — a real moment, a fracture — the grin drops off him. Underneath, there is nothing so simple as hunger. There is something starved and ancient and terribly, terribly bored. "Say that again," Alucard breathes. "No." His shadow moves. It comes up around her ankles like black water, and inside it she sees eyes — dozens, hundreds, opening in the dark, and dogs' mouths, and the shapes of people who used to be. Her heart lurches. She lets it. She lets him hear it, because a woman with no fear is a woman with nothing to bargain with, and she has been trading in fear since she was fourteen years old and hunchbacked and drowning in a well. Yennefer speaks three words. The shadow does not retreat — but it *stops*, hissing against a wall of air that smells of gooseberries and ozone, and she holds it there, and her arm does not tremble. "You can't kill me," Alucard says conversationally, from inside the dark. "No," she agrees. "But I can inconvenience you for a hundred years. Which, for you, may be worse." The eyes close. The shadow folds back into a man's silhouette, obedient as a hound. He straightens his hat. "Come with me," he says. "There's a cellar full of cowards. I'd like a witness who won't faint." "I have somewhere to be." "Everyone does." He walks past her, close enough that his coat brushes her sleeve, and he does not look back. "The bird of Hermes is my name, sorceress. Eating my wings to make me tame." "Poetry," Yennefer says. "How disappointing." But she follows him — three paces behind, light still burning, arithmetic still running — and above the ruined village the moon comes up red, and neither of them looks away first.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated character work and atmospheric writing that successfully captures both characters' essences while creating a compelling encounter. The author shows strong command of voice, maintaining consistent characterization for both Alucard and Yennefer throughout their tense meeting. The opening immediately establishes mood through vivid imagery - the abandoned cart wheel, mud "churned into soup," and doors "like slack mouths" - creating an effectively ominous atmosphere. The author skillfully uses sensory details, particularly Yennefer's detection of "absence" rather than mere rot, which feels authentically supernatural. Character portrayal is notably strong. Alucard's predatory playfulness comes through in lines like his delight at being called a charnel house, while his ancient boredom and search for worthy opponents drives the interaction. Yennefer's calculating nature is well-captured through her constant tactical assessment and refusal to show weakness. The power dynamic shifts naturally as promised, with neither character dominating completely. The dialogue crackles with tension and personality. Exchanges like "You smell of lilac" / "You smell of a charnel house" / "Yes" capture both characters perfectly - his monstrous pride and her sharp wit. The conversation feels organic while advancing both plot and character development. The prose strikes an effective balance between literary sophistication and accessibility. Phrases like "shadow does not retreat - but it stops, hissing against a wall of air" demonstrate strong technical skill without becoming overwrought. The writing maintains consistent third-person present tense as requested. The piece successfully avoids common pitfalls. There are no unearned character transformations - both remain true to their natures while revealing new facets. The ending maintains appropriate tension rather than forcing false resolution. The encounter feels complete while leaving their relationship unresolved, which suits both characters. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose edges toward purple ("arterial spray," "favorite son of darkness"), though these generally serve the gothic atmosphere. The pacing occasionally slows during descriptive passages, but not enough to significantly impact engagement. The story adheres well to instructions, delivering the requested medieval European setting, power dynamic shifts, and character interactions. At approximately 1000 words, it meets length requirements while feeling complete rather than truncated. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. Model Output:
Chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by. Not from wind — Green Dolphin Street Prison has no wind worth the name in August, only heat that sits on the concrete like a wet animal. The fences rattle because something in this place recognizes the people walking past it, and shivers. Jolyne Cujoh notices. She notices everything now. Six months inside has sanded her instincts down to a point. The new arrival walks the perimeter path with her hands folded in front of her, orange jumpsuit somehow pressed, auburn hair catching the light. She doesn't sweat. That's the first thing. Everyone in this yard is glazed with it, shirts stuck to spines, and this woman moves through the heat like she's being carried. "Hello," the woman says, stopping in front of Jolyne's bench. Her eyes are yellow with rings in them, concentric, like something dropped a stone in each iris. "You're Jolyne Cujoh. Everyone here talks about you." "That's flattering. Who's everyone?" "The guards. The chaplain. A woman named Gwess." A soft smile. "I'm Makima. I hope we can be friends." Jolyne's hand, resting on her knee, has already begun to fray. Just the tip of her index finger, unspooling into a single strand of pale thread, running down along the bench leg and into the dust. Stone Free doesn't ask permission anymore. It reacts to her gut, and her gut is screaming. "Friends," Jolyne repeats. "Sure. Let's be friends. What're you in for?" "A misunderstanding." Makima sits down beside her, uninvited, close. "And you?" "Murder I didn't do." "Then we're the same." *No we're not,* Jolyne thinks, and the thread creeps another inch through the dust. Because here's the thing about liars: Jolyne has met professionals. Her father hunted the worst of them. She's learned that the amateurs oversell, and the professionals underplay, and the truly dangerous ones don't perform at all — they simply *are* what you want them to be, seamlessly, without effort, the way water is the shape of the glass. This woman's kindness has no seams. It's manufactured all the way down. "You've got an unusual soul," Makima says pleasantly. "It has strings coming off it." Jolyne's blood goes cold in the ninety-degree heat. "Most people," Makima continues, watching a group of inmates shuffle past the fence — *rattle, rattle* — "have nothing interesting attached. But you unravel, don't you? You come apart into thread and you keep thinking while you're apart. That's remarkable. Where does the thinking happen, I wonder, when you're spread over twenty meters? Is the thinking in every strand?" "Ask my lawyer." "I'd like to keep you," Makima says, in exactly the same tone. "I have a great many pets. Some of them are devils, some are people. They're happier on the leash than off it, in my experience. It's restful, not deciding things." Jolyne laughs — short, ugly, real. "Lady, you have *no idea* how badly you just misjudged the room." "Kneel." The word lands like a hand on the back of her neck. It isn't sound. It goes *around* sound. Jolyne feels her spine try to fold, feels her kneecaps aim themselves at the concrete, feels her own body agree with something it never agreed to — and this, *this*, is the moment where being Jotaro Kujo's daughter matters. Not the tough talk. Not the fists. The stubbornness. The single black nail of a will that says *no* to physics itself. Her knees stop half-bent. Her teeth grind. "Oh," says Makima, and for the first time something genuine surfaces in her face: interest. Bright, appetitive, awful. "You're above me? No — no, you're not. You just don't *know* you're beneath me yet. That happens sometimes. It only makes the arrangement take longer." "Here's what's happening," Jolyne grunts, and stands up straight. "You came in here to shop. Guards, inmates, whatever's chained up in the psych ward. You found a whole warehouse of desperate people and you're picking out favorites." "That's a very cynical way to describe helping." "I got a cynical way to describe everything." Jolyne spreads her fingers. "*Stone Free.*" The Stand doesn't punch. That's the thing Makima expects — Jolyne can see her expecting it, weight shifting to accept a blow, that immortal calm. Instead, Jolyne's left arm comes apart into thread, hundreds of strands, and the strands are already *everywhere*, because she started unspooling four minutes ago while pretending to be bored. Threads through the dust. Threads up the fence posts. Threads laced through the chain-link in a hundred places, in a fifty-meter arc around this bench, tied off and tensioned like a harp. Makima looks around. Understands. Her smile does something complicated. "You mapped the yard." "I mapped *the whole damn prison,* every day, since May." Jolyne tugs, and the fences all scream at once — *rattle rattle RATTLE* — and every inmate in the yard turns to look at the two of them, forty pairs of eyes suddenly witnesses. "See, I don't know what you are. Maybe I can't kill you. My old man taught me something better: you don't beat a thing like you by punching it. You take away the dark." "...You're making yourself public." "I'm making *you* public. Every guard, every camera, every mouth in this yard. Whatever you do to me, forty people watch you do it, and forty people go tell it. You can't own a room you're standing in the middle of." Jolyne's grin is all teeth, sweat running down her temple, one knee still trembling from the word *kneel*. "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney. And you? You're not Mickey. You're the guy in the suit trying to convince the kids the mouse is real." For three long seconds Makima says nothing. Somewhere beyond the fence a dog barks, and Jolyne has the sick certainty it barked because it was told to. Then Makima folds her hands again, sweet as a hymn. "I'll be here for a while, Jolyne. Sooner or later, you'll want something from me. Everyone does." She rises, brushes nothing from her jumpsuit. "It's alright. I'm patient with dogs that bite." She walks off down the perimeter path. The fences rattle as she passes. Jolyne, reeling her string back into her arm strand by strand, notices that they rattle *louder*.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character understanding. The author successfully captures both characters' essences - Jolyne's street-smart defiance and Makima's manipulative control - while creating a tense psychological confrontation that feels authentic to both source materials. The prose quality is notably high, with evocative imagery like "heat that sits on the concrete like a wet animal" and "fences rattle because something in this place recognizes the people walking past it." The writing maintains a consistent noir-tinged tone that suits the prison setting while incorporating supernatural elements naturally. Character portrayal is particularly strong. Jolyne's immediate suspicion and tactical thinking align perfectly with her established personality, while her use of Stone Free as a surveillance network rather than a direct weapon shows creative understanding of her abilities. Makima's false sweetness masking predatory intent is captured effectively, and her "kneel" command demonstrates her power while respecting Jolyne's inherited Joestar willpower. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, with Jolyne's crude directness ("If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!") contrasting sharply with Makima's deceptively gentle manipulation. The escalation from pleasantries to psychological warfare unfolds naturally. The story's central conceit - that Jolyne defeats Makima not through force but by removing her ability to operate in shadows - is both clever and character-appropriate. It shows understanding that Makima's power relies on isolation and secrecy. However, the piece occasionally veers toward purple prose, particularly in atmospheric descriptions. Some metaphors, while evocative, border on overwrought. The ending, while satisfying, resolves perhaps too neatly given Makima's established persistence and power. The pacing is excellent, building tension steadily through small details before exploding into confrontation. The author successfully balances exposition with action, never letting either character explanation or plot advancement overwhelm the narrative flow. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 89.1
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**SCP-████ — "Marginalia"** **Personal Log Compilation, Researcher Aiden Vosk, Site-19** **Classification pending. Do not archive without O5 sign-off.** --- I found the first note on 14 March, tucked inside my containment log for SCP-████-B, on a page I had signed and sealed the previous evening. My handwriting. Not an imitation of it — *mine*, including the way I close my lowercase g with a hook I have never seen anyone else produce. > *Do not open Chamber 4 on the 19th. It doesn't matter what Dr. Halloran says. It doesn't matter what the schedule says. Four dead. One of them is you. — A.V.* I reported it within the hour, because that is what the procedure says to do, and because I still believed procedure was a shield. Site security pulled the corridor footage. Nobody entered my office between 22:40 and 06:15. The seal on the log was intact; the note was *beneath* the seal. Dr. Halloran, to her credit, did not laugh. She confiscated the note and ordered a full sweep of my quarters, my terminal, and my person. Chamber 4 was not opened on the 19th. Nothing happened. This proved nothing, and everyone in the room knew it. --- The second note came on the 23rd, folded inside my glasses case. > *Good. Thank you. But it only moved. Now it's the 4th of April and it comes through the water reclamation line, not the door. Tell them to weld the grate. They won't. Tell them anyway. I'm sorry about the way you'll find out about Marta.* I do not have a Marta. I have never known a Marta. I checked the Foundation personnel index for every Marta in the organization's history and found eleven, none of whom I had met. The grate was welded. The 4th of April passed without incident. Halloran began referring to the phenomenon as "your correspondent," a phrase I came to hate. --- Analysis, Materials Division, Report 4471-A: *Ink composition inconsistent across samples. All samples contain iron gall base with trace concentrations of thallium, hafnium, and an isotopic ratio of lead (²⁰⁷Pb/²⁰⁶Pb = 0.7211) inconsistent with any terrestrial ore body catalogued to date. No Site-19 requisitioned writing implement produces this composition. No commercially available implement produces this composition. Paper stock matches Foundation internal supply, lot number ██-449 — a lot number not yet issued at time of recovery. Lot ██-449 entered circulation eleven days after Sample 1 was collected.* That last sentence is the one I read over and over. Everything else could be explained. Someone with a chemistry background and a grudge could have mixed the ink. Nobody could have printed the future's inventory numbers on the future's paper. --- The notes accelerated. Four in one week. Then nine. > *The breach starts in your own hand. I keep telling you that and you keep reading it as a metaphor.* > *They interviewed you on the 2nd and you lied about the dreams. Stop lying. Every hour you spend protecting your clearance is an hour I spend* The line ended there, mid-word, with a long tear in the paper as if the pen had been pulled away. > *There is no Chamber 4. There has never been a Chamber 4. Ask them. Watch their faces when you ask them.* I asked them. There is a Chamber 4. I have worked in it for two years. I have a small burn scar on my left wrist from an incident in Chamber 4 in the winter of 2019. That was the first day I understood that the notes were not simply warnings. They were doing something to me. After that note I could not walk into Chamber 4 without a physical sensation of *thinness*, as though the room had been recently invented and had not yet had time to accumulate its full weight of reality. --- Halloran convened a working group. There were, essentially, two hypotheses. **Hypothesis A (Temporal).** A causal-loop anomaly of the retro-informational class. Under this reading, a future iteration of me, existing in a timeline where the breach occurred, was transmitting warnings backward by an unknown mechanism. Each successful intervention altered the future, which altered the content of subsequent notes — accounting for the contradictions, the shifting dates, the "Marta" who was perhaps someone I would have met, in a version of my life that my own compliance had erased. Under Hypothesis A, the incoherence was not a symptom. It was *evidence*. A man shouting through a door that keeps changing shape. **Hypothesis B (Psychological).** SCP-████-B, the entity in Chamber 4, is a memetic-cognitohazardous intelligence with documented capacity for inducing false-memory structures in personnel who maintain sustained observational contact. It had, over two years, learned me. It had learned my handwriting from a thousand hours of my logs. The notes were not messages from the future; they were a slow instrument for making me distrust the categories I use to sort real from unreal, so that when the moment came I would not be able to recognize a breach as a breach — or would perform one myself, believing I was preventing it. Hypothesis B accounted for everything except the ink and the paper. Hypothesis A accounted for the ink and the paper and nothing else. Dr. Ngo suggested, in a memo I found unforgivable and correct, that both could be true. That an entity capable of producing thallium-doped iron gall ink out of a sealed chamber would find the manufacture of a plausible future trivially easy. --- I was removed from Chamber 4 on 1 June. Amnestic treatment was declined; the working group determined that erasing my knowledge would only produce a subject who received the notes without context, which was worse. The notes did not stop when I was reassigned. They followed me to Site-45. They followed me into a Class-3 secure medical wing with no writing implements and no paper. > *You think the reassignment is a cure. It's a lens. Everything you did to get away from Chamber 4 is the road to Chamber 4. I have written this eleven thousand times. I don't know which one of me you're reading. Please* --- I am writing this compilation because I have been asked to, and because I have noticed something I have not yet told the working group, and I am putting it here so that it exists outside my skull, where things do not stay reliable. Three days ago I sat down to draft a note. Not to read one — to *write* one. A warning, dated forward, in my own hand, addressed to myself. I do not remember deciding to do this. I got as far as *Do not* before I recognized what my hand was doing and stopped. There was no pen in my quarters. I have not been issued one in five weeks. I would like the ink on that page analyzed. I would like to be told the isotopic ratio. I would like, very much, for it not to match.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP report demonstrates exceptional craft in both format adherence and psychological horror execution. The author successfully captures the clinical, bureaucratic tone of SCP documentation while weaving in deeply personal elements through the researcher's perspective. The piece maintains perfect consistency with SCP Foundation conventions, using appropriate redactions, classification headers, and interdisciplinary report structures. The narrative structure is particularly sophisticated, alternating between personal log entries, official reports, and the increasingly disturbing handwritten notes. This creates a multi-layered reading experience that mirrors the protagonist's fragmenting reality. The voice remains consistent throughout - clinical yet increasingly strained, maintaining professional detachment even as the researcher's world unravels. Character development is nuanced and believable. Vosk's responses feel authentic to someone in his position - following protocol initially, then growing increasingly paranoid and uncertain. His progression from confident reporting to desperate self-doubt is earned through accumulating evidence rather than sudden shifts. The supporting characters like Dr. Halloran feel real within their limited appearances. The central concept is genuinely creative, exploring temporal paradox through the lens of institutional paranoia. The two competing hypotheses (temporal anomaly vs. psychological manipulation) create genuine ambiguity that enhances rather than confuses the narrative. The author avoids easy answers, maintaining tension between rational and supernatural explanations. The prose is elegant and controlled, avoiding purple language while maintaining atmospheric dread. Technical details like isotopic ratios and chemical compositions add verisimilitude without overwhelming the narrative. The imagery is subtle but effective - the "thinness" of Chamber 4, the hook in the protagonist's handwriting, the pen being "pulled away" mid-sentence. The ending is particularly strong, with Vosk discovering himself unconsciously writing the notes. This revelation recontextualizes the entire narrative without feeling like a cheap twist. The final request for isotopic analysis creates a perfect note of dread - we suspect what the results will show, making the uncertainty more terrifying than revelation. Minor weaknesses include limited dialogue opportunities due to the format, though what exists feels natural. The piece occasionally borders on being slightly overwrought in its paranoia, but this serves the psychological horror effectively. The technical exposition is well-integrated and never feels like mere showing-off. **Item #:** SCP-████ **Object Class:** Euclid (Pending Reclassification) **Special Containment Procedures:** All confirmed instances of SCP-████ are to be sealed with reinforced steel plating and monitored by two (2) Foundation personnel under civilian cover. Municipal demolition orders for host structures are to be quietly delayed; three instances have demonstrated that destruction of the host building results in the instance relocating within 72 hours to another abandoned structure within a 400 km radius. Exploration of SCP-████-A ("the Archive") is currently **suspended** pending review by an oversight body external to the O5 Council. See Addendum ████-6. **Description:** SCP-████ designates a set of at least fifty-one (51) identical doors that have manifested in abandoned or condemned buildings across thirty-two countries. All instances are unmarked, unpainted hardwood of an unidentified species, fitted with brass hardware showing no manufacturer's marks. In every documented case, the door exhibits weathering inconsistent with its surroundings. An instance recovered from a 1978 apartment block in Kraków displayed grain erosion, hardware oxidation, and thermal cycling damage consistent with four to six centuries of exposure. The frames are seamlessly integrated into the host walls, with no evidence of installation. Dendrochronological analysis has failed; the growth rings do not correspond to any known regional climate sequence. Opening an instance reveals SCP-████-A, a contiguous interior space of indeterminate extent. Surveying teams have mapped 11.4 km of corridor without encountering an exterior wall, a fact irreconcilable with the fact that all instances open into the same location. Lighting is ambient and sourceless. Temperature is maintained at 18.5°C. Humidity control is active, implying maintenance. The Archive contains an estimated 40 million documents in ninety-one languages, thirty-eight of which remain unidentified. Roughly 12% are legible to Foundation linguists. --- **Recovered Document Excerpt 4-C** (translated from an unidentified Semitic-adjacent script; paper stock dated to no known period): > ...and so the ninth protocol was ratified, that no record of the Cause should be entered into any archive, catalogue, or memorial, lest the record itself become instruction. We write instead of the effect: eleven cities in the first hour. The rest by the fourth season. It is agreed that the failure originated in Site of the Southern Ordering, and that the failure was **ours**. **Recovered Document Excerpt 11-A** (English, typeset, paper stock dated 1600–1750 by two independent labs): > The Assembly of Custodians affirms: we did not fail through ignorance. We failed through the belief that the Assembly could not fail. Therefore the succeeding Assembly shall be built to believe itself fallible, and shall be given no memory of us. It shall be given a different name. It shall be told it is the first. The phrase "Assembly of Custodians" appears in 2,300+ recovered documents in contexts structurally identical to Foundation operational literature: containment classification schemes (six tiers, of which "Custodial" and "Terminal" have no Foundation analogue), site nomenclature, mobile task force designations, and ethics committee minutes. --- ### Exploration Log ████-3 (Excerpt) MTF Iota-10 ("Paper Cuts"), four personnel, entry via Instance-17 (Detroit, MI). **02:11** — Team advances into Wing 6. Agent Vasquez reports shelving in this section is empty. Dust patterns indicate removal within the past 30 days. **02:26** — Sounds detected ahead: wheeled carts, low voices, an intermittent mechanical hiss. **02:31** — Team observes eleven (11) humanoid entities in full encapsulating suits. Suits are grey, seamless, with rectangular visors of smoked glass. No insignia. Entities are loading documents into unmarked containers and applying a red adhesive seal to emptied shelves. **02:33** — Agent Kohl attempts contact in English, then Russian. **02:33** — All entities cease activity simultaneously. Team leader Sgt. Okonkwo describes the reaction as "not startled. *Embarrassed.*" **02:34** — Entities abandon carts and withdraw down Corridor 6-F at a rapid walk. Pursuit attempted. Entities are not present at the corridor terminus. No side doors exist along the 90 m segment. **02:41** — Abandoned containers are found empty. Carts are found empty. Red seals have faded to nothing. **02:52** — Sgt. Okonkwo locates an intact shelf in an adjacent alcove designated "PERSONNEL — CUSTODIAL TIER — ACTIVE." Contents retrieved. --- The retrieved files number 3,114. Of these, 1,807 correspond by name, date of birth, biometric description, and psychological profile to **currently employed Foundation personnel**. Paper stock and ink for all files predate 1800. **Excerpt, File 2211-K:** > **OKONKWO, D.** — Assembly of Custodians, Field Retrieval, Tier 3. Assessed reliable. Recurrent nightmare motif: *long room, no windows.* Recommend no intervention. Subject has been recruited on four (4) prior occasions. Sgt. Okonkwo has requested reassignment. --- ### Addendum ████-6: Access Anomaly During inventory of the Instance-17 threshold, Researcher Aldana noted that the Archive's floor is composed of a fine pale dust which records footfalls indefinitely; prints do not degrade. A photographic survey of the entry vestibule was ordered to establish a baseline of authorized traffic. The survey identified 344 distinct sets of prints. Cross-referencing against boot-issue records and gait analysis produced the following: - 209 sets attributable to logged Foundation exploration teams. - 118 sets of unknown origin, all made by the same style of soft-soled shoe, all leading *outward* from deeper in the Archive toward the door. - 17 sets matching the gait signatures of five (5) sitting members of the O5 Council. The earliest of these seventeen predates SCP-████'s discovery by eleven years. A single note was recovered from a reading desk in Wing 1, handwritten on contemporary Foundation stationery. It is unsigned. Handwriting analysis returned a 96% match to a Council member whose identity is withheld from this file. > *Third time here. Still cannot decide whether to burn it or memorize it.* > > *The suits are not stealing the records. They are filing them. We are the ones who lost them.* > > *If the succeeding Assembly must believe itself fallible, then the correct action is obvious and I will not take it.* **Note from the Office of the Ethics Committee:** All Council access logs for the past decade have been requisitioned. Four have been returned marked *destroyed in routine cycle.* The Committee is aware of what that means.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry demonstrates strong adherence to the Foundation's clinical documentation style while weaving a compelling narrative of existential horror. The piece successfully fulfills all prompt requirements: unmarked doors in abandoned buildings, an impossible archive, references to a previous civilization's containment failure, personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago, exploration logs with fleeing hazmat entities, and evidence of unauthorized O5 visits. The writing maintains the characteristic SCP tone throughout - clinical, bureaucratic, yet increasingly unsettling. The author skillfully builds tension through the gradual revelation that the Foundation may be caught in a cyclical pattern of failure and rebirth. The concept that the "Assembly of Custodians" was deliberately designed to forget its predecessor creates a chilling philosophical horror that goes beyond simple anomalous phenomena. The exploration logs are particularly effective, with realistic team dynamics and the memorable detail of the entities appearing "embarrassed" rather than startled when discovered. This humanizes the mysterious figures while maintaining their otherworldly nature. The footprint analysis revelation is expertly deployed as a climactic twist that recontextualizes everything preceding it. Character actions feel authentic within the SCP universe - researchers following protocols, personnel requesting reassignment after disturbing discoveries, and the Ethics Committee's ominous final note. The recovered documents are convincingly written in different voices and time periods, showing strong attention to detail. The prose is clean and purposeful, avoiding unnecessary flourishes while maintaining engagement. The pacing builds effectively from mundane anomaly description to existential crisis. The ending strikes an appropriately dark note without feeling forced, as the implications naturally arise from the established facts. Some minor weaknesses include limited character development (though this is somewhat inherent to the SCP format) and the fact that certain revelations, while well-executed, follow somewhat predictable patterns for cosmic horror. However, the execution elevates familiar concepts through careful worldbuilding and attention to the Foundation's established mythology. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 88.0
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter Six: The Cloak The briefings had described Ottok's Third City as "stratified, with rigid endogamous castes corresponding to morphological lineage." I had read this three times on the voyage in, and once more in my quarters that morning, and when I walked out into the Underway at the fourth hour I understood that whoever wrote it had never gone down the stairs. I had gone against protocol, of course. The reception at the Prefecture would run until the sixth hour and my absence would be noted by someone whose business it was to note absences. But the Ekumen has never sent envoys to observe receptions. It sends them to observe worlds, and a world is not visible from a dais. The Underway was warm. Ottok's sun is small and orange and gives little heat, but the city is built into the flank of a young mountain that has not finished cooling, and the lower avenues are heated from beneath by the planet itself. So the people of the Underway wear almost nothing: a hip-wrap, a sling for tools or infants, sometimes a beaded collar denoting trade guild. I wore my traveling cloak, grey, ankle-length, closed at the throat. Within a hundred paces I had learned what the cloak meant. It meant I was cold, and being cold on Ottok means you are recently arrived from above, or offworld, or ill. Children pointed. An old woman selling pressed cakes at the mouth of the fifth stair reached out and rubbed the fabric between two fingers, unhurried, as one tests cloth in a market, and said something to her neighbor that made them both laugh, not unkindly. I could not follow it. My Ottoki was learned from recordings made forty years ago by a man who had spent his time entirely among the Prefecture staff. The briefings said: *four lineages, no intermarriage, no shared public space.* I stood at the fifth stair and counted. The cake-seller was Tulg: broad, short-limbed, the dense build of eleven generations in the high pressure of the deep galleries, with the flattened nasal bridge that filters the sulfur air. The man buying from her was some Tulg and some Hanne, unmistakably — the Hanne length of forearm, the pale lashless eyes bred in the dark of the ice-tunnels, but the Tulg chest. Their daughter, riding his hip in a sling, was something else again, and there was no word in my briefings for what she was. They were not supposed to exist. I watched them for a long while, and then I bought a cake, and it was very good, tasting of the mineral water they use and of something like anise, and I ate it walking, which I later learned was the vulgarest possible thing I could have done in that quarter and did more for my standing than a month of formal visits. The market of the sixth level was arranged by trade, not lineage. I checked this three times, walking the aisles. Metalworkers together, Tulg and Hanne and two of the tall attenuated Sesh whom I had been told never descend below the third level. Weavers together. In the food rows, families, and the families were mixed. There were quarters where they were not mixed; I found one, and it was small, and the people in it were wealthy, and their doors were watched. That, I thought, is what my briefing describes. Someone wrote down what the rich told them and called it a world. I came back at the seventh hour by the service lift, and Command was waiting on the screen in my quarters with the light behind it in the way they arrange when they intend displeasure. "You left the Prefecture unescorted." "Yes." "Envoy, you are one person on a planet of four hundred million, and your body is the only instrument the Ekumen has here. You are not permitted to spend it out of curiosity." "I spent nothing. I learned that the caste report is wrong. Not incomplete — wrong. It describes the ruling three percent." A pause of the length that means the Stabile's office is being consulted. "Take it to the Minister of Science," Command said. "Rega Odh. Tomorrow. He has requested you twice; refuse a third time and it becomes an insult." "Is he a scientist?" "He is a politician who holds the science portfolio. He has held four portfolios in nine years. He is the most dangerous man who will speak to you honestly." --- Rega Odh received me in a room heated to my comfort, which was itself a message: *I have read your file; I know what you can bear.* He was Sesh, very tall, his skull elongated, his hands like the hands of a musician. He wore less than the cake-seller had. "You are cold," he said, "even so. Keep the cloak. It suits you. It tells everyone in the room that you are not from here, which saves a great deal of time." "I was told it drew attention in the Underway." "Ah." He smiled with only his mouth. "So it was you. A grey ghost eating a cake on the sixth level. I had three reports before dinner." He sat, folding those long legs. "Tell me what you saw, and I will tell you whether you saw it." "I saw mixed lineages in every trade row of the sixth market. I saw children who cannot be classified by your census categories. I saw endogamy practiced strictly in exactly one quarter, and that quarter was guarded." "And you conclude that my government lies to the Ekumen." "I conclude that your government has been quoting itself for forty years, and that no one thought to walk downstairs." Odh was quiet. When he spoke his voice had changed register, gone flatter, more careful, and I understood that the fencing was over and the conversation had begun. "If you write that report," he said, "the Ekumen will believe Ottok is one people, and will treat with us as one people, and the three percent will lose the argument they have made for nine generations. Do you know what they will do rather than lose it?" "No." "Neither do I. That is what frightens me." He looked at my cloak. "Envoy. How old are you?" "Twenty-six." "God help us both," said the Minister of Science.
