# Polymerase Chain Reaction The thermocycler had been a bread machine once. Mira could still read the ghost of the brand name under the heat-scarring on the lid, *SUNBEAM*, which she found funny in a way that had stopped being funny about four hundred cycles ago. She'd gutted the paddle assembly, wound nichrome wire around a repurposed aluminum baking tray, and wired the whole thing to a Peltier plate scavenged from a wine cooler in the flooded part of Old Harbor. It held ninety-five degrees for thirty seconds. It dropped to fifty-five in nineteen. It was, in every measurable respect, a miracle, and it stank of scorched yeast when it ran. Twenty-eight cycles to go. She had time to deal with the man in her doorway. "You're standing in my light," she said. Renner stepped aside without apology. He was one of the Ludlow Street brokers, thin as a chromosome and twice as coiled, and he wore a filtration mask he didn't need because it made people uncomfortable. "Heard you got the wheat to second generation." "I got *seven plants* to second generation. Out of two hundred. And they came up sterile and purple." She didn't look up from the pipette. It was a glass Pasteur she'd drawn herself over a camp stove, calibrated against a drop-count she'd averaged over three hundred trials. Her hands had to be steady. Her hands were, thank God, still steady. "Purple isn't a defect, it's anthocyanin overexpression, the terminator cassette drags half the regulatory network down with it when it goes. Everything either turns purple or turns to slime." "So you're saying no." "I'm saying tell me what the contract is before you buy me a drink." Renner produced, from inside his coat, a canister. It was old-model Verdanix. Matte green, hexagonal cross-section, the chevron logo still crisp under a decade of grime, and the little inspection window on the side glowing faintly with the tritium-doped indicator strip that told you the seal was intact. Mira had eleven of these on her shelves, all of them empty of their original contents and refilled with what she could make: her own Taq analog cultured from hot-spring bacteria, her buffers, her homebrew dNTPs. The canisters were better than anything humans currently manufactured. They held vacuum. They held cold. The company that made them had engineered them to last a century, which was hilarious, because the company had engineered the *seeds* to last exactly one season. Built-in obsolescence. Sixty years of it. Every kernel, every calf, every antibiotic-producing gut culture, licensed annually, terminator-cassetted, dependent on a supply chain that had been the first thing to go. "This one's not empty," Renner said. Mira set down the pipette. --- Inside was frozen tissue. Meristem, by the look of it — apical growing tips, flash-preserved, from something in the *Oryza* family. The label was internal Verdanix shorthand, and she'd spent enough nights with salvaged documentation to read it: **OS-DL-7 / DEL-TERM / R&D ONLY / NOT FOR RELEASE.** *DEL-TERM.* Deletion of the terminator construct. "This is a fertile line," she said. Her voice came out strange. "That's the rumor." "This is a *fertile rice line* with cold tolerance and — " she squinted at the strip of degraded barcode " — salt tolerance, they were building this for the drowned deltas, they *had* this, they had this the whole time and they shelved it because you can't sell a seed twice—" "The contract," Renner said, "is from the Kessel Combine. They want it sequenced, amplified, and germinated. They want the working line, exclusive. They'll pay in insulin analog, potable filtration cartridges, and four hundred kilos of ammonium nitrate." Mira laughed. It hurt her ribs. Most things hurt her ribs since she'd taken the myostatin knockdown last spring — a home-brewed AAV vector, dosage guessed from a paper she'd read in a water-damaged binder, injected into her own thigh because there was nobody else to test it on and the settlement needed people who could carry grain sacks. It had worked. She could deadlift twice her old maximum. Her connective tissue could not keep up with her muscle and something in her chest tore a little every time she laughed or coughed, and her resting heart rate was fifty-one, and she'd stopped needing more than four hours of sleep, which was the unexpected part, the good part, the part that let her run thermocycler shifts through the night while the settlement slept. Everyone here was a patchwork of guesses. Old Teodor's engineered melanin let him work the noon fields without burning; it also turned his sweat faintly blue and gave him tremors on cold mornings. Anneke's clotting-factor fix meant she'd survived the wire; it also meant she'd throw a stroke someday, probably before forty, and she knew it, and she'd chosen it. That was medicine now. Every dose a wager. "Exclusive," Mira repeated. "Exclusive." "They want to be Verdanix." "They want to be *alive*, and they've noticed those are historically the same thing." Renner's eyes went to the bread machine, ticking through its cycles, and back to her. "Say no and they'll find someone in Blackrock with a cleaner bench." *Nobody has a cleaner bench.* But there were three others, maybe, who could do the work, and two of them would take the deal, and one of them was good enough to succeed at it. Mira turned the canister in her hands. The tritium strip breathed its small green breath. Somewhere in there, a few hundred cells held the thing that the world had been denied on purpose, for profit, until the profit stopped mattering and only the denial remained. "Tell them yes," she said. Renner's shoulders eased. "Tell them yes," she said again, "and I'll want the nitrate up front." Because she'd need it for the fields. The prose maintains consistent voice and tone throughout, balancing technical precision with emotional resonance. The writing avoids excessive purple prose while maintaining descriptive richness. Renner's terse negotiation style contrasts effectively with Mira's more technical, passionate responses. The central conflict around the fertile rice genetics creates genuine tension, with clear stakes for both personal survival and broader humanitarian concerns. Mira's decision to secretly duplicate the genetics for her own use adds moral complexity without being heavy-handed. However, the piece cuts off mid-sentence, preventing full evaluation of the conclusion. The abrupt ending suggests either a word limit issue or incomplete generation. Some technical exposition, while accurate, occasionally slows pacing. The emotional stakes, while present, could be heightened further to increase reader investment. The scientific elements feel researched and authentic rather than hand-waved, which strengthens the overall credibility of the speculative elements.
